text:
The Trump administration is charging ahead with its immensely unpopular deportation campaign, now by planning to send Afghan and Iranian refugees to their home countries to face severe consequences.

To circumvent court rulings preventing the removal of immigrants to countries where they face certain persecution or death, the administration recently arranged for an aircraft to fly more than 150 Afghan asylum seekers from Louisiana to Pakistan, which would in turn deport them to Afghanistan, The New York Times reported. A lack of diplomatic relations with the Taliban also prevents the administration from arranging direct deportations to the country, and some are protected from removal by court order.

Among the Afghan group are relatives of people who worked alongside American military forces during the Afghan war, which ended in 2021 with as many as 200,000 lawfully fleeing to the U.S. for safety. Also among them are at least one woman and at least one gay man, The Times reported.

“You don’t hand the people who stood with our troops to the Taliban.”

But the plan has drawn a strong opposition in Congress, in the courts and among veterans and immigration rights advocates.

“Our nation made a promise to stand by Afghans who risked their lives and their families’ safety to stand by U.S. service members,” 66 U.S. House and Senate Democrats and Republicans wrote in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

Deporting the Afghans would be a moral failure and violation of a promise to care for those who helped American troops during the war. “The State Department lists Afghanistan as a Level 4 ‘Do Not Travel’ country, and for those who aided U.S. forces, ‘their assistance to U.S. troops puts a target on these individuals and their families to this day,’” the letter states.

The Afghanistan TPS Act has been introduced in both houses of Congress with bipartisan support to restore Temporary Protected Status to Afghans, including some of the 150 immediately tagged for deportation.

The legislators also raised concerns about the administration’s ongoing efforts to deport Iranians, also through Pakistan. That targeted group includes Christian converts, women and pro-democracy advocates. “Sending people who sought protection from the Islamic Republic of Iran back to a war zone and a repressive regime is unconscionable,” the letter says.

ABC News reported that a Nov. 13 deportation flight carrying Iranians was aborted moments after takeoff because Pakistan refused to accept it. A similar flight was canceled a few days earlier. “Both flights come after a federal judge blasted the administration for planning to send people back to Iran — ‘a declared enemy’ — during the ongoing war there.”

A flurry of court activity over the flight resulted in a federal court placing an indefinite temporary restraining order against the plan. “The complaint more than adequately alleges that the Afghan nationals face a likelihood of irreparable harm if deported from this country and transported to Pakistan to be turned over to the Taliban,” U.S. District Judge Victor Marrero said in his Nov. 7 ruling in New York.

In addition, a federal judge in New Mexico temporarily blocked Immigration and Customs Enforcement from putting one of the Afghans, Sardar Akbari, on the flight because he faces persecution in Pakistan, the American Civil Liberties Union said.

“Mr. Akbari’s case is a window into the abject horrors of our immigration system, and the government’s ‘third country removals’ in particular,” said co-counsel Shaw Drake, a professor at the University of New Mexico Law School.

“Everyone at risk of being forcibly sent to a country to which they have no connections is entitled under the Constitution to safeguards against suffering harm there,” added Becca Sheff, senior staff attorney at the ACLU of New Mexico. “Sixty-six members of Congress, from both chambers, needed less than 24 hours to say what every veteran of the Afghanistan war already knows: You don’t hand the people who stood with our troops to the Taliban.

“This flight isn’t immigration enforcement. It’s a betrayal with a boarding pass.”

Afghan war veteran Shawn Vandiver said the attempt to send Afghans back to Afghanistan is reprehensible.

“When even the Taliban are voicing ‘serious concern’ about your deportation plan, you’ve lost the moral argument and the national security one,” he said. “This flight isn’t immigration enforcement. It’s a betrayal with a boarding pass, and the whole world is watching whether America keeps its word.”

Global Refuge President Krish O’Mara Vignarajah urged consideration of the terrible fate awaiting Afghans in their home nation, including prison, torture and death: “For their families here, some of whom served alongside U.S. servicemembers, it means losing a loved one without knowing whether they’ll ever hear from them again.”

And arriving in Pakistan can be very dangerous for Afghans, she said. “Pakistan is patently unsafe for Afghans. Its own government has made that clear by hounding them out of the country by the millions. Deporting Afghans into that crackdown is a deliberate decision to put them in harm’s way.”

The broad opposition the administration is facing over the impending Afghan and Iranian deportations was mirrored in the 2026 midterms that swept Democrats into power on the state and federal levels. Exit polling showed that 57% of Americans agreed the administration’s deportation campaign had “gone too far.”

title: Is Trump planning to use 1950s immigration act to ban Muslims from public office? - Snopes
description:
Claim: President Donald Trump plans to “revive” the 1952 McCarran-Walter Act to bar Muslims from holding public office in the United States.
Even if he was, it would be impossible to use that specific act to bar Muslims from holding public office.
For example, one Facebook user wrote (archived): BREAKING: President Trump is reportedly pushing to ban Muslims from holding public office!
Reports suggest that President Trump wants to revive the 1952 McCarran-Walter Act to bar Muslims from holding public office.
FactCheck.org, a fellow fact-checking organization, also reported on fake claims about the scope of the McCarran-Walter Act in 2018.
text:
Claim:

President Donald Trump plans to “revive” the 1952 McCarran-Walter Act to bar Muslims from holding public office in the United States.

Rating:

False

About this rating

Context

There is no evidence Trump plans to revive the legislation. Even if he was, it would be impossible to use that specific act to bar Muslims from holding public office. It would also likely be unconstitutional.

In November, a claim spread that President Donald Trump was planning to "revive" immigration and nationality legislation from 1952 in order to bar Muslims from holding public office in the United States.

For example, one Facebook user wrote (archived):

BREAKING: President Trump is reportedly pushing to ban Muslims from holding public office!

Reports suggest that President Trump wants to revive the 1952 McCarran-Walter Act to bar Muslims from holding public office.

(David J Harris Jr., accessed via Facebook)

The rumor also circulated on X and TikTok, starting at the end of October, while Snopes readers searched our site seeking more information.

Snopes investigated part of this claim in 2018. At that time, social media users falsely claimed the McCarran-Walter Act of 1952, which is named in the posts above, barred people of Muslim faith from holding public office.

This remains false in 2026, as the 1952 act is unchanged.

There is also no evidence the Trump administration is seeking to use the act, which upheld controversial immigration quotas, to bar Muslims from holding public office, as of this writing. His administration has invoked the act before, according to reputable news reports, but never to bar people from public office.

Trump has also previously talked about a "Muslim ban" on social media, though this also refers to immigration policy rather than blocking anyone from public office. As of this writing, he has not explicitly mentioned the McCarran-Walter Act on Truth Social — his social media app where he regularly discusses his policy ideas — according to Trump's Truth, which archives his posts on the platform.

Using the legislation in this way would not only be impossible, given what it actually governed, but also potentially unconstitutional due to the Constitution's Article Six, Clause Three, which bars "religious tests" from ever being used to determine whether a person can hold public office.

We contacted the White House Press Office for comment on the claim that Trump is planning to use the 1952 act, or any other legislative powers, to ban people of the Muslim faith from running for office. We await a reply to our inquiries.

Snopes wrote about the McCarran-Walter Act in 2018. Rather than barring people from public office, the legislation focused on denying people entry into the U.S. if they were deemed a threat to the government:

The McCarran-Walter Act of 1952 allowed the U.S. to deny citizenship to persons belonging to organizations deemed to be a threat to the government. While that singular aspect of the law remains on the books, not one aspect of that law or its successors is concerned with the suitability of any person to hold public office, and therefore the claim that this act bars Muslims from holding office is false.

The Constitution's Article Six, Clause Three, reads (emphasis ours):

The Senators and Representatives before mentioned, and the Members of the several State Legislatures, and all executive and judicial Officers, both of the United States and of the several States, shall be bound by Oath or Affirmation, to support this Constitution; but no religious Test shall ever be required as a Qualification to any Office or public Trust under the United States.

FactCheck.org, a fellow fact-checking organization, also reported on fake claims about the scope of the McCarran-Walter Act in 2018.

The outlet says that social media posts claiming the act could be used to bar people of the Muslim faith from public office first circulated after Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib, both Muslim women, were elected to the House in Minnesota and Michigan, respectively, that year.

title: Trump signals amnesty deal openness as experts weigh pros and cons | Fox News
description:

"They are potentially making higher wages, they're able to negotiate for different jobs and different wages because they have that legal work authorization," Collins said.
GOP NEEDS TO PROVE IT AGAIN She argued that with legal work authorization, some illegal immigrants would be able to fulfill their full potential in higher-level jobs.
"Well, to begin with, it's not going to happen," he said of an amnesty deal.

text:
After President Donald Trump signaled in a "60 Minutes" interview that aired shortly after the midterm elections that he was willing to "work on a deal" with Democrats to allow some illegal immigrants to gain legal status, Fox News Digital spoke with several immigration experts about the potential ramifications of such an agreement.

The interview came just days after Republicans suffered crushing losses in the midterm elections, raising questions about whether Trump might be willing to compromise on immigration. But the president later ruled out amnesty, saying, "There won't be amnesty," while maintaining that his immigration policy had not changed.

While Trump has not outlined a specific proposal, his comments have raised questions about what a potential deal could look like and how granting legal status to some illegal immigrants could impact the rule of law, assimilation and fiscal policy.

TRUMP ADMITS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT MAY HAVE BEEN TOO 'TOUGH' IN FIRST INTERVIEW SINCE MIDTERMS

Fox News Digital spoke with three immigration experts about what a potential agreement could mean for the country, including its impact on the rule of law, assimilation and taxpayers.

Rule of Law:

"I think one of the first things we have to always consider is the impact on the rule of law and does it undermine it. It's very hard to argue that the best way to restore the rule of law and deal with illegal immigration is to reward some large fraction of people who've broken the law," said Steven Camarota, the director of research at the Center for Immigration Studies (CIS).

Camarota believes that amnesty begs the question of basic fairness, and impacts how people who have come to the United States legally view the immigration system.

"It seems like it mocks them," he said.

He used the example of a person who illegally overstays a visa to illustrate his point, saying that person shouldn't be rewarded with citizenship after overstaying a visa, especially when there are millions of people who have already followed the law and left the country when their visas expired.

Laura Collins, director of immigration policy at the George W. Bush Presidential Center, acknowledged those concerns but argued that the country's immigration laws are part of the problem.

AMERICA NEEDS WORKERS, BUT TRUMP'S POLICIES ARE SHARPLY CUTTING LEGAL IMMIGRATION

"I understand people's concerns about the rule of law," said Collins. "I also think you have a set of immigration laws that are not working as intended. The reason we have so many people who are here undocumented is because we have an economy that pulls in a lot of people's work, but an immigration system that restricts that labor flow."

She says the United States is at a crossroads: the country can choose a system where illegal immigrants cannot stay and fix their mistakes while also contributing to the economy, or they can stay and be offered a chance at restitution.

"Almost every single piece of legislation that has had a chance at passage on immigration that involves legalization program has had things like paying back taxes, going through a background check, paying some sort of fine or fee or restitution payment in order to make up for the fact that these people did something illegal by either overstaying a visa or crossing the border," she said.

But Camarota questioned whether a future amnesty agreement would actually require immigrants to complete those restitution payments before obtaining citizenship.

Assimilation:

Camarota also said that one of the main reasons for restricting immigration in the first place is to ensure that the United States isn't overwhelmed.

"We don't want the numbers to be so large that they overwhelm the assimilation process, where you can go to a school where everyone's from your background or you don't ever have to learn English, because there's enough people around you who you don't [and] who you speak your native tongue So that's one reason to limit immigration," he said.

"In effect, an amnesty throws that out the window and says, well, we have these limits, but we're not going to enforce them," he continued.

TRUMP SAYS DEPORTATION PUSH HASN’T PUT 'SAME PRESSURE' ON FARMWORKERS, HOTEL STAFF: 'NOT EVEN CLOSE'

Drawing from the findings of a 2022 book called "Streets of Gold: America's Untold Story of Immigrant Success," Collins argued that today's immigrants are assimilating at a pace similar to that of immigrants of prior generations. America's current foreign-born population has matched a historic peak similar to late 1800s and early 1900s levels. About 15% of the current population is foreign-born.

The book, she said, compared people's memories of how their grandparents and great-grandparents assimilated when they came to the United States.

"And what they found was actually that immigrants are integrating it pretty much the same rates," she said.

She also said that work helps people to assimilate faster, and thus, if illegal immigrants were given the opportunity to work legally, assimilation would be a smoother process.

"I do think that one of the things America really is good at is us taking newcomers and turning them into Americans, and so I worry less about that" she said. "But I understand why there is a scenario where people could be afraid of that. But the data doesn't support it."

Fiscal Policy:

Camarota estimated that households headed by illegal immigrants receive approximately $50 billion annually in government benefits, often through programs for which their U.S.-born children are eligible. He cited Medicaid, Supplemental Security Income (SSI), Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) and free school lunches as examples, although illegal immigrants themselves are generally barred from receiving many federal welfare benefits.

TRUMP TELLS DHS CHIEF TO WORK WITH DEMOCRATS ON IMMIGRATION REFORM, BUT NO AMNESTY

Illegal immigrants use welfare not because they're lazy, but because most of them do not have educations higher than 11th grade level, Camarota said.

text:
A federal judge threw out a Trump administration rule limiting how long foreign students can stay in the U.S., finding it arbitrary and contrary to Congress’s intent, Politico reports.

Massachusetts District Judge Dennis Saylor, appointed by President George W. Bush, ruled Monday against the Department of Homeland Security rule issued in July. It would have ended the “duration of status” system and capped stays for F and J visa holders at four years, whatever the program’s length, forcing students, researchers and professors who needed more time to apply for extensions.

Saylor found DHS didn’t properly weigh the rule’s costs and benefits, and that its fraud and national security rationale didn’t hold up. He also found it ran counter to Congress. “DHS is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity... that Congress sought to permit and encourage,” he wrote.

The ruling keeps the existing definition in place.

Education groups sued in August, arguing the rule was arbitrary and would deter international students. Miriam Feldblum, president of The Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, a plaintiff, said it would have worsened falling enrollment and burdened campuses. A report from the Institute of International Education puts the drop in new international enrollment at 15% this fall.

Administration officials say stricter student visa policies fight fraud and keep Americans from competing with international students for work. DHS earlier said the rule would fix a system in which students stay indefinitely and take advantage of U.S. generosity.

text:
Five European countries and Rwanda announced Monday that they are exploring the establishment of the first return hub outside Europe, aiming to reach an agreement and begin transferring rejected asylum seekers by 2027.

Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands said in a joint statement published by Denmark's Immigration Ministry that the proposed facility would accommodate migrants without legal permission to remain in the participating EU countries and who are subject to enforceable return decisions.

The initiative would allow transferred migrants to integrate into Rwandan society or voluntarily travel to their countries of origin or other countries where they can legally reside, with international support, according to the statement.

Speaking at a press conference in Vienna, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called the announcement a turning point.

"For me today marks a crucial step towards a new migration system, a system that safeguards the cohesion of our societies and answers the concerns of our citizens," she said.

Frederiksen said the participating countries are seeking fundamental changes to migration policy, arguing that human smuggling networks are profiting from dangerous journeys to Europe.

Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the partnership would provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants," while addressing economic inequalities driving irregular migration.

Danish Minister of Immigration and Integration Morten Bodskov called the announcement "a huge breakthrough," saying the proposed hub would help address difficulties in returning migrants without legal residence.

Return hubs offer "a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said, particularly when their countries of origin do not cooperate on repatriation.

Greek Minister for Migration and Asylum Athanasios Plevris said "combating illegal immigration and dismantling human trafficking networks is one of our key priorities," adding that return hubs could reduce irregular migration and increase returns.

Lastly, Dutch Minister of Asylum and Migration Bart van den Brink said the initiative aimed to "increase returns and provide a new chance for migrants to settle in Rwanda.

"This is how the Netherlands, with its partners, will contribute to a modern, effective and well-functioning asylum system," he said.

The joint statement said the proposed arrangement would comply with EU, Rwandan and international law, while the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) is providing advice on human rights standards.

Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner said concrete negotiations with the East African country would begin Monday.

Karner described the initiative as a pilot project intended to curb irregular migration, disrupt smuggling networks and reduce pressure on the population.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is no longer pursuing a lawsuit against the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), according to Collin County court records.

The state filed a notice of nonsuit without prejudice on Monday, court records show. Paxton filed the suit in February to stop CAIR and its Texas chapters from operating in the state. The lawsuit also sought to name CAIR and its Texas affiliates as foreign terrorist organizations.

CAIR's website states the group was established to challenge stereotypes about Islam and Muslims. Most of its work focuses on civil rights and anti-defamation.

Gov. Greg Abbott designated CAIR as a foreign terrorist and transnational criminal organization last year. Among several things in Abbott's proclamation letter, he cited accusations that CAIR was created as a "front group" for Hamas. CAIR denies those claims.

Abbott also claimed CAIR has "repeatedly employed, affiliated with, and supported individuals promoting terrorism-related activities."

Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa told the Washington Post that she would remove CAIR's terrorist designation when she assumes office.

"We have to use public safety measures for public safety," she said, dismissing what she called "nonsense happening with power that should be used for public safety, money that should use for public safety, that is not being used for safety."

CAIR hopes to see a push toward unity under the new administration, said Mustafaa Carroll, the CAIR-Dallas executive director.

"We're tired of fighting this fight," Carroll said. "We want to get along with folks."

KERA has reached out to Hinojosa and the attorney general's office for comment on this story and will update with any response.

text:
(Bangkok) – Humanitarian education programs for Rohingya refugee children in Bangladesh are struggling amid a collapse in donor funding, Human Rights Watch said today. Donors should fully fund the education programs, while Bangladesh should recognize and the United Nations should support a separate Rohingya-led school network.

Humanitarian education programs have enrolled 312,000 out of approximately 500,000 school-age Rohingya children in the Bangladesh refugee camps. But the programs, which aid cuts had shuttered for months in 2025, are barely adequate even for the children they reach and may close again, humanitarian officials told Human Rights Watch. While resources are shrinking, about 90,000 more refugee children need schooling this year, due to population growth and new arrivals fleeing atrocities in Myanmar. The donor-supported programs have largely ignored the schools that Rohingya teachers set up in the camps, which are well-regarded by refugees for their quality of education, but lack legal status and reach only about 30,000 students.

“Donor governments have turned their backs on education for half a million Rohingya students stuck in the world’s largest refugee camp, but so much could be done to mitigate this crisis,” said Bill Van Esveld, associate children’s rights director at Human Rights Watch. “Bangladesh should accelerate steps to end bans on education for refugees, and humanitarian agencies should work with the Rohingya-led schools.”

On November 19, 2026, the International Court of Justice will deliver its judgment in the case brought by Gambia alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya during the 2016-2017 “clearance operations” constitute genocide and violate the Genocide Convention.

Bangladesh’s Awami League government, overthrown in 2024, had banned Rohingya children’s access to certified education and higher education in the camps or in the Bangladesh school system. It allowed donor-funded education programs but prohibited Rohingya community-led schools, demolished several, and threatened teachers with exile to Bhasan Char, a remote island.

The current government has taken positive steps and should lift remaining restrictions on refugees’ access to education amid the donor funding crisis, Human Rights Watch said.

In October, Bangladesh for the first time allowed a few dozen Rohingya primary students to take an internationally recognized primary school examination, supported by the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

Also for the first time, Bangladesh in October approved a Rohingya nongovernmental organization’s plans to build a primary school in the camps for 240 students and to provide a structured curriculum. The Rohingya Centre UK, set up by the diaspora Rohingya community, said that the 10-subject curriculum will be taught from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., significantly more instruction than students receive in donor-funded education programs. The organization is also running training on the new curriculum for other Rohingya-led schools in the camps.

Teachers in the camps established the Examination Board of Rohingya Refugees in 2025, which now comprises more than 125 community-led schools with up to 30,000 students, and is working to ensure quality education, including standardized exams in the Myanmar curriculum. Establishing the examination board took a year of volunteer outreach in the camps.

However, the Bangladesh government has still not accredited any curriculum for Rohingya children, and because community-led schools lack legal status, they cannot receive foreign support directly. As a result, while the UK organization’s school is able to hire and train Rohingya teachers, the project is formally being implemented through a registered Bangladeshi group. Most community-led schools have to charge students small fees to operate, limiting access, and rely on refugees to donate the use of their small living shelters as makeshift classrooms.

Eight teachers at community-led schools said that to reach more students, they need Bangladesh to grant their schools official status, allow official certification of education and a pathway to higher education, and for the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and humanitarian organizations to acknowledge their work and engage with them.

A teacher at one of the schools said, “We are spending money to ensure education quality, as if we were a government, but we are not a government, we are simply refugees.” Leaders and teachers offered to collaborate with UNICEF and humanitarian organizations on examinations, quality assurance, and improved teaching.

The vast majority of Rohingya students rely on donor-funded humanitarian education programs. Humanitarian groups providing education, coordinated by UNICEF, received just US$29 million from donors towards their 2025 budget request of $72 million, resulting in “learning centers” in the refugee camps closing for months. The education sector laid off teachers, cancelled an early education program, and cut teacher trainings and other programs. In October 2026, a humanitarian education official told Human Rights Watch: “We are struggling to maintain the most basic services. Even textbooks are [insufficient].… We cannot ensure children receive materials like a pencil, a notebook.... Learning centers were damaged by mudslides and climate events, but we do not have funding to carry out repairs.”

Several Rohingya instructors at learning centers that rely on humanitarian funds confirmed the lack of resources. A grade 1 instructor said his classroom had no whiteboard, markers, desks, or benches, and students had to share textbooks, pens, and exercise books. A grade 3 instructor worried that “three students are using one set of textbooks.” Rather than teaching one class for the full school day, learning center instructors teach students in two “shifts” per day.

Even after humanitarian agencies reduced their education funding request to $53 million for 2026, donors had pledged only $36 million by mid-October, leaving learning centers at risk of closing again, humanitarian officials said. The World Bank and Education Cannot Wait have provided or pledged funding, but this alone is insufficient. The United States had paid for half the Rohingya education budget before halting its funding in 2025. Globally, humanitarian education funding has fallen by 20 percent since 2023.

All states are obligated to provide children access to quality education without discrimination, regardless of their refugee status. The Inter-Agency Network for Education in Emergencies’ Minimum Standards emphasize the importance of community leadership and participation in the design and implementation of education programming.

“Rohingya children are eager to learn,” said a Rohingya teacher in the camps. “The problem is that their education has been repeatedly interrupted by circumstances beyond their control. Education needs to be treated as a right, not a temporary humanitarian project.”

text:
Attorney General Ken Paxton has dropped a lawsuit that sought to ban the country’s largest Muslim civil rights group from operating in Texas, state court records show.

The lawsuit, filed in February, had asked a Collin County judge to declare the Council on American-Islamic Relations a foreign terrorist and transnational criminal organization. It alleged that CAIR was working with the Muslim Brotherhood, an international Sunni Muslim group, to “usurp governmental power and establish dominion through Sharia law.” At the time, CAIR said it was being punished for its opposition to Israel’s war in Gaza.

The petition came after Gov. Greg Abbott slapped the same designation against the two groups and urged Paxton to take legal action against CAIR amid a surge in Republican candidates running anti-Islam campaigns.

Paxton’s office filed a notice of nonsuit Monday, voiding the lawsuit nearly two weeks after a blue wave sunk Paxton’s U.S. Senate bid and swept Abbott out of office. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she will remove the “foreign terrorist organization” label against CAIR.

The organization didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment about the lawsuit’s end, which was first reported by Bloomberg Law.

CAIR and its Texas chapter have cheered Hinojosa’s pledge, which she announced during an interview with The Washington Post.

“Greg Abbott, Ken Paxton, Bo French, and Mayes Middleton staked their political campaigns on shredding the First Amendment to target Texas Muslims, but the people of Texas rejected this un-American bigotry,” the groups added in a statement. “Anti-Muslim hate is no longer an effective political weapon in Texas, and it must no longer have any place in state governance.”

text:
Immigrants facing deportation would have just 10 days to appeal many immigration court decisions under a Trump administration rule that revives a major change blocked by a federal judge earlier this year.

The rule, due to be published in the Federal Register by the Department of Justice (DOJ), would cut the normal appeal period from 30 days to 10 days and restore other restrictions on appeals before the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA), amid efforts to speed up a system that has become overwhelmed by a growing backlog.

The DOJ tried to do this in February, but faced legal challenges that led to a federal judge partially setting the policy aside. After a notice and comment period, the DOJ policy is back as a final rule.

Read More on U.S.

"This rule is a part of the Trump Administration's efforts to provide only a facade of due process," Jill family, a professor at Widener University Commonwealth Law School, told Newsweek. "These procedures do not provide meaningful internal review of immigration judge decisions. Addressing the backlog requires more resources and procedural innovation, but that innovation must maintain, if not improve, the process. The administration's approach is to say, 'the line is too long; let's eliminate the service.'"

Under the Trump administration, immigration court hearings have spiked, in part due to the rise in the number of people detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) suspected of having no legal status. The court system has also faced a growing backlog due to sweeping firings of longtime immigration judges, who have been gradually replaced.

Newsweek reached out to the Department of Justice, as well as Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, which brought the original challenge, for further comment Monday afternoon.

What is Changing for Immigration Appeals?

The BIA is the Justice Department's highest administrative body for interpreting and applying immigration law, handling large numbers of appeals from removal decisions made by immigration judges.

Under the plan laid out in the Federal Register filing, the appeal window for many cases would fall from 30 to 10 days, with appellants needing to identify the issues they are raising in their Notice of Appeal. Some asylum cases would keep the 30-day window.

The new system substantially expands summary dismissal, meaning an immigration judge's decision to issue a removal order would be the final government decision unless the BIA accepts the case through a vote by the majority of BIA members.

The DOJ said the changes are needed because of a spike in the number of waiting cases, which it called a "lengthy and unprecedented" backlog.

In Fiscal Year 2017, the BIA had a pending caseload of 35,837 cases. That rose to 325,774 in Fiscal Year 2026, a near ninefold increase.

Hunter Hammill, policy and practice counsel at the American Immigration Lawyers Association (AILA) told Newsweek Monday that the changes would increase efficiency "at the great cost of dismantling due process in the court system."

"It will be nearly impossible, even for people with attorneys, to file an appeal in 10 calendar days, rather than having the 30-day window," Hammill said. "Detained individuals and people who do not have legal counsel will have a harder time because they will have barely received notice of a decision and there will be no time as a practical matter to find an attorney to help with an appeal."

Why Was the 10-Day Deadline Blocked?

On February 6, the DOJ issued its interim final rule laying out this proposal. That sparked a legal challenge to the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, with plaintiffs arguing that the new deadline would severely curtail meaningful BIA reviews.

The lawsuit included claims under the Administrative Procedure Act, the Immigration and Nationality Act, and the Constitution.

On March 8, Judge Randolph D. Moss set aside parts of the rule, with the DOJ then telling immigration judges the 10-day deadline had been set aside and the correct appeal deadline was still 30 days.

The March ruling did not declare that immigrants were constitutionally entitled to 30 days. Instead, Moss focused on how DOJ had gone about implementing the policy, saying the department had bypassed notice-and-comment requirements for substantive changes to policy.

Does a 10-Day Deadline Violate Due Process?

The restored deadline could renew a deeper fight over how much process the Constitution requires before the government can deport someone.

The Justice Department argued that while noncitizens are entitled to due process in removal proceedings, the Constitution does not independently guarantee an administrative appeal before the BIA.

Once the government establishes an appeal process, the question becomes whether it can impose conditions that effectively prevent people from using it.

Under the 10-day time frame, an immigrant facing deportation would need to obtain the judge's decision, find counsel, understand what went wrong, and prepare a Notice of Appeal identifying the issues being challenged, potentially while in ICE custody and without English proficiency.

The organizations fighting the original rule argued it would disproportionately affect people who are detained, unrepresented, disabled, children, or speakers of less-common languages.

"The BIA Interim Final Rule makes a mockery of due process," Emilie Raber, Senior Attorney at the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, said in a February press release. "In addition to taking away virtually any benefit the BIA could provide immigrants, it will wreak havoc on people with cases in immigration court or federal appellate courts."

In 1994, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals considered a 20-day immigration appeals deadline in Gonzales-Julio v. INS, which the DOJ also refers to in its 2026 rule.

The court found then that a 10-day deadline was unconstitutional in certain circumstances, with the case examining an immigrant in Hawaii who needed to file an appeal in San Diego, California, within that time.

The DOJ argues in 2026 that technology has mitigated that issue, with electronic filing allowing documents to be sent at any time over the internet.

What Happens Next

The DOJ plan is due to be published November 17, with the rule taking effect 30 days later and applying to cases filed after that date. Cases already pending would not face the shorter deadline.

The department likely expects further legal challenges, with its plan outlining concerns around due process, access to counsel, and meaningful case review.

While the BIA is the last immigration tribunal layer, immigrants who still see their cases dismissed could take their case to a federal court for further examination.

text:
Today, Congresswoman Veronica Escobar (TX-16) led a group of 22 other Democrats in a letter to U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Office of Inspector General (OIG) Joseph Cuffari urging him to investigate the nearly $7.5 billion in taxpayer funds for border infrastructure projects in the Big Bend Border Patrol Sector.

Joining Congresswoman Escobar (in alphabetical order) are Representatives Greg Casar (TX-35), Joaquin Castro (TX-20), Jasmine Crockett (TX-30), Lloyd Doggett (TX-37), Lizzie Fletcher (TX-7), Sylvia Garcia (TX-29), Dan Goldman (NY-10), Vicente Gonzalez (TX-34), Al Green (TX-9), Jared Huffman (CA-2), Julie Johnson (TX-32), Raja Krishnamoorthi (IL-8), Stephen Lynch (MA-8), Seth Magaziner (RI-2), Christian Menefee (TX-18), Dave Min (CA-47), Brittany Petterson (CO-7), Emily Randall (WA-6), Rashida Tlaib (MI-12), Paul Tonko (NY-20), Gabe Vazquez (NM-2), and Nydia Velazquez (NY-7).

The full letter can be found here or below:

Inspector General Cuffari:

We write to urgently request that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Office of Inspector General (OIG) investigate the contracting process, potential political influence, and award of $7.5 billion in taxpayer funds for massive border infrastructure projects in and around the Big Bend Border Patrol Sector in Texas, including Big Bend National Park.

On October 15, 2025, former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem waived virtually every provision of federal law “with respect to all contracting actions necessary for the construction of physical barriers and roads” in the Big Bend Sector of Texas. This was followed by additional waivers of environmental, historic preservation, and other laws that would ordinarily provide independent review of federal actions affecting more than 500 miles of borderlands. In addition to Big Bend National Park, one of the nation’s most treasured landscapes, these waivers also impact Big Bend Ranch State Park, Texas’ largest state park, and hundreds of miles of privately owned land.

Publicly available information raises serious questions about how these contracts were awarded, whether political relationships played any role in contractor selection, whether the circumvention of normal contracting and oversight safeguards was in the public interest, and whether the enormous expenditures are justified by an operational need.

The Big Bend Sector, and especially Big Bend National Park, encompasses some of the most remote, rugged, and waterless terrain along the southern border. Local law enforcement officials and elected leaders from across the political spectrum, as well as former National Park Service officials, have questioned the need for extensive physical barriers or other major border security infrastructure in this region.

The available data further raises questions about the justification for the waivers or these massive contracts. The Big Bend Sector includes 26% of the southern border, but CBP’s published data shows that in the 5 years that DHS used to justify these actions, it accounted for less than 1% of the apprehensions of migrants across that same border. The national park accounted for only 0.016% of apprehensions in the same period despite spanning 6% of the southern border. DHS’ own press releases cites that apprehensions in the sector have fallen sharply in recent years.

Nevertheless, DHS designated the region an "area of high illegal entry" with an "acute and immediate need" for border infrastructure. “High illegal entry” is a legal necessity established by the Congress under Section 102(a) of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA) to allow the Department to waive legal requirements and expedite construction.

We believe the DHS Office of the Inspector General has a responsibility to scrutinize how the Department has made the decisions, and the impact of those decisions, regarding whether the area in question is truly an area of high illegal entry, whether the subsequently awarded contracts were properly issued (even in light of the waivers), and whether the resulting expenditures are in the public interest. The scale of the expenditures is enormous. Five contracts, totaling $7.5 billion, have been awarded in the Sector.

These contracts include:

$1.0 billion to Barnard Construction (BB1 Project)

$1.2 billion to Fisher Sand & Gravel (BB2 Project)

$960.4 million to Barnard Construction (BB3 Project)

$1.7 billion to Southwest Valley Constructors for work associated with Big Bend National Park. (BB4 project)

$2.6 billion to Fisher Sand & Gravel for work in the Lower Canyons region downstream of the national park (BB5 project)

These expenditures warrant scrutiny because of the contracting practices and political relationships surrounding some of the companies receiving them. Public reporting has documented substantial political connections involving contractors that have received significant border construction awards.

Barnard Construction Chairman Tim Barnard and his wife donated approximately $1 million to a Trump campaign fundraising committee during the 2024 election cycle. Barnard Construction has subsequently received billions of dollars in border construction contracts, including a $1.6 billion contract for approximately 112 miles of border wall in New Mexico that was awarded without competitive bidding based on an asserted need for urgency.

Fisher Sand & Gravel has also been the subject of previous scrutiny over political influence in federal contracting. During President Trump's first term, the company received a $400 million border wall contract after President Trump personally and repeatedly urged federal officials to consider Fisher for the work. Those circumstances prompted a Department of Defense Inspector General review. Public reporting has also connected Fisher to a consulting firm formerly associated with White House Border Czar Tom Homan. Fisher reportedly paid Homan's consulting firm as much as $186,000 while seeking border wall work. The administration has stated that Mr. Homan does not participate in the actual awarding of contracts.

These facts do not by themselves establish that contracts were improperly awarded. They do, however, create a strong public interest in an independent review of whether political relationships, communications, or influence played any role in DHS contracting decisions.

The processes CBP used to award these contracts lacked any transparency, and there has been no opportunity for public oversight of the contracts, or even for the public to understand the scope of the contracts.

A lawsuit brought by a competing contractor – that was subsequently withdrawn -

- alleged that solicitations for broader Texas border work were not genuine competitive opportunities and that winningbidders were subsequently required to perform work outside the scope originally advertised. When discovery was sought in that litigation, DHS moved to seal materials including depositions and affidavits.

At the same time, DHS and CBP have repeatedly changed their public descriptions of what is being built in the Big Bend Sector.

CBP materials initially showed a border wall through the region. The wall later disappeared from public maps, then reappeared. In May, CBP publicly stated that there would be no wall in Big Bend National Park. Approximately one week later, DHS awarded a $1.7 billion contract whose contracting records described work associated with a border wall in the national park. More recently, CBP has described construction inside the park as involving roads, technology, and vehicle barriers.

Taken together, these circumstances warrant an independent investigation. We therefore request that the DHS Office of Inspector General examine:

Whether political relationships, communications, campaign contributions, or other political considerations played any role in the selection of contractors or award of contracts for border infrastructure in the Big Bend Sector;

Whether contracts awarded for work in the Big Bend Sector were awarded through full and open competition and, where they were not, whether DHS properly justified the use of noncompetitive or expedited procurement procedures;

Whether DHS adequately evaluated the operational need, cost effectiveness, and alternatives before committing billions of taxpayer dollars to border infrastructure in a region with comparatively low and declining levels of unlawful crossings;

Whether the scope of work ultimately assigned to contractors materially differed from the work described during the solicitation and bidding process, and whether any such changes disadvantaged competing bidders or increased costs to taxpayers;

Whether any current or former administration officials participated in, attempted to influence, or communicated with DHS or CBP officials concerning the selection of particular contractors;

Whether DHS's waiver of environmental and other statutory requirements, together with limitations on public access to contracting information, diminished safeguards against waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement; and

Whether the contracts and expenditures associated with these projects comply with applicable ethics, appropriations, and other federal requirements.

Big Bend National Park is an irreplaceable public resource. Taxpayers deserve confidence that decisions affecting it and the surrounding region— and billions of dollars in federal spending — are based on legitimate public needs rather than political influence or private advantage.

We expect a written response to this letter with an associated timeline for an OIG investigation no later than November 27, 2026. We further expect that the findings of such an investigation be made public.

I wondered if your guests could comment on the effectiveness.

This ordinance details down the line that no city or county employee will collaborate with any federal law enforcement official without a judicially signed order. And it goes on to say they won’t use property, won’t use buildings, will not be allowed entrance to buildings without a warrant.

Caller: Mm-hmm.

Bob: Now, you know, that doesn’t mean we’ve effectively, you know, put that in process yet, but I just wanted to say this is the result of two years of considerable focused work. But I just wonder —

Alexis Madrigal: Bob, no, I really appreciate it. Let’s take it to the panel here. Tyche, let us get your perspective first, and then, Deep, I’m going to ask you about this kind of thing nationally.

Tyche Hendricks: Yeah, I mean, I think, you know, this is something that we’re seeing, in addition to our statewide laws, which over, you know, really beginning in the first Trump administration, were saying, look, law enforcement — you know, the job of state and local law enforcement is to protect public safety. It’s not to conduct immigration operations.

But on top of those statewide laws, a lot of localities are increasingly being pushed by grassroots efforts, like the caller was describing, to specify and spell out, like, unless they have a judicial warrant signed by a judge, not just a warrant for somebody that was signed by an ICE supervisor, then we’re not going to, you know, let them onto the property or so forth.

And our attorney general has spelled out some best practices for public institutions, going all the way to public hospitals, public schools, and universities, for how to interact with ICE and keep nonpublic spaces off-limits and so forth. And records, also, documents.

But the enforcement is the question, or the implementation. It seems we’re seeing ICE basically saying, “Yeah, that doesn’t apply to us.”

So then I think it’s most likely to get kicked to the courts.

But one other thing I wanted — we started out talking about the nursing professor at USF and the student at UC Berkeley. And another area where we have seen kind of a response has been from the universities that those women are affiliated with.

And a real — I mean, their advocates say that the universities just sprang into action to connect these people with legal support, to provide letters from the chancellor, and to rally support from members of Congress, to open channels through the congressional offices with ICE to try to locate them and so forth.

And a kind of a protocol, and in particular, UC Berkeley’s protocol.

Advocates have said, and lawyers who are doing this work — in fact, this young woman, Paola’s lawyer, was saying, “I spoke with my other stakeholders in the county and said, like, this protocol that UC Berkeley’s developed is a great model for other institutions.”

And so there’s other kinds of pushback where universities, in some cases, early in the Trump administration, were a little bit wary of standing up to this administration, but here they really seem to be coming to these women’s support.

So there’s a lot of different parts of society that seem to be stepping into this arena.

Alexis Madrigal: Deep, what else? Yeah, I mean, this is interesting. Maybe there’s a proliferation of different models by local actors who are kind of opposing this one larger national or federal force. What else do you see?

Deep Gulasekaram: Yeah, so I think, to the listener’s question, certainly these local ordinances, state ordinances, county ordinances that highly restrict the communication, what local officers can do, what types of questions they can ask, who they can communicate with, can be highly effective and are completely within the control of state and local county boards and supervisory legislative bodies.

And so I think that is an important right to assert.

Tyche was saying public institutions like universities — they have rights with regard to the types of privacy they can create for their students, the nature under which they need to allow enforcement officers on their campuses. They have rights they can assert.

It gets trickier, though, as to the question that was asked, when we deal with public property. Certainly counties and localities own property and therefore can assert some rights over it.

But the tricky legal question is that you cannot, as a state and local county or jurisdiction, simply have a blanket prohibition on federal authorities coming upon your public property.

Federal authorities, like everyone else, have rights to access, especially when it’s a public area. And this is where it gets tricky, right?

So if there’s a public area where people are generally allowed to go on that public land, so should ICE agents and federal agents.

On the other hand, if the presence of those ICE agents is starting to compromise the types of services provided, so especially thinking about state courts and scaring away witnesses and litigants, county health institutions, and the presence of ICE officials is scaring away people who need care, it becomes a much harder question.

And these are the questions that are currently being litigated in federal court.

Alexis Madrigal: So interesting. Let’s bring in one last caller here. Let’s bring in Amy in Concord.

Amy: Thank you so much for taking my call. Thank you very much, Alexis. I feel like I know you even though we’ve never met. I’ve been with you every day, and I feel a good day to you.

Alexis Madrigal: Thank you, Amy. Thank you.

Amy: Well, I’ve been thinking about this. The main thing is they’ve got to shut down the money because they can’t have an unlimited amount of money to go out and violate human rights.

These immigrants are being put in jail without any due process, and they aren’t really even criminals. You know, Trump sold it to us that we were going to be taking criminals away, but no, we’re just taking immigrants away. They may have been under a protected status just a few short months ago. That’s part of the biggest problem.

The other part is that these jails are not ever — there’s no oversight. There are young women who are pregnant, who are becoming pregnant in these jails. How is that happening? And there’s not oversight.

You know, I’m just wondering, when is the time going to come where we decide that we have to collect all the people who have red hair and freckles and put them in jail? Because that’s really all that we’re doing. We’re just selecting a group of people, and we’re putting them in jail.

And it’s not even a jail. It really is. You can call it a detention center if you have to, but —

Alexis Madrigal: Amy, I appreciate it. Thanks, friend, for this perspective.

You know, maybe I’ll give you the last kind of sense. I do think there’s many people who are expressing Amy’s sense of frustration about this and maybe are expecting Congress to be able to go after the money. Is there any sense that might happen?

Tyche Hendricks: Well, I mean, yeah, I guess a question, and maybe our folks who are looking at the federal picture: Can the Democratic Congress claw back some of those tens of billions of dollars that were appropriated by this current Congress? Can they put restrictions on how ICE conducts itself? Can they, you know, dare the president to veto legislation?

I mean, these are going to be the questions that face the next Congress. And there’s a lot of questions that are going to face the next Congress.

So how much of a priority immigration rises to is partly going to come from constituents and from the grassroots, as far as, you know, making that a priority with their lawmakers.

Alexis Madrigal: Thank you so much, Tyche Hendricks, immigration reporter at KQED. Thanks so much for joining us.

Tyche Hendricks: My pleasure.

Alexis Madrigal: We’ve also had Deep Gulasekaram, who is professor of law at the University of Colorado Boulder Law School. Thank you so much, Deep.

Deep Gulasekaram: Thank you for having me.

Alexis Madrigal: And we’ve had Jasmine Garsd, immigration correspondent at NPR. Thank you so much for coming back, Jasmine.

Jasmine Garsd: Always a pleasure.

Alexis Madrigal: Thanks so much to all of our callers, our listeners, and commenters. Thanks so much.

I’m Alexis Madrigal. Stay tuned for another hour of Forum ahead with Mina Kim.

text:
WASHINGTON — Some Texas Democrats argue Congress should immediately tackle immigration reform following their party’s decisive victories across the country this month, including in Hispanic-majority districts in South Texas that have experienced the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

In his first public appearance after winning the U.S. Senate race in Texas, Democrat James Talarico visited the memorial of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, the Houston man fatally shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer. Talarico, like many others, placed his “I Voted” sticker at the site.

“People were moved by this situation, and I do think it was the turning point in the election and in our country as a whole,” Carlos Eduardo Espina, a Spanish-language content creator from Houston, told Spectrum News.

Espina said President Donald Trump’s hard-line immigration approach was a motivating factor for many Texans to vote. Espina has more than 25 million followers across different social media platforms, where he discusses immigration and politics.

“There's a difference between going after someone who has a criminal record who's done things they shouldn't do, and going after someone who's been here for 10, 15, 20 years, working hard, paying taxes, contributing to society,” Espina said.

Espina joined Texas Democrats, immigration advocates and business leaders at a press conference in Washington last week, calling for protections for undocumented immigrants who have lived and worked in the U.S. for years.

Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, a Democrat who flipped a Hispanic-majority district in South Texas, said mixed-status families have been living in fear.

“I do want to fight for a pathway to citizenship for those that have been here, and I say this because that's going to be their protection. We don't know. What if we in the future get somebody even more anti-immigrant than Donald Trump? The only thing that would protect them is citizenship, because we don't know what the future holds,” Pulido said.

Before leaving the White House Monday for the Philippines and China, President Trump was asked about the possibility of immigration reform.

“A lot of people would like me to look at it, and I'll always look at it, and it'd be wonderful, but we'll see. I mean, it has to be tough, and no amnesty, et cetera, et cetera,” the president told reporters.

The president said his immigration policies “helped and hurt” him at the polls and that they may have been “too tough.” But the president’s promotion of Stephen Miller, the architect of many of his hardline immigration policies, to White House chief of staff is being seen by many as a sign that a dramatic change of course is unlikely.

“To me, immigration and the economy go hand in hand,” Espina said. “When someone gets detained by ICE, let's say the head of household, that creates economic issues for that family. Immigration becomes an economic issue when you own a business and half your clients don't want to show up anymore because they're afraid of ICE enforcement."

Espina said Republicans need to strike a deal on immigration reform if they want to be successful in the 2028 elections.

“People on both sides of the aisle can agree that the current system just doesn't work. It's completely broken. It's completely outdated, and there needs to be some change, and I think we can make it happen,” Espina said.

Some Texas Democrats argue there is no need to wait for the new Congress to begin in January to tackle immigration. Meanwhile, the Trump administration recently touted its 483,000 deportations and nearly half a million immigration arrests made this year.

title: Victory: Federal court sides with NewsGuild and allies in challenge to DHS visa rule ...
description:
The coalition challenged the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) final rule ending the Duration of Status (D/S) policy for international students, exchange visitors, and representatives of foreign media.
The court set aside the rule in its entirety under the Administrative Procedure Act and denied the government’s motion for summary judgment.
If implemented, this rule would have further weakened our ability to attract international talent, disrupted educational plans, and burdened campuses.
This outcome underscores the importance of defending international education through principled, strategic, and sustained advocacy.
International students and scholars deserve to have a level of predictability in pursuit of their dreams and it is in our nation’s best interest to provide it.
text:
Media Contacts: media@nafsa.org, press@presidentsalliance.org, press@aft.org, highered@uaw.net, press@newsguild.org

Washington, D.C. — Today, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts ruled in favor of NAFSA: Association of International Educators; the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration; the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM); the American Federation of Teachers (AFT); Graduate Labor Organization, AFT Local 6516 (GLO); International Union, United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (UAW); United Auto Workers Local 2322; and The NewsGuild-CWA. The coalition challenged the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) final rule ending the Duration of Status (D/S) policy for international students, exchange visitors, and representatives of foreign media.

The court set aside the rule in its entirety under the Administrative Procedure Act and denied the government’s motion for summary judgment. The ruling preserves the longstanding D/S framework and prevents the rule’s new fixed admission periods, extension-of-stay requirements, and restrictions on academic mobility from taking effect.

The court held that the rule was arbitrary and capricious because DHS failed to appropriately weigh its costs and benefits, justify the changes based on its stated fraud and national security concerns, consider less burdensome alternatives, or adequately respond to significant public comments. The court further emphasized that DHS failed to meaningfully consider improvements to the existing Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) as an alternative to imposing a costly new system.

The court also held that the rule’s restrictions on academic studies exceeded DHS’s statutory authority because they were not reasonably related to the nature and purpose of the F-1 student visa program. As the court explained, “The statute simply does not grant DHS such broad and open-ended authority to undermine the F-1 visa program.”

The rule would have replaced the longstanding D/S policy with fixed admission periods of no more than four years and required international students and exchange visitors to apply for extensions of stay. It also would have restricted students’ ability to change educational objectives, transfer institutions, or pursue additional programs of study. The coalition challenged the rule in court because of the uncertainty and administrative burdens it would create, their interference with academic decision-making, and the disruption it would cause to educational and professional plans.

The coalition is represented by Paul Hughes, Partner, at McDermott Will & Schulte.

Jon Schleuss, President of The NewsGuild-CWA, stated:

“International journalists working in the United States have been on pins and needles waiting for a decision in this case and we are thrilled that Judge Saylor struck down the Trump administration’s rule. We are grateful that Judge Saylor understands that a free press is an essential ingredient to protect democracy. We will continue to defend journalists everywhere.”

Miriam Feldblum, President and CEO of the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, stated:

“Today’s ruling is a clear and important victory for international students and scholars and the colleges and universities that welcome them. Preserving Duration of Status gives students greater certainty as they pursue their education and allows institutions to support their academic progress without arbitrary hurdles and unnecessary barriers. The harmful consequences of the current administration’s policy actions and efforts are already evident in the significant declines in international student enrollment and interest we are witnessing. If implemented, this rule would have further weakened our ability to attract international talent, disrupted educational plans, and burdened campuses. We are proud to stand with our coalition partners in defending international education, and the contributions that international students and researchers bring to our campuses, communities, and country.”

Fanta Aw, PhD, Executive Director and CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators, stated:

“With this ruling, the judge has sent an unequivocal and resounding message: the longstanding Duration of Status policy is retained. This outcome underscores the importance of defending international education through principled, strategic, and sustained advocacy. At a time when uncertainty continues to affect our field, this decision is a powerful reminder that our collective voice matters and that standing firm in defense of educational opportunity can make a meaningful difference for institutions, students and this nation. We owe a huge debt of gratitude to our legal counsel, our fellow plaintiffs, and the many members and institutions whose experiences and expertise helped inform this effort. International students and scholars deserve to have a level of predictability in pursuit of their dreams and it is in our nation’s best interest to provide it. Their contributions, combined with domestic talent, make our country stronger.”

Robert J. McCarron, President and CEO of the Association of Independent Colleges & Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM), stated:

“We are pleased that the court vacated the entire Duration of Status rule as arbitrary and capricious and reiterated in its ruling that the “nature and purpose” of the F-1 visa is to permit, and indeed encourage, international students to pursue educational opportunities here. International students add to the vibrancy of our campuses, drive innovative research, and support the Commonwealth’s economic vitality.”

Randi Weingarten, President of AFT, stated:

“Today’s final order will have resounding impacts for generations of scientists and scholars from every corner of the globe that make America the worldwide leader in cutting-edge research. The Trump administration’s proposed limits on how long international scholars have to complete their studies were arbitrary and hostile. We stand united with our 420,000 higher education members, international and American alike, so they can continue to pursue difficult questions, challenge conventional wisdom, publish findings without political interference and make US colleges and universities the envy of the world.

WASHINGTON — Today, the United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) announced that CBP’s October encounters reached the lowest level ever recorded to start a fiscal year. Additionally, October marked the 18th consecutive month of zero releases at the border.

“President Trump unleashed the full strength of DHS to secure the border and enforce the law,” said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “The results speak for themselves. In Fiscal Year 2026, our officers and agents drove illegal crossings to historic lows. DHS carried that momentum into October, when CBP saw its fewest nationwide encounters ever to open a fiscal year. Under President Trump’s leadership, we will continue to deliver the most secure border in American history and save American lives.”

The sustained decline in illegal border crossings and apprehensions—at levels not seen in over three decades—shows the profound impact of robust enforcement policies. With daily Border Patrol apprehensions along the southwest border down 95% over the past year compared with the previous administration, the border remains more secure than at any point in history.

“Under the leadership of President Trump and Secretary Mullin, CBP has been empowered to enforce the law, giving us an unprecedented level of control over our borders,” said CBP Commissioner Rodney S. Scott. “We know more about who and what is entering our homeland than at any time in our nation’s history. America is safer because we are enforcing the rule of law, keeping threats out of our communities, and putting the security of the American people first.”

Below is a snapshot of October’s key figures. Full monthly reporting can be viewed on CBP’s Stats and Summaries webpage.

Border Enforcement at Historic Levels

Illegal crossings remain historically low:

CBP’s nationwide encounters in October were the lowest ever to start a fiscal year

Additionally, CBP’s nationwide encounters in October (27,890) were 7% lower than September, and the lowest for a month since February.

U.S. Border Patrol apprehensions decreased in October

The U.S. Border Patrol’s apprehensions along the southwest border in October (8,288) were 7% lower than September.

Southwest border apprehensions in October were 95% lower than under Biden

The U.S. Border Patrol’s apprehensions along the southwest border in October (8,288) were 95% lower than the monthly average of the Biden administration; 97% below the peak of the Biden administration (December 2023); and less than the number of apprehensions recorded in 5 days in October 2024.

Drug Interdictions That Save Lives

CBP remains on the frontline against drug smuggling, seizing dangerous narcotics before they reach American communities.

Nationwide in October, seizures of cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, fentanyl, and marijuana (combined, by weight) increased 44% from September 2026. Total drug seizures in October 2026 (combined, by weight) increased 13% from October 2024 during the Biden administration.

Individual drugs compared to September 2026:

Marijuana seizures increased 29% in October (14,748 pounds seized in October 2026)

Methamphetamine seizures increased 59% in October (14,745 pounds seized in October 2026)

Cocaine seizures increased 60% in October (9,032 pounds seized in October 2026)

Heroin seizures increased 95% in October (246 pounds seized in October 2026)

Trade and Tariff Enforcement

CBP plays a central role in enforcing U.S. trade law and supporting economic security.

$391 billion in imports processed in October 2026.

$26 billion in duties identified for collection in October 2026.

Agriculture Stats/Seizures – Securing American Agriculture

In October, CBP agriculture specialists helped protect America’s agriculture, natural resources, and economic prosperity.

CBP issued 6,020 emergency action notifications for restricted and prohibited plant and animal products.

title: FP Predictions: SCOTUS Will Hand Major Win to Agricultural Employers by Blocking DOL ...
description:
Quick Background Sun Valley Orchards, a family-run farm in New Jersey, was investigated by the DOL over its H-2A practices during the 2015 growing season.
While a federal district court in New Jersey sided with the DOL, the 3rd Circuit reversed in favor of Sun Valley Orchards.
The Supreme Court heard arguments in DOL v. Sun Valley Orchards on November 10.
On behalf of Sun Valley Orchards, Robert Johnson argued that this is fundamentally an employment and contract dispute, not an immigration proceeding.
This could potentially significantly reduce H-2A employers’ exposure to such financial liability.
text:
The Supreme Court will likely rule in favor of a family farm in a critical separations-of-power case, ending the Department of Labor’s ability to adjudicate proceedings to collect financial penalties from agricultural employers for alleged violations of the H-2A temporary visa program. That’s according to the predictions of our firm’s thought leaders monitoring DOL v. Sun Valley Orchards, a pending case that centers on whether the agency’s use of administrative law judges (ALJs) to impose H-2A penalties is constitutional (if authorized by federal law at all) or whether ag employers have a right to a trial before an independent federal judge. Read on for an analysis of the issues, our specific predictions on how SCOTUS will decide the case, and how a final decision in 2027 could impact ag employers for years to come.

Quick Background

Sun Valley Orchards, a family-run farm in New Jersey, was investigated by the DOL over its H-2A practices during the 2015 growing season. The agency determined that the farm had committed several violations and owed back wages and civil penalties. After Sun Valley requested a hearing, an ALJ issued a decision that mostly aligned with the DOL’s determination, requiring the farm to pay over $500K to the agency. The DOL’s Administrative Review Board affirmed the ALJ’s decision on appeal.

The farm then sued the DOL in federal court, claiming, among other things, that the agency’s administrative system for imposing financial liability was unconstitutional, and that cases involving orders to pay money to the government must be tried before an Article III court. While a federal district court in New Jersey sided with the DOL, the 3rd Circuit reversed in favor of Sun Valley Orchards. Earlier this year, the DOL officially asked the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case, and SCOTUS granted that petition on April 27.

Overview of the Issues Before SCOTUS

The Supreme Court will ultimately decide whether the DOL’s adjudication system for collecting monetary remedies from employers that have allegedly violated the terms and conditions of employment of H-2A workers (and domestic workers in corresponding employment) is:

prohibited by Article III of the Constitution; and, if not,

authorized by the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) (8 U.S.C. §1188(g)(2)).

The DOL argues that that agency’s administrative penalty procedure for H-2A violations is permissible because:

this procedure involves immigration-related “public” rights;

Congress may empower the executive branch to impose monetary penalties in cases involving public rights; and

Congress has done so through Section 1188(g)(2) of the INA, which authorizes the Secretary of Labor to “take such actions, including imposing appropriate penalties…as may be necessary to assure employer compliance with terms and conditions of employment under this section.”

On the other hand, Sun Valley Orchards argues that:

this case is fundamentally a labor dispute involving private contractual rights and therefore falls outside of the narrow “public rights” exception (especially in light of the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in SEC v. Jarkesy); and

Section 1188(g)(2) of the INA allows the DOL to pursue penalties in court, but not to create this type of in-house agency court system where they write the rules, prosecute cases, provide witnesses, and then issue judgments.

What’s the Latest?

The Supreme Court heard arguments in DOL v. Sun Valley Orchards on November 10. Below are some of the highlights.

Chief Justice Roberts repeatedly challenged the government’s attempt to characterize this dispute as an exercise of immigration authority, drawing a line between admission to the country via the H-2A program versus subsequent employment conditions.

Sarah Harris, a principal deputy solicitor general for the Department of Justice, argued on behalf of the DOL that the H-2A program’s conditions are governmental obligations rather than private employment contracts, and that immigration authority over those continuing obligations does not stop at the physical border.

On behalf of Sun Valley Orchards, Robert Johnson argued that this is fundamentally an employment and contract dispute, not an immigration proceeding. He said the nature of the allegations in this case are employment-related (“for instance, almost half the liability, a large chunk of the liability, involves the three-quarters guarantee issue”), whereas “immigration adjudication involves the question of whether to admit, exclude, or deport.”

Justice Kagan pushed back and said that the H-2A program has nothing to do with contract rights: “Essentially, this is a kind of visa fraud or immigration fraud. The employer says I’m certifying a set of things in order to get a set of foreign workers, and in exchange for that, I’m going to treat them a certain way, treat them the way that will not undercut domestic workers. And then, allegedly, the employer does the exact opposite, treats them in ways that do undercut domestic workers.”

Justices Alito, Kavanaugh, and Barrett, who seemed the most undecided, raised concerns about the broadest possible arguments on both sides and where lines should be drawn.

FP SCOTUS Predictions: Court Will Strike Down DOL’s ALJ Use for H-2A Penalties

Rebecca Hause-Schultz and Joshua Viau, leaders of FP’s Agriculture Industry Team, predict that the Court will rule 6-3 for Sun Valley Orchards, with Chief Justice Roberts writing the majority opinion. We anticipate that the decision will continue this Court’s recent trend limiting administrative agency authority and deference. The majority is likely to emphasize the substance of the underlying claims rather than the immigration-policy-based purpose and preserve the distinction between the government’s authority to regulate participation in a federal program and its authority to adjudicate monetary liability.

What’s at Stake for Agricultural Employers?

If the Supreme Court rules in favor of Sun Valley Orchards, agricultural employers will gain a new tool to fight back against back wages and monetary penalties by the DOL for H-2A program violations. The DOL would have to bring these types of claims in federal court, which is a slower, more burdensome, and less favorable process for the government. This could potentially significantly reduce H-2A employers’ exposure to such financial liability.

Further, a win for agricultural employers could benefit employers across all industries as it could potentially influence other courts to curb ALJ authority in similar challenges. Stay tuned for an upcoming FP Insight that will dive deeper into the broader implications at stake for all employers.

Conclusion
