text:
The U.S. Supreme Court late last week agreed to take on a case central to the Trump administration's immigration agenda concerning the conditions under which migrants can request asylum.

While the announcement ended up being buried in a Friday afternoon news cycle that saw the unforeseen ground stop of U.S. air travel, it means that the top court will now hear at least three major immigration-related cases in its session that runs through June 2027.

The Trump administration's "retinterpretation of certain detention and deportation policies" has led to a "particularly high number of immigration disputes" compared to previous sessions," according to SCOTUSblog, which tracks the work of the top court. The blog, in an October post, also highlighted a handful of other cases that, while narrower in scope in terms of their ramifications, could also be described as immigration-related.

The top court in the 2025-2026 session rejected a Trump administration bid to end birthright citizenship going forward, but it made an impactful ruling that has paved the way for the federal government to deport large numbers of Haitian Americans and other residents who have been in the U.S. for years after fleeing natural disasters or turmoil in their home countries.

Overall, these new cases could lead to Supreme Court rulings that further reshape the American immigration and asylum system, or at least provide clarity in response to actions, some very controversial, that have been undertaken by President Donald Trump's second administration.

Here is a look at the three major cases, so far, of the 2026-2027 docket:

Executive authority to limit asylum

Generally speaking, U.S. laws have recognized through the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) and other legislation the rights of migrants to make an asylum claim when arriving at a border entry point, or even if they are caught trying to cross into the country between entry points. In most years, denials have been greater than asylum claims being granted, though the percentage has fluctuated.

In his final year in office, former president Joe Biden sought to stem the tide of surging arrivals at the southern border and encourage appointment-based claims with what was described as an executive order meant to be temporary, which limited asylum eligibility based on the daily number of encounters at the border.

On the very first day of his second presidential term in 2025, Trump signed an executive order deemed necessary due to an "invasion" at the southern border.

Trump's order has essentially amounted to a blanket asylum ban for migrants caught crossing between border points. The prohibition has also applied to migrants who arrive at official border crossings and lack certain medical or criminal history information, a requirement that advocates say is often impossible to meet for people fleeing violence.

It was blocked first by a federal judge and then in April by the U.S. Court of Appeals in D.C. The panel ruled 2-1 that the INA doesn't "allow the president to remove [migrants] under summary removal procedures of his own making."

In a partial dissent, Judge Justin Walker wrote that the administration can broadly deny asylum applications, but that the INA and other laws forbid sending people back to countries where they would be persecuted.

Whether that has been practised in the asylum claims the government does consider is arguable. Denial rates in some cases have climbed to over 90 per cent, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse at Syracuse University. Denial rates that high have not been seen for decades, if ever.

Democratic House Rep. Rob Menendez of New Jersey, posting Friday after it was learned the Supreme Court would take on the case, said "fixing our broken immigration system means upholding our values as a nation of immigrants" while "protecting the right to seek asylum."

Third-country deportations

The Supreme Court justices will gather to hear oral arguments on Dec. 9 regarding a controversial plank of the Trump administration's deportation policies, also related to executive orders the president signed on his first day back in the Oval Office in 2025.

The U.S. traditionally has followed a principle of non-refoulement. That is, not returning persons to countries where it could be reasonably expected they'd face persecution or torture due to race, religion, sexuality, political views or other factors.

Flowing through the Trump executive orders, however, the administration has sought workarounds through third-country deportations. According to a website run by two human rights organizations, the Trump administration has spent more than $95 million US to deport over 28,000 people to 31 different countries and has struck agreements to potentially send people to four additional countries.

In many cases, people are being sent to countries to which they have no connection. In addition, some of the countries that have struck agreements with the U.S. have had questionable track records in terms of upholding human rights and freedoms.

"These migrants are being transferred to countries or territories with which they have no ties, which can be a traumatizing and isolating experience that compounds harms already suffered which triggered their fleeing to the U.S. in the first place," the UN's Human Rights Council said in a statement earlier this year condemning the practice.

The administration has said that it has struck deals with foreign governments where the safety of the deportees has been assured. But the New York Times reported last week after an extensive investigation that it had it identified 110 persons who were deported to a third country but then put on a plane back to their home country of origin, even after U.S. courts had established they had reasonable fears in leaving those countries to seek asylum.

LISTEN | Amy Fischer, director for Refugee and Migrant Rights at Amnesty International USA:

Access to bond hearings

Under past administrations, most non-citizens without a criminal record who were arrested away from border points had an opportunity to request a bond hearing. In many cases, that allowed them to work and remain free while their cases, which would ultimately determine if they would be deported, wound their through immigration court.

The Trump administration has ended that practice, citing an interpretation of existing 1996 legislation. After conflicting rulings in federal courts across the U.S., the Supreme Court will take up the issue after the American Civil Liberties Union filed a lawsuit on behalf of Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha.

The Brazilian man entered the U.S. without authorization two decades ago and, according to his lawyers, has never been charged or convicted of a crime. Nevertheless, after federal immigration agents detained him on his way to work in September 2025, an immigration judge subsequently denied him a bond hearing.

According to the Deportation Data Project at UC Berkeley and UCLA, the number of detention beds for people arrested within the U.S. has more than quadrupled in the past two years, meaning the stakes for this case are considerable.

As with the asylum case just announced Friday, no date has been set yet for oral arguments.

Today, a federal district court vacated the Department of Homeland Security regulation that sought to subject F, J, and I nonimmigrants to fixed periods of admission. Judge Dennis Saylor of the federal district court for the district of Massachusetts granted the plaintiffs’ motion for summary judgment and struck down the regulation, finding that the regulation exceeded DHS’s authority and was inconsistent with Congress’s intent in creating the affected visa programs. text:
BRUSSELS/VIENNA ― Five European countries are set to announce plans on Monday to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda, two sources familiar with the plans said.

Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands said in September they were working towards a deal with a non-EU country to host so-called return hubs, part of a broader European push to increase deportations and curb irregular migration.

The deal, expected to be announced in Vienna, follows the approval of the EU's new Returns Regulation, which seeks to speed up deportations and allows member states to establish return hubs outside the block.

With elections approaching in several EU countries and anti-immigration sentiment widespread, governments are under pressure to show they can control migration. Deportation hubs offer a highly visible demonstration of that resolve, analysts say.

The scheme differs from Britain's abandoned Rwanda deportation plan in that it would only apply to migrants who have exhausted all legal avenues to remain in the European Union, rather than those whose claims are still being processed.

Accountability questions

Leaders from the five countries have repeatedly said their plans would comply with EU and international law, but rights advocates have questioned whether migrants' rights could be violated if they are transferred to a country they have no connection to.

"What recourse do people have if their rights are violated and who is accountable?" said Céline Mias, EU director at the Danish Refugee Council. "If responsibility rests with the European member state, how would that work in practice?"

The Council of Europe, a pan-European human rights body, said in July that return hubs posed "considerable human rights risks."

European officials backing the hubs say the policy's main purpose is deterrence rather than large-scale removals.

They argue that the prospect of paying smugglers thousands of euros for a dangerous journey to Europe, only to be sent to a third country, could dissuade some migrants from making the trip.

Critics, however, say there is little evidence that tougher enforcement measures and deportation schemes reduce migration over the long term.

“Enforcement changes how people travel, not whether they travel. Some pause or change route, and smugglers adapt and raise their prices,” said Roberto Forin of the Mixed Migration Centre, a research institute that collects data along migration routes.

A willing host

Rwanda has positioned itself as a destination for migrants that Western countries want to remove, despite longstanding concerns about its human rights record.

President Paul Kagame has won praise from Western and regional leaders for helping end Rwanda's 1994 genocide and rebuilding the country into a destination for investment and aid.

Critics, however, accuse his government of suppressing dissent and supporting the M23 rebel group in neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo, which rights groups say has committed killings, rapes and other abuses.

Rights advocates also point to restrictions on political freedoms and free speech.

Freedom House rates it "Not Free" and cites what it describes as the suppression of political dissent through surveillance, intimidation, arbitrary detention and torture.

The United States last year began transferring migrants to Rwanda under an agreement allowing it to deport up to 250 people.

Britain abandoned its own plan to send asylum seekers to Rwanda after it was ruled unlawful by the country's Supreme Court 2023. Kigali sought a 50 million pound ($63.6 million) payment after the UK scheme was scrapped.

During a September visit to Kigali, two European Parliament lawmakers were shown facilities earmarked for Britain's abandoned scheme that could potentially house migrants transferred from EU countries, including a hotel.

description:
The Netherlands and four other European Union countries are preparing to establish a deportation center in Rwanda for rejected asylum seekers.
The proposed facility would allow European governments to transfer rejected asylum seekers to a third country while arrangements are made for their eventual return home.
The plan follows changes to European migration rules introduced in June, which expanded the legal options for transferring rejected asylum seekers to countries outside the European Union.
The financial implications are a particular concern because only a relatively small number of asylum seekers are expected to be transferred initially.
Human rights organizations and refugee advocacy groups have opposed the use of third countries to accommodate rejected asylum seekers.
text:
The Netherlands and four other European Union countries are preparing to establish a deportation center in Rwanda for rejected asylum seekers. The proposed facility would house migrants who cannot be returned to their home countries. The plan is expected to be formally announced at a meeting in Vienna on November 16.

The proposed facility would allow European governments to transfer rejected asylum seekers to a third country while arrangements are made for their eventual return home. Migrants would not need to have any previous connection to Rwanda.

The agreement is expected to be formally announced at a migration conference in Vienna on November 16, according to sources cited by RTL. Germany, Austria, Denmark and Greece are joining the Netherlands in the initiative after months of discussions about establishing deportation facilities beyond European borders.

Rwanda is the first country selected for the proposed arrangement. One possible location is the Hope Hostel in Rwanda’s capital, Kigali. The facility was originally developed under a British agreement to accommodate migrants deported from the United Kingdom. The agreement collapsed following legal challenges, and Britain’s new government abandoned the plan in 2024.

The plan follows changes to European migration rules introduced in June, which expanded the legal options for transferring rejected asylum seekers to countries outside the European Union. However, the legality of the arrangements has yet to be tested in court.

The previously mentioned Hope Hostel now stands empty and has space for about 100 people. Its facilities include shared bedrooms, communal washing areas, a dining hall, gardens and sports fields. A nearby residential development, also financed by Britain, could provide accommodation for hundreds more.

Rwanda already accommodates refugees from neighboring Congo and other countries. It also works with the United Nations and the African Union to receive migrants evacuated from detention centers in Libya. Dutch Asylum Minister Bart van den Brink has also backed the concept but has been more cautious about setting a timetable or specifying how many people could be transferred.

The proposal is included in the Dutch governing coalition agreement, which commits the government to pursuing reception facilities for rejected asylum seekers outside the European Union. In February, the Tweede Kamer adopted a motion introduced by the JA21 party calling for a concrete plan within six months.

The financial terms of the Rwanda agreement have not been settled. Rwanda is expected to seek economic compensation for hosting the migrants, but the participating countries have not disclosed how much the arrangement could cost.

The financial implications are a particular concern because only a relatively small number of asylum seekers are expected to be transferred initially. Britain previously paid Rwanda hundreds of millions of pounds under its abandoned deportation agreement. The two countries have since disputed the payments, with Rwanda refusing to return the money.

The proposal has exposed some differences within the Dutch governing coalition. The conservative VVD and Christian Democratic CDA support the plan, while the centrist D66 party has raised serious objections. D66 considers Rwanda, as well as Uganda, an unsuitable destination for transferred migrants.

Human rights organizations and refugee advocacy groups have opposed the use of third countries to accommodate rejected asylum seekers. They argue that transferring migrants to countries outside Europe could expose them to inadequate protections and make independent monitoring more difficult.

The Dutch Council for Refugees has criticized the proposal, citing concerns about Rwanda’s human rights record. “One of the primary reasons for our opposition is our serious concern regarding the human rights situation in Rwanda,” said Sjoerd Warmerdam, the organization’s director.

“Independent human rights monitoring is virtually impossible in Rwanda. Furthermore, the Dutch Immigration and Naturalization Service (IND) has itself concluded that Rwanda cannot be classified as a safe third country. The United Kingdom previously attempted to negotiate an agreement with Rwanda, but that arrangement was rightfully rejected because of concerns surrounding the country’s human rights record.”

The European coalition is also considering similar arrangements with Kenya, Uzbekistan, Ghana and Uganda. The Netherlands previously held discussions with Uganda about establishing a return hub but suspended its participation in those talks.

text:
The Briefing

On November 13, 2026, the Supreme Court agreed to hear Mullin v. RAICES, a challenge to President Trump's January 2025 proclamation that eliminated asylum access at the entire southern border — including at official ports of entry.

Both a D.C. federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit have already ruled the proclamation unlawful, but the ban has remained in effect while the case works its way to the justices.

A final ruling is expected before the Court closes its term in June 2027; the decision will settle whether an executive proclamation can override a congressional statute specifically designed to protect people fleeing persecution.

A presidential order that has shut people out of the asylum system at the southern border for nearly two years is now on its way to the highest court in the country. On November 13, 2026, the Supreme Court agreed to review the Trump administration's asylum restrictions in Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services — widely known as Mullin v. RAICES. The justices will decide whether a sitting president can use an executive proclamation to override a statute that Congress wrote specifically to give people fleeing persecution the right to request protection on American soil.

A Proclamation That Left No Door Open

On the first day of his second term, President Trump signed Proclamation 10888, declaring an "invasion" along the southern border and suspending asylum access for everyone crossing there — including those who approached official ports of entry. That last detail set the order apart from previous Trump-era restrictions: unlike earlier policies, this one left no legal pathway to asylum whatsoever, closing even the door that had traditionally remained open at official checkpoints.

The legal scaffolding for the proclamation rested primarily on Section 212(f) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which authorizes a president to suspend the entry of noncitizens when deemed in the national interest. The administration added the "invasion" framing to invoke what it argued were additional emergency powers under both the Constitution and the statute.

The legal problem, as courts below identified it: Congress separately enacted INA § 208, which explicitly grants any person physically present in the United States — regardless of how they arrived — the right to apply for asylum. No executive proclamation, however sweeping, can override a congressional statute that was written to function as an unconditional floor of protection.

Two Courts Said No — Yet the Ban Kept Running

The federal district court in Washington, D.C. ruled the proclamation unlawful, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld that ruling in April 2026. Even so, the appellate panel paused its own decision to allow the Supreme Court to weigh in — meaning the ban has remained operational throughout, permitting the rapid removal of people who crossed the border without authorization.

The plaintiffs in the case include 13 individuals who fled countries including Afghanistan, as well as three nonprofits that provide legal services to migrants at the border: RAICES, the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project, and Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center. Some of the individual plaintiffs were deported to third countries and then pushed back to the very nations they had originally fled; others endured extended detention without meaningful access to legal proceedings.

The Two Questions the Justices Will Answer

The Supreme Court narrowed its grant of review to two specific legal questions. The first asks whether the proclamation and related Department of Homeland Security guidance lawfully bar both asylum claims and withholding-of-removal claims. The second involves a procedural question about scope: whether a provision of federal immigration law, 8 U.S.C. § 1252(f)(1), prohibited the lower court from extending its relief to an entire class of migrants rather than adjudicating each case individually.

The stakes of the first question could not be higher. A ruling in the administration's favor would validate the use of a presidential proclamation to override a federal statute — a legal tool that future administrations of either party could then deploy against any congressionally protected right. A ruling for the plaintiffs would reaffirm that Congress, not the White House, sets the floor for who may seek safety in the United States.

"Our system of checks and balances exists for moments precisely like this — to ensure no single branch can consolidate power at will," said Faisal Al-Juburi, co-chief executive officer of RAICES.

A Supreme Court Term Defined by Immigration

Mullin v. RAICES does not stand alone on the Court's docket. This term has shaped up as one of the most consequential for immigration law in decades, with the justices having accepted review in a cluster of related cases since late spring.

One companion case involves the administration's practice of deporting noncitizens to countries not identified in their removal orders — a third-country removal policy the Court has repeatedly allowed to continue while litigation plays out. That case, Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., was scheduled for oral argument in December and centers on whether migrants have the right to contest a deportation destination before being removed to a country where they have no ties.

The other, Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, concerns the government's policy of holding immigrants in mandatory detention without access to bond hearings, regardless of how long a person has lived in the United States or how deep their community ties run. In July 2025, the Department of Homeland Security issued guidance declaring that immigrants who entered the country without inspection are subject to mandatory detention for the entire duration of their removal proceedings — a sharp break from nearly three decades of established practice.

Together, these three cases form an interlocking framework: Can the president eliminate asylum at the border? Can those already living in the country be held indefinitely without a hearing? Can they be deported to countries they never identified as home? The answers — arriving from a Court with a 6-3 conservative majority — will define the rights of millions of immigrants, disproportionately from Latin America, for a generation.

What Happens Between Now and the Ruling

Until the Supreme Court issues its decision, the asylum ban remains in force. Oral arguments in Mullin v. RAICES are expected in spring 2027, with a final ruling anticipated before the Court wraps up its term that June. No specific argument date has been set.

text:
Five European countries have announced a plan to send rejected asylum seekers to a processing centre in Rwanda as early as next year, drawing condemnation from rights groups who said it would leave vulnerable people at risk of abuse.

The planned scheme, which is still being negotiated with Rwanda, would send people to a centre where the migrants could choose to return home, settle or go somewhere else where they had a right to stay, Kigali said on Monday.

Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands said that the plan aimed to deter more people from migrating to Europe. The European Union has worked for years to tighten migration rules, reduce the number of asylum seekers arriving and increase deportations of migrants who are not entitled to stay.

“I think this will be a game changer, making us able to confront the massive challenges with illegal migration,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said. “We will break down the business model of human smugglers. We will take back control of our borders and we will remove the incentives for illegal migration.”

Rwanda’s interior minister, Vincent Biruta, said his country would give a “second chance” to people who have no right to stay in Europe.

He added that arrivals would be able “to voluntarily return to the countries of origin, integrate into Rwandan society or relocate to another destination where they have the legal right to reside, according to their preference”.

When asked how Kigali would ensure refugees’ human rights, Biruta said, “There will be an independent monitoring mechanism” and that it would cooperate with the United Nations’ refugee agency.

Human rights groups criticised the plans, saying that EU countries could not guarantee their rights would be respected there.

In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged ‌the five countries to abandon the Rwanda plan — echoing criticisms of a different migration settlement plan between Britain and Rwanda in the early 2020s.

The plan “signals that Member States accept the risk of serious human rights violations against one of the most marginalized groups in society, in return for a deterrence goal that evidence clearly suggests they will not reach,” read the statement from the International Rescue Committee, the Dutch Council for Refugees and other groups.

A Human Rights Watch researcher said the deal “would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad”.

Germany’s interior minister said the European plan was not comparable to a scrapped 2022 deal with the United Kingdom because only those whose asylum claims are rejected will be sent to Rwanda.

text:
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents pepper-sprayed a pregnant US citizen and threw her to the ground during a protest in California on Sunday, according to her family’s attorney, who shared footage of the incident.

Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, 23, was filming and protesting the presence of several ICE officers outside the Stanislaus county jail in Modesto, in California’s central valley, before she was taken down by officers and arrested on her stomach during a chaotic encounter.

Vargas Andrade, who is 12 weeks pregnant, said in a press conference on Sunday evening that she is part of a group of local residents who monitor ICE sightings, and that she had gone to the jail parking lot after agents were spotted in the area.

A commotion erupted when ICE agents moved to arrest a man who, it appeared, had just been released from the jail, video shows.

Footage filmed by Vargas Andrade’s husband, Adolfo Talavera, captured a tumultuous scene as several people protested the agents making the arrest. The circumstances of the man’s arrest were not immediately clear, and he has not been identified. Agents wore law enforcement vests and ICE badges, and at least two of them had masks covering their faces.

It was unclear what exactly happened right before Vargas Andrade’s arrest, with the sound on the footage repeatedly cutting out. One woman was heard screaming at the agents to get away from her and another cursed at the agents, telling them, “You should be embarrassed … you guys are so fucked up.”

Vargas Andrade had her phone in one hand as she and an agent then appeared to bump into each other, footage showed. That agent then grabbed her and started to handcuff her. Another agent then pulled out what appeared to be a pepper-spray canister and pointed it at the direction of Vargas Andrade and her husband who was filming.

The footage partially captured the agent deploying the pepper spray, though it was difficult to discern how long he sprayed it and where the chemicals landed. Soon after, the footage captured Talavera shouting, “She’s pregnant with child!” as the agents moved to detain his wife. Seconds later, two agents took Vargas Andrade to the ground where she was handcuffed on her stomach with her hands behind her back, before one of the agents moved her onto her side.

Vargas Andrade was taken into custody and transported to an ICE field office in Stockton, according to her attorney, Patrick Kolasinski. Vargas Andrade’s sister had called for an ambulance, which then arrived at the ICE facility and transported her to a hospital, her family and a local advocate said at the press conference.

Vargas Andrade said officers had told her she was accused of assaulting an ICE agent, an accusation she denied. She was released later that day, and she has not been charged with any crimes, according to Kolasinski.

Spokespeople for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) did not immediately respond to inquiries on Monday. A spokesperson for the Department of Justice (DoJ) declined to comment. A spokesperson for the Stanislaus sheriff’s office, which runs the jail, said sheriff deputies were not involved in Vargas Andrade’s arrest.

“They threw me to the ground, they maced me, then they handcuffed me,” Vargas Andrade recalled to reporters on Sunday night. “I told the ICE agent … ‘I’m pregnant, so don’t put your hands on me.’ … They right away threw me on the floor … I was burning. I couldn’t breathe. The mace went up my nose.”

Another ICE agent then gave her water to wash her face, she recalled.

“I got scared,” Talavera said. “I was like, what if she has a miscarriage?”

Vargas Andrade said she was particularly worried because she had suffered two previous pregnancy losses, but she said doctors did an ultrasound after the incident and did not identify any concerns.

The encounter happened amid reports of increased ICE activity in California’s central valley region, which is home to the state’s agricultural industry. DHS and the justice department have repeatedly accused anti-ICE protesters of assaulting agents, though many of those prosecutions in California have fallen apart in federal court.

“We’re not going to stop helping the community even though this happened,” Vargas Andrade said. “We want our immigrants to feel safe here.”

text:
By Georg von Harrach

Five European countries have announced that they will send failed asylum seekers to Rwanda after reaching an agreement in principle with the central African country.

In a deal with Austria, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece, migrants, who have had their right to asylum rejected, could be sent to Rwanda to seek a new life.

The model differs from the now defunct British scheme to send migrants to Rwanda while their asylum applications were processed.

Announcing the outline of a deal in Vienna this afternoon, Denmark’s Prime Minister, Mette Frederiksen, pictured at the top, said “we need to take back control of our borders”.

Ministers would not be drawn on the number of migrants involved or the cost, which they insisted were still under negotiation.

Pilot phase

Some reports suggest a pilot phase could involve up to 100 migrants, but Frederiksen said it would put off a much bigger number - in the “thousands” - from making the attempt to try to get to Europe in the first place.

Standing alongside European ministers at the press conference, Rwanda’s Foreign Minister, Olivier Nduhungirehe, said migrants would be given the option to settle in Rwanda or volunteer to return to their home country.

Unlike the British scheme, which saw dedicated facilities built in Kigali, Nduhungirehe said migrants from the five EU member states would not be “kept in a camp or a dedicated area, they will be integrated in our society”.

But the details still need to be finalised.

Denmark’s Immigration Minister, Morten Bødskov, said he hoped the full agreement could be completed “within the next few months”, with the aim of sending the first set of migrants to Rwanda before the end of 2027.

‘Safe third country’

Under EU rules, it was previously only possible for member states to send failed asylum seekers to a country where they have some kind of family connection and one with which the EU, or a member state, had a bilateral agreement, if they refused to return home voluntarily.

But under the terms of a new European law, which only recently came into force, migrants can be sent to a designated “safe third country”, even if it is a country with which the migrant has no previous connection.

Share Channel 4 News

According to data from the European Commission, 28% of all non-EU migrants “ordered to leave” actually did so last year.

An estimated 350,000 failed asylum seekers neither voluntarily left nor could be forced to do so.

The EU has been signing more so-called readmission agreements, including one with Nigeria last week. But many countries refuse to take migrants back or - like war-torn Syria - are not in a position to do so.

Tougher stance

Immigration has become a political hot potato across Europe with governments under pressure - particularly from right wing parties - to take a tougher stance.

In the first 10 months of this year, there were around 110,000 attempts to illegally enter the EU, according to the EU’s border agency, Frontex. That’s down 29% on last year, but the numbers are still seen as too high.

Before the announcement, Human Rights Watch said the Rwanda scheme was a “deceitful misnomer” to send migrants to a country where they have never set foot.

“Paying Kigali to host a deportation program would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad,” said Clementine de Montjoye.

Share

The EU’s Return Regulation requires that deals “may only be concluded with a third country where international human rights standards and principles in accordance with international law, including the principle of non-refoulement, are respected”.

But the regulation is untested and many expect the scheme to end up in court. In the past that has put paid to other similar schemes.

Huge political pressure

The British government previously reached a deal worth £715 million to send migrants to Rwanda while their asylum claims were being assessed in the UK.

The UK paid for asylum facilities to be built in Rwanda that could house up to 200 people per year at Hope Hostel in Kigali.

After facing hurdles from the European Court of Human Rights and huge political pressure, the scheme was dropped when Labour came to power.

Meanwhile, Italy has struggled with its deal to send migrants to Albania, with court cases forcing the Italian government, under Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, pictured below, to move the goalposts.

But only a handful of migrants have ended up there.

Other countries to follow suit?

Meloni has called it an “innovative solution” that set the precedent for the change in European law.

The Italian scheme is set to cost taxpayers €653 million over five years.

The European Commission said that it “welcomed” the initiative taken by five member states to work towards a deal with Rwanda which it said had been taken following “careful preparatory work, including with regard to ensuring respect for human rights and the close cooperation with UN agencies”.

The Rwandan government said it believed other countries would likely follow suit and accept migrants from Europe once the concept was proven to be a success.

text:

A section of the U.S.-Mexico border wall near El Paso, Texas, on June 6, 2024.

The U.S. Supreme Court Friday granted the Trump administration’s request to decide whether the federal government can ban asylum claims at the southern border.

One of President Donald Trump’s first proclamations he signed at the start of his second term was a ban on asylum claims at the southern border on the grounds that there was an “invasion,” which the administration argued was a condition that allowed the president to invoke a section of the law to suspend asylum claims.

A federal judge found the policy unlawful, but decided to allow it to remain while litigation pursued. An appeals court upheld the lower court’s decision.

The justices agreed to answer two questions, whether the proclamation that bans asylum is lawful and if a class action suit should be allowed. The case will be argued sometime during the coming months.

This is the third major immigration-related case the high court has agreed to hear this term. The justices also will decide whether the Trump administration can deport immigrants to countries to which they have no ties to and whether immigrants can be indefinitely detained.

The justices earlier this year allowed the Trump administration to use a policy known as “metering” which allows immigration officials to turn away migrants applying from asylum at the southern border.

The American Civil Liberties Union is representing the three immigration groups that brought the suit: the Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, the Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center and the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project.

“The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger,” Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement. “The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court.”

A decision from the justices is likely next summer.

text:
Media contacts:

media@sikhcoalition.org

media@asianlawcaucus.org

Federal Court Strikes Down Determination, Reaffirms NY Immigrant Truck Drivers’ Ability to Work

SAN FRANCISCO — Last week, a federal appeals court struck down the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration’s (FMCSA) determination that the State of New York and its Department of Motor Vehicles’ (DMV) are out of compliance with the federal commercial drivers license (CDL) program, FMCSA issued its Final Determination in April which risked the removal of $73.5 million in highway funds and threatened the decertification of the state’s entire CDL program.

“The decision is a much-needed win for immigrant commercial drivers,” said Josh Rosenthal, workers’ rights program director at Asian Law Caucus. ‘They have done everything right only for the Trump administration to take away their livelihoods and thrust thousands of families into economic instability. Commercial drivers are essential workers that our communities depend on, and the entire country suffers when the government targets immigrant workers with these hurtful policies.”

“Following the devastating attack on California truckers’ livelihoods as a result of FMCSA’s threats, this development in New York is a significant victory,” continued Sahel Kaur, Managing Attorney at the Sikh Coalition. “We continue to believe that it is callous to deprive law-abiding drivers of the ability to provide for their families—and that it is reckless to threaten entire states’ transportation funding packages in service of doing so.”

Asian Law Caucus and Sikh Coalition submitted an amicus brief to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit in July urging the court to set aside FMCSA’s determination as it would mean the loss of 25,000 CDL holders’ livelihoods and it attempted to rewrite long-standing policy. The brief was submitted on the behalf of Asian American Legal Defense and Education Fund, Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project, Chinese for Affirmative Action, National Immigration Law Center, Sikh American Legal Defense and Education Fund, South Asian Legal Defense Fund, Stop AAPI Hate, Truckers Movement for Justice, and United Sikhs.

California received a similar determination from FMCSA, which led it to cancel thousands of CDLs this spring. Asian Law Caucus, Sikh Coalition, and Weil, Gotshal & Manges LLP brought a class-action lawsuit on the behalf of the class of commercial drivers and the Jakara Movement challenging these cancellations. California later challenged the FMCSA determination in a separate lawsuit.

The affected California drivers—as well as many immigrant drivers with lawful status in New York and across the country— remain unable to renew expiring CDLs, due to a Trump administration rule. That rule is also subject to a lawsuit in the United States Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit.

###

About the Organizations

For nearly 25 years, the Sikh Coalition has fought to defend and expand Sikh civil rights in the United States. For more information about this lawsuit, the Sikh community’s impact on the U.S. trucking industry, or the Sikh Coalition’s additional work to fight for truckers’ rights, email media@sikhcoalition.org.

text:
The American Nurses Association (ANA) and the American Association of Colleges of Nursing (AACN) condemn the continued detention of Ann Lawani, PhD, MSN, RN, a nurse educator at the University of San Francisco. Detained in Lodi, California, on September 16, she remains in federal immigration detention thousands of miles from her family and community. We call for her immediate release and return to California while her legal proceedings continue.

Dr. Lawani’s detention raises broader concerns about the consequences of separating nurses from the people who depend on them. Nurses provide essential patient care, educate the next generation of healthcare professionals, strengthen public health, and care for their own families. Their absence can disrupt care and education, with consequences that extend throughout their communities.

ANA and AACN are deeply concerned about the detention of nurses who hold valid federal work authorization, as Dr. Lawani reportedly does. Federal authorities must account for the human and community consequences of enforcement decisions, including disruptions to healthcare and nursing education.

Guided by the Code of Ethics for Nurses and our shared commitment to the nursing profession, ANA and AACN advocate for the dignity, human rights, and fair treatment of every person, regardless of immigration status. These principles apply to the patients nurses serve and to nurses themselves.

We urge federal authorities to uphold due process and humane treatment and ensure that enforcement practices take account of the effects on nurses, their families, and the patients, students, and communities who rely on them.

###

About the American Nurses Association

As the preeminent organization representing more than 5 million nurses, the American Nurses Association harnesses The Power of Nurses® to champion the profession and drive transformation in healthcare. Through legislative and political advocacy, comprehensive educational services, and the profession’s leading Code of Ethics and Scope and Standards, the association empowers nurses across every specialty and practice setting. The association is committed to ensuring healthy work environments, shaping pioneering policies, and cultivating partnerships that enhance both the nursing profession and the broader healthcare experience.

title: Democracy Works Newsletter 2026 - League of Women Voters of California
description:
Your extraordinary dedication helped deliver significant victories for democracy, voting rights, and justice in California.
Together, we also celebrated the 61st anniversary of the Voting Rights Act through Unite & Rise events statewide, carrying that momentum into a landmark victory: passage of the California Voting Rights Act of 2026.
When we asked members to attend court hearings in our litigation defending California voters’ privacy, they showed up.
Protecting Democracy California took a major step to protect voting rights in 2026, strengthening state law in the face of the Supreme Court’s relentless assault on federal voting rights protections.
Democracy Works When We Do The votes are counted, but our work to defend democracy never stops.
text:
A Year of Courage, Commitment, and Collective Action

The year’s end invites us to reflect with gratitude. To you – the engine of the League – we offer our deepest appreciation. Your extraordinary dedication helped deliver significant victories for democracy, voting rights, and justice in California.

This year, voters across California and the nation made their voices heard, delivering historic firsts, including the election of California’s first Latino governor. Here at home, voters resoundingly rejected Proposition 39, protecting access to the ballot box and reminding us of the power of participation and the importance of our work with each and every voter.

To safeguard our democracy as it was threatened, you bravely showed up in countless ways: educating voters, organizing No Kings protests, responding to Action Alerts, and supporting the League’s defense of democracy. When the U.S. Department of Justice demanded sensitive personal information about California’s 23 million voters, LWVC stood firm, successfully challenging federal overreach in court.

Together, we also celebrated the 61st anniversary of the Voting Rights Act through Unite & Rise events statewide, carrying that momentum into a landmark victory: passage of the California Voting Rights Act of 2026. As federal voting rights protections faced unprecedented threats, California strengthened its commitment to protecting voters.

Our legislative accomplishments were equally remarkable. Governor Newsom signed 43 of 46 League-supported bills that reached his desk, including 11 of our 12 highest priorities. These victories advanced voting rights, government transparency, immigrant protections, reproductive freedom, housing access, and more.

Among them was AB 2599, championed by Assemblymember Isaac Bryan, requiring corporations to disclose historical connections to slavery. Working alongside the Alliance for Reparations, Reconciliation, & Truth and coalition partners, we helped advance accountability and racial justice.

These achievements belong to you. Every email to a legislator, response to an action alert, donation, and heartfelt conversation moved this work forward. In a year marked by uncertainty and challenges to our democratic institutions, you continued to act with the courage and purpose that led to the victories we achieved for all Californians.

Finally, we thank you for entrusting us with a historic first for LWVC: a shared presidency. Serving together has allowed us to draw on each other’s strengths, embrace collaborative leadership, and act as a possible example of a presidency partnership for future generations.

Thank you for sustaining each other over the last year, thank you for your time, thank you for your spirit, and unwavering commitment to the League. We look forward to all we will accomplish together in the year ahead.

Reflections on My First Year

What a year to join the League of Women Voters of California! As I reflect on my first year as Executive Director, I am struck by two things: the extraordinary strength of the League’s voice and the remarkable dedication of the people behind it. At a time when our public discourse was driven by outrage, fear, and whoever can shout the loudest, the League offered something different: a trusted, principled voice grounded in facts, integrity, and a deep commitment to democracy.

This past year, I watched partners, journalists, and community members turn to the League time and time again for clarity and leadership. In the weeks leading up to the historic midterm election, our phones rang off the hook as folks turned to the League for our perspective on everything from California’s 14 ballot propositions to the escalating attacks on our democracy. Amid all the noise and confusion, we helped cut through the rhetoric with trusted information and a reassuring voice reminding Californians that their participation mattered.

League Members Show Up!

One of the greatest joys of this year has been discovering just how reliably League members answer the call. When we asked members to attend court hearings in our litigation defending California voters’ privacy, they showed up. At rallies and press conferences about Propositions 4 and 39, they showed up. Everywhere I’ve traveled across California, from Annual Meetings to community gatherings and celebrations, League members have welcomed me with open arms.

I’ve also had some fun along the way! A performance of Suffs with the Los Angeles League inspired a musical party trick that I trotted out at events across the state. (I need to find a new song for next year…) From those gatherings to my first national Convention, I’ve been continually inspired by the warmth, energy, and commitment of this community.

I’m especially grateful to our incredible Staff and Board, who have been extraordinary mentors and partners throughout this first year. Thank you all!

Building a Democracy For All

This year has reinforced for me that our mission is about more than simply increasing voter turnout (although let’s keep working on this!). It’s about ensuring that the people who participate in our democracy truly reflect the wonderfully diverse communities of California.

That’s why our work strengthening the California Voting Rights Act and co-chairing the Yes on Proposition 4 and No on Proposition 39 campaigns was so meaningful to me. At a time when powerful forces were working to narrow the electorate, intimidate voters, and concentrate political power in fewer hands, the League fought and continues to fight to open doors wider. Because we believe democracy works best when power is shared, every voice can be heard, and everyone has a meaningful opportunity to participate.

Looking Ahead, Together

The coming year will undoubtedly bring new challenges. But I enter it with tremendous optimism because I’ve seen firsthand what this community can accomplish.

Even amid the chaos, confusion, and attacks on our democracy, this year brought me moments of genuine joy and inspiration. I’ve found a community of people who aren’t simply fighting against what is wrong but working together to build something better – a democracy rooted in fairness, belonging, kindness, and mutual care.

Thank you for welcoming me into this extraordinary organization, for showing up again and again, and for reminding me that democracy isn’t just something we defend. It’s something we build together, every day.

Year in Review

In 2026, California faced mounting federal threats to our democracy, efforts to roll back voting rights, escalating attacks on immigrant communities, and growing concerns about intimidation at the polls. The League of Women Voters of California responded on multiple fronts by advancing legislation, defending voting rights in court, supporting local Leagues, and engaging voters on consequential ballot measures.

Protecting Democracy

California took a major step to protect voting rights in 2026, strengthening state law in the face of the Supreme Court’s relentless assault on federal voting rights protections. As co-sponsors working through the California Democracy Partnership, the League was instrumental in passing the following two bills that together make up the California Voting Rights Act of 2026:

SB 1164 (Cervantes) expands California’s protections against voter suppression and vote dilution, giving voters stronger tools to challenge election rules and systems that unfairly burden racial and language-minority communities or weaken their ability to elect candidates of their choice. It establishes state law protections against discriminatory effects, even without proof of discriminatory intent.

SB 1360 (Cervantes) strengthens language access by preserving existing federal language assistance requirements in state law and establishing a future state process for identifying additional language coverage obligations. Voters should not lose access to election materials because federal protections are weakened.

Safeguarding California’s Elections. As threats to California’s elections intensified, the League responded with urgency. We championed the following legislation to defend election systems from interference and protect voters from intimidation at the polls:

SB 73 (Cervantes) strengthens protections against improper law enforcement interference with California’s elections, including unauthorized access to or seizure of voter lists and election materials.

AB 1664 (Jackson) requires local election officials to notify the Secretary of State and Attorney General about warrants, subpoenas, and investigations involving election records or voting technology. Early notification is critical because it allows the state to respond before interference disrupts an election.

SB 884 (Umberg), the Protect Our Polls Act, focuses on voters themselves. It prohibits law enforcement arrests within 200 feet of polling places on Election Day while polls are open, with specified exceptions. It also permits election officials to extend polling hours when violations disrupt voting and requires ballot drop-off locations to open at least 30 days before Election Day. We worked alongside Senator Umberg to advance these protections in time for the November 2026 election.

We also helped stop SB 1310 (Choi), which would have canceled voter registrations based on unreliable juror records that could be outdated or inaccurate. Had this bill passed, voters could have been kicked off the voter rolls before receiving notice or a chance to correct mistakes. The League organized coalition opposition to stop this dangerous bill from advancing further.

Finally, our co-sponsored bill, AB 868 (Carrillo), would have ensured that the final choice for nonpartisan county offices is made in November, when more voters participate, rather than allowing contests to be decided in low turnout primaries earlier in the year. Although the bill did not advance this year, we are planning to bring it back in 2027.

Civil Rights, Immigration & Reparations

The No Kings Act. Ongoing federal overreach and violations of civil rights and liberties demand accountability, which is why we championed SB 747 (Wiener). The law gives Californians a new path to sue federal officers, including immigration agents, for violations of federal constitutional rights. SB 747 reinforces the principle that no official, federal or state, is above the law.

Detention Facility Transparency Act. Reports of deaths, medical neglect, sexual abuse, and other atrocities in immigration detention facilities have raised serious questions about accountability. We fought for SB 423 (Gonzalez) to bring more public scrutiny to these conditions. The legislation makes specified records concerning incidents at private detention facilities accessible under the California Public Records Act. The new law will help prevent important information about these incidents from being hidden behind a wall of secrecy.

Establishing Accountability & Truth. AB 2599 (Bryan), the Truth in Disclosure Act, takes an important step toward confronting the legacy of slavery by requiring certain large businesses operating in California to examine their records and disclose whether they or their predecessors participated in or profited from slavery, slaveholding, or the slave trade. While acknowledging these injustices cannot undo the lasting harm inflicted on Black Americans or erase persistent racial disparities, establishing the truth is essential to holding institutions accountable and securing reparations. LWVC worked to advance this legislation and will continue to partner with organizations leading reparations efforts in California.

Criminal Justice

Those who are charged with a crime have the right to effective legal counsel under the U.S. and California Constitutions. We strongly supported AB 690 (Schultz), the Fair Representation Act, which establishes standards for indigent defense contracts beginning in 2028. These safeguards can help ensure defense attorneys have the time and resources to provide effective representation.

Unfortunately, the Assembly failed to pass our co-sponsored bill, AB 1958 (Kalra), following last-minute intensive lobbying of legislators by law enforcement groups. This bill would have strengthened the Racial Justice Act by improving procedures for establishing racial disparity claims. We intend to return to these important accountability reforms in 2027.

Housing, Clean Energy & Affordability

An important housing and climate victory this year was the passage of SB 772 (Cabaldon), sponsored by Prosperity California. The new law modernizes California’s Infill Infrastructure Grant Program, expanding opportunities for affordable housing development, particularly in smaller cities and towns where inadequate infrastructure can be a major barrier to building new homes. It will help communities build much needed housing while supporting thriving local economies and California’s climate goals.

Remove Barriers to Clean Energy. Heat pumps can lower energy use, reduce indoor air pollution, and help households move away from fossil fuels. However, complicated permitting can discourage installation. LWVC advocated for SB 222 (Wiener), the Heat Pump Access Act, which streamlines permitting and inspections for qualifying residential heat-pump systems. These practical changes can make cleaner, more efficient home heating and cooling easier to install.

Protecting Utility Customers as Data Centers Expand. The rapid growth of AI is driving proposals for large data centers, with substantial demands on California’s electric grid. We championed SB 886 (Padilla), the California Technology Innovation and Ratepayer Protection Act, because households and other businesses should not have to absorb the costs of serving these new facilities. As electricity demand grows, protecting affordability needs to be part of the equation.

Beyond Legislation

Our advocacy in 2026 also took us into the courts, where we fought to protect voting rights, voter privacy, and California’s Constitutional authority to administer its own elections.

In United States v. Weber, the League successfully intervened to fight the Trump administration’s sweeping demand for California’s complete voter file, including sensitive personal information such as driver’s license and Social Security numbers. That information could be used to check California voters against flawed federal citizenship databases, putting eligible voters at risk of being wrongly identified as noncitizens. A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department’s lawsuit in January, although the administration has since appealed and the threat didn’t end. In October, the danger reared its head again when the Justice Department demanded that California set aside ballots from more than 20,000 voters flagged as possible noncitizens through error-prone data matching. These escalating actions demonstrate why the League’s fight to protect voter privacy and prevent eligible voters from being disenfranchised is so important.

In Issa v. Weber, we intervened to defend California’s law allowing mail ballots postmarked by Election Day to be counted if they arrive within seven days. Following a June U.S. Supreme Court ruling upholding states’ authority to count timely cast ballots received after Election Day, Issa voluntarily dismissed his lawsuit. California voters have therefore retained this critical safeguard against mail delays.

In Cervantes v. Bianco, the League and Common Cause filed an amicus brief challenging Sheriff Chad Bianco’s extraordinary seizure of nearly 650,000 ballots from the November 2025 special election. In September 2026, the California Supreme Court unanimously ruled the seizure unlawful and ordered the ballots returned, reaffirming that sheriffs cannot take control of election materials outside the procedures established by state law.

In California v. Shasta County, we joined the LWV of Redding Area and other voting rights organizations in challenging local Measure B, which would have required photo ID to register and vote, virtually eliminated mail and early voting, and mandated hand counting of ballots. A court blocked the measure before the November 2026 election.

Ballot Measures. The League devoted significant work to researching the November 2026 statewide ballot measures and explaining our recommendations to voters. We published Vote with the League recommendations and a deeper analysis online. LWVC also co-chaired the campaign committees for both Yes on Prop 4 (to reduce the influence of wealthy donors and give everyday Californians a stronger voice in elections) and No on Prop 39 (to protect voting rights and prevent new barriers that could keep eligible voters from casting their ballots and having their votes counted). We helped guide campaign strategy, coordinated coalition partners, developed messaging, and engaged voters through public events, social media, and extensive media outreach.

Voter Protection. We provide voting information through our hotline (888) 870-VOTE (8683) and cavotes.org, bring together Know Your Rights resources, and help voters understand how to cast a ballot that will count. We also monitor threats to voting access with partners and work with state and county election officials to resolve problems when they arise.

Looking Ahead

Whatever the political and budget environment, important work remains unfinished. We are already planning to reintroduce legislation to reform county primary elections and strengthen the Racial Justice Act, building on the work we did to advance both bills this year.

A Word of Thanks

None of this would be possible without the tireless work of our advocacy team and grassroots leaders. Our work depends on volunteers, members, and local Leagues who turn policy goals into action. As we enter 2027, we will keep defending the right to vote, pushing for accountable government, and building a democracy in which everyone can participate. Thank you for making it all possible.

Support Our Work

The threats to our democracy are not letting up. From federal interference in California elections to attacks on voting rights and accountable government, the challenges ahead demand a strong response. The League is fighting back in the courts, at the Capitol, and in communities across California. But we cannot do it without you. Your contributions help us respond quickly, defend voters, and stand up for democracy when it matters most. Please donate to the League of Women Voters of California Action Fund to support this important work.

2026 Voter Engagement

A Year of Impact: Empowering California Voters

The 2026 election year was a powerful reminder of the importance of an informed and engaged electorate – and the vital role that trusted, nonpartisan voter education plays in strengthening our democracy. Through the dedication of our volunteers, staff, and community partners, the League of Women Voters of California Education Fund (LWVCEF) worked tirelessly to ensure that voters across California had access to the information, resources, and tools they needed to navigate the election and make their voices heard with confidence.

From expanding access to voter education resources to connecting voters with reliable information about candidates and ballot measures, our collective efforts have helped make the voting process more accessible and meaningful for Californians. We are deeply grateful to everyone who has contributed their time, expertise, and passion to this work.

In 2026, the LWVCEF’s voter engagement efforts included:

• Producing the Easy Voter Guide (EVG): We made trusted, nonpartisan election information easier to understand and access through the Easy Voter Guide, available in five languages – English, Spanish, Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese. Designed to provide clear, “snack-sized” information, the EVG broke down the 14 state propositions into easy-to-understand, accessible summaries. More than 125,000 printed copies were distributed through partnerships with community organizations across California, helping bring essential voter information directly to the communities that needed it. The guide was also available online at easyvoterguide.org, making this resource accessible to voters wherever they were.

• Running the VOTE411 website: Our comprehensive online election guide, VOTE411, continues to be an invaluable resource for California voters, offering nonpartisan insights into candidates and measures at federal, state, and local levels. Thanks to the dedication of over 120 volunteers, we reached out to more than 5,700 candidates and entered detailed information on 450 local measures. VOTE411 also offers essential guidance on polling places, ballot return processes, and more. Dive into the wealth of information at vote411.org.

• Engaging Communities Across California: Local Leagues across California brought voter education directly into their communities by hosting candidate forums, ballot measure presentations, and other nonpartisan educational events. LWVC’s Pros&Cons and InDepth resources provided clear, balanced information about state ballot measures, helping voters better understand the issues before them. To support local presentations, we also provided a ready-to-use slide deck that Leagues could customize to meet the needs of their communities and audiences.

As we close out the 2026 election year, we are deeply grateful to everyone who helped bring trusted, nonpartisan election information to voters across California. Your time, dedication, and commitment made it possible for voters and communities to access the information they needed to participate fully and confidently in our democracy.

This year’s work is a powerful reminder of what we can accomplish when we come together with a shared commitment to informed and engaged voters. From volunteers and local Leagues to staff and community partners, every contribution helped strengthen our collective impact.

Thank you for being part of this important work and for helping empower voters across California. While this election may be coming to a close, our work continues. We look forward to building on what we have accomplished together and reaching even more voters in the year ahead.

Leaguer in Action

When did you become a Leaguer?

I joined the league in 2022, so about 5 years.

What did you dream of doing when you were young?

I wanted to solve problems for our communities and for people. I felt the calling to help those that can’t help themselves and to bring solutions to problems/challenges. I always knew I wanted to help my fellow man and I wanted to put my talents at the disposal of those who need the assistance most.

How has your work influenced the League and/or your community?

I am a firm believer in strategic and focused collaboration and leveraging of resources from all sectors of our society to uplift and support an important cause. I have worked my entire career as an Engineering Project Manager, so my work has always revolved around collaboration and integration of resources for the purpose of completing or reaching an intended goal. I have worked towards bringing together organizations and working with local agencies on the common goal of informing our communities, particularly those of color and the youth, about the importance of civic engagement and how it benefits their daily lives.

Where do you see the League going in the future?

My vision for the League is that of a leadership organization upholding and uplifting voting rights, human rights and defending our democracy through purposeful and strategic collaborations with other organizations. I see the League as a very logical leader of the effort to bring people together from all walks of life through meaningful coordination of efforts from multiple organizations with a clear focus on the improvement of the lives of all individuals.

Democracy Works When We Do

The votes are counted, but our work to defend democracy never stops.

The 2026 midterms are over, but the work to protect our vote never stops. Amid nationwide threats to voting rights and rising disinformation, California remains a beacon of hope because people like you invest in grassroots power.

title: American Council of Learned Societies v. McDonald - Constitutional Accountability Center
description:
The plaintiffs, leading scholarly organizations in the humanities, challenged the grant terminations in a New York district court.
They argued that, among other claims, the grant terminations violated the Fifth Amendment right to equal protection.
First, the text and history of the Fourteenth Amendment show the breadth of the Fifth Amendment’s parallel guarantee of equal protection.
The grant terminations here follow exactly that pattern, and therefore violate the Fifth Amendment right to equal protection.
DOGE’s grant terminations cannot survive any level of scrutiny, and the Second Circuit should hold that they were unconstitutional.
text:
The National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH) is a federal agency that awards competitive grants to fund scholarly humanistic work. This case concerns the April 2025 revocation of more than 1,400 previously awarded NEH grants worth over $100,000,000. The grants were terminated by staffers from the federal Department of Government Efficiency Service (DOGE) because they involved projects touching on race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, sex, and sexual orientation. DOGE staffers used keyword searches to identify grant descriptions that included, among other terms, “BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, People of Color),” “Minorities,” “Native,” “Tribal,” “Indigenous,” “Immigrant,” “LGBTQ,” “Homosexual,” and “Gay.” There were no similar searches for “white,” “Caucasian,” or “heterosexual.” DOGE staffers also used ChatGPT to identify “grants involving DEI,” which classified grants as “DEI” because they involved specific races, ethnicities, religions, or genders.

The plaintiffs, leading scholarly organizations in the humanities, challenged the grant terminations in a New York district court. They argued that, among other claims, the grant terminations violated the Fifth Amendment right to equal protection. The district court agreed. The Trump administration appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, and CAC filed an amicus brief in November 2026 explaining that the cuts to the grants violated the Fifth Amendment.

First, the text and history of the Fourteenth Amendment show the breadth of the Fifth Amendment’s parallel guarantee of equal protection. As courts have long recognized, the Fifth Amendment’s equal-protection component is coextensive with the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause, such that the history of the latter is directly probative in considering the scope of the former. The Framers of the Fourteenth Amendment were deeply concerned about violence and discrimination targeting Black communities during Reconstruction, as well as the documented violence and discrimination faced by white allies targeted based on their association with Black Americans. In line with this history, the Supreme Court has never limited equal-protection liability to discrimination based on one’s own constitutionally protected traits, recognizing constitutional violations when people are targeted for adverse treatment based on the race of their spouse or companion.

Second, the Constitution’s equal-protection guarantee bars the government from using protected traits like race to impose negative consequences. Here, DOGE identified NEH grants by searching their descriptions for references to race, religion, ethnicity, national origin, sex, and sexual orientation and then terminated them. Longstanding equal-protection doctrine forbids this sort of government action. Although the government attempts to frame its classification of these grants as making viewpoint-based distinctions, the Supreme Court—more than half a century ago—identified a similar sorting scheme as an “explicitly racial classification” subject to heightened constitutional scrutiny. In that case, the Court held that a city amendment that imposed extra procedural hurdles for laws that dealt with race and other protected traits (and only those laws) violated the Equal Protection Clause. The grant terminations here follow exactly that pattern, and therefore violate the Fifth Amendment right to equal protection.

DOGE’s grant terminations cannot survive any level of scrutiny, and the Second Circuit should hold that they were unconstitutional.

title: Urgent Need for Legal Funding for Vulnerable Children - Inside Philanthropy
description:
This is happening as courts and immigration agencies accelerate cases and children face increasingly aggressive enforcement.
Providers with specialized expertise in immigration law and child trauma can and should continue representing the children who are already their clients.
Funding these attorneys preserves continuity of counsel and ensures that children retain independent advocates whose ethical obligation is to them, rather than relying on legal services selected by the government.
The answer has two parts: stabilize the legal capacity children need today while building a more resilient legal access system for tomorrow.
Philanthropy can help preserve independent, child-centered legal representation now while a more diversified and sustainable funding base is built.
text:
For two decades, a national network of nonprofit legal organizations, reaching from major metropolitan areas to rural communities where access to attorneys is scarce, has helped ensure that children who arrive in the United States without a parent or guardian do not have to navigate one of the most complicated legal systems in the country entirely on their own.

Today, that network is at risk of unraveling — and children are already feeling the consequences.

Federal funding for this national network has ended, despite decades of bipartisan support. Unaccompanied children’s immigration cases have not. Providers remain committed to representing their young clients, but they are now doing so without the resources that sustained this work.

This is happening as courts and immigration agencies accelerate cases and children face increasingly aggressive enforcement.

Independent representation makes an enormous difference in this environment. A child’s attorney has an ethical obligation to the child — not to the government, a detention facility, or an immigration agency. That attorney can defend a child abused during apprehension or in custody, challenge unlawful removal, and advocate for safe family reunification.

Federal funding should not determine who a child’s lawyer is — or whether that lawyer can continue to access their client in custody. Providers with specialized expertise in immigration law and child trauma can and should continue representing the children who are already their clients. Funding these attorneys preserves continuity of counsel and ensures that children retain independent advocates whose ethical obligation is to them, rather than relying on legal services selected by the government.

To take just one recent example, a provider learned that a child newly separated from his family and placed in federal custody was scheduled for deportation the next day. Attorneys mobilized immediately, filed to reopen the child’s case in immigration court, and went to the facility to advocate directly with government officials attempting to remove the child. They ensured the child received the individualized legal process to which he was entitled.

This is what is at stake.

Funders are understandably asking: What comes next? What are we building toward?

The answer has two parts: stabilize the legal capacity children need today while building a more resilient legal access system for tomorrow. The urgency of funding both cannot be overstated.

We do not know exactly what that future system will look like. It will likely combine strong local representation with regional and national coordination, training and technical assistance, pro bono engagement, litigation, technology, and more diversified public and private funding.

But we cannot build it if we allow the current field to collapse first.

Innovation cannot substitute for stabilization. Stabilization is what makes innovation possible.

Philanthropy can act now. Flexible funding can ensure experienced attorneys continue representing children, support attorneys who already have access to their clients in shelters and detention, and give providers the capacity to respond when new children are apprehended, rights are violated, or rapid intervention is necessary to prevent removal or protect family reunification.

This is not only the responsibility of immigration funders alone. It is a child-welfare, anti-trafficking, civil rights, and access-to-justice issue.

The United States has made a commitment to protect the due process rights of unaccompanied children. States including New York and California have demonstrated that public partners can step forward. Philanthropy can help preserve independent, child-centered legal representation now while a more diversified and sustainable funding base is built.

The children cannot wait for the perfect funding strategy or next innovation. They need their lawyers now.

title: John Oliver remembers 'Alligator Alcatraz': 'the utter disgrace' - The Guardian
description:
He is going to build this network for the American people.” “What are you doing going on TV to demand $50bn?” Oliver mocked.
“You might understandably have forgotten about Alligator Alcatraz given, you know, everything else,” said Oliver.
“For one thing, Alligator Alcatraz is a pretty good encapsulation of the performative cruelty of Trump’s second term,” he said.
Even though Alligator Alcatraz is no more, “we should remember the utter disgrace that it was”, he concluded.
