text:
John Oliver opened the season finale of Last Week Tonight with a brief reaction to the Federal Aviation Administration’s shock grounding of all US flights on Friday afternoon, which brought nationwide travel to a halt and stranded travelers across the country. He zoned in on transportation secretary Sean Duffy, whose Friday press conference in the midst of a crisis left much to be desired. “Rather than use that press conference to dispense information, which would have been ideal, he instead took it as an opportunity to air grievances and make demands,” Oliver noted.

Duffy blamed “old, legacy equipment that failed” and asked for $50bn from Congress to upgrade the system. “I can’t build things if i don’t have money,” Duffy said. “I want $50bn. President Trump is a builder. He is going to build this network for the American people.”

“What are you doing going on TV to demand $50bn?” Oliver mocked. “You sound less like a secretary of transportation trying to calm people down and more like a Batman villain trying to hold Gotham hostage: ‘I need $50bn unless the Batman can solve my riddles in time!’”

Duffy, said Oliver, was right about one thing: the US flight system is outdated. But as the host pointed out, Republicans have controlled both houses of Congress as well as the presidency for the past two years, making them responsible for any complaints about underfunding. And the Republican-led Congress, along with the Trump administration, collaborated to triple Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)’s budget last year to $28bn, for a total that surpasses the annual budgets of almost all federal law enforcement agencies combined.

“It is hard to take a panicked shakedown from Duffy,” said Oliver, “not just because his cost estimate jumped by $20bn mid-sentence, but also because he’s part of a flagrantly corrupt administration who spent a chunk of his time in office shooting a shitty reality show with his family to encourage Americans to take more road trips.” (Duffy, his wife and their nine kids shot The Great American Road Trip over seven months from 2025 to 2026.)

“To that end,” said Oliver in reference to reports of stranded travelers renting cars last minute, “guess what, Sean? Mission fucking accomplished!”

In his main segment, Oliver tracked the rise and fall of “Alligator Alcatraz”, the prison opened last year in the Florida Everglades by the state’s then governor, Ron DeSantis, to curry favor with immigration hardliners like Trump.

“You might understandably have forgotten about Alligator Alcatraz given, you know, everything else,” said Oliver. “And this is the rare story where I’m actually going to tell you up front how it ends, and an even rarer one, given that it’s actually good news.” Because back in June, the Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, announced that the prison was closing down immediately. “And that is a genuinely good thing,” said Oliver. “Which is almost hard to absorb, isn’t it? The last few years, whenever you hear something was shut down, you naturally assume it’s an important clinical trial, or critical repairs at national parks, or maybe a beloved celebrity’s heart, not actually something you want to see end.”

But though it’s now closed, Oliver argued that the erstwhile prison is still worth talking about. “For one thing, Alligator Alcatraz is a pretty good encapsulation of the performative cruelty of Trump’s second term,” he said. “But also, one of the key men behind it, Ron DeSantis, is now being floated as a possible replacement for Pete Hegseth, and there’s even rumors that he’s planning another White House run.”

“And I am sure that DeSantis, like many of those who were behind Alligator Alcatraz, would like nothing more than for people to forget about it and move on. But … that should not happen.”

The host then retraced the prison’s “incredibly stupid origins” as a “mashup of two different ill-thought-through ideas that Trump floated”. One was his first-term interest in a border wall with a water-filled trench stocked with snakes and/or alligators. Another was his proposal to reopen Alcatraz, the infamous island prison located within the San Francisco Bay. Florida attorney general James Uthmeier, one of many “mid-tier villains in Trump’s orbit”, appears to have smushed together the two slapdash ideas into a proposal pitched via social media, claiming such a prison would be “efficient and low cost” because one doesn’t have to invest too much in a “perimeter”.

Trump’s team loved the idea, and the facility was assembled in under eight days – “slower than God, sure, but a lot faster than most high-intensity builds”, Oliver noted. To do so, the Florida state government relied on no-bid emergency contracts, including $219m to a portable restrooms company called Doodie Calls. In all, Alligator Alcatraz cost more than $1bn to construct, by using funds set aside for hurricanes, floods and other natural disasters because DeSantis declared US immigration in Florida to be a “state of emergency”. The vast majority of people incarcerated there, it should be noted, were neither convicted of a violent crime nor on a “final removal” order.

Perhaps unsurprisingly for a swamp prison, conditions were reportedly terrible – cramped and unsanitary, with open toilets, rotten food and literal cages branded as “calming areas” for men to “reflect on their behavior choices, manage their emotions, reduce stress and practice self-directed behavior”.

“That’s just straight-up torture,” Oliver corrected.

Though one would think inhumane practices would close the prison, what actually shut Alligator Alcatraz down “wasn’t everyone suddenly having an attack of conscience”, said Oliver: “Instead, it seems to have been a very stupid oversight on Ron DeSantis’s part.” The governor had said that the costs of the prison would be fully reimbursed by the federal government, but the federal government legally had to declare it a state project, sticking Florida with all of the costs.

The passing of the buck is one of many, many reasons, Oliver argued, states should not be allowed to run immigration detention facilities, full stop. “I’d actually argue that we shouldn’t be running immigration detention facilities in general, but that is a different story that we have already done,” he added.

Even though Alligator Alcatraz is no more, “we should remember the utter disgrace that it was”, he concluded. Ultimately, Alligator Alcatraz was “a shoddy, shameless attempt to gain political points with public cruelty”.

title: Five EU countries unveil plans for Rwanda deportation hub | CNN
description:
Five European countries unveiled plans on Monday to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda, drawing condemnation from rights groups who said it would leave vulnerable people at risk of abuse.
‘The risk of violations’ In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged the five countries to abandon the Rwanda plan — echoing criticisms of a different migration settlement plan between Britain and Rwanda in the early 2020s.
Rwanda a willing host Rwanda has positioned itself as a destination for migrants whom Western countries want to remove, despite longstanding concerns about its own human rights record.

Britain abandoned its own plan to send asylum seekers to Rwanda after it was ruled unlawful by the country’s Supreme Court in 2023.
text:
Five European countries unveiled plans on Monday to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda, drawing condemnation from rights groups who said it would leave vulnerable people at risk of abuse.

Under the planned scheme — which is still being negotiated with Rwanda — Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands would send people to a center where the migrants could choose to return home, settle or go somewhere else where they had a right to stay, Kigali said.

“I think it will be a game changer, making us able to confront the massive challenges of illegal migration,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told a press conference in Vienna with her Austrian counterpart and ministers from the countries involved.

The five countries have been working towards a deal for a so-called return hub for several months, officials have said — part of a broader push inside the European Union to increase deportations and curb irregular migration.

With elections approaching in several EU countries, centrist governments have been toughening immigration policies to try to counter growing public support for far-right parties.

‘The risk of violations’

In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged the five countries to abandon the Rwanda plan — echoing criticisms of a different migration settlement plan between Britain and Rwanda in the early 2020s.

The plan “signals that Member States accept the risk of serious human rights violations against one of the most marginalized groups in society, in return for a deterrence goal that evidence clearly suggests they will not reach,” read the statement from the International Rescue Committee, the Dutch Council for Refugees and other groups.

Although officials say such a hub would only handle about 100 people at a time, the countries championing it say it would send an important signal that they hope will discourage would-be migrants from making the often perilous journey to Europe.

The project follows the approval of the EU’s new Return Regulation, designed to speed up deportations.

The scheme differs from Britain’s abandoned Rwanda deportation plan in that it would only apply to migrants who have exhausted all legal avenues to remain in the European Union, rather than those whose claims are still being processed.

Rwanda a willing host

Rwanda has positioned itself as a destination for migrants whom Western countries want to remove, despite longstanding concerns about its own human rights record.

“Under this partnership, Rwanda would provide a second chance to people who no longer have the legal right to remain in the partner countries,” Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said on Monday.

Rwanda was not looking to be paid for the arrangement, but partner countries would meet the cost of relocation and the integration of any who chose to stay in Rwanda, he added.

Veteran President Paul Kagame won praise from Western and regional leaders for helping end Rwanda’s 1994 genocide and rebuilding the East African country into a destination for investment.

However, critics accuse his government of suppressing dissent and supporting rebels alleged to have committed killings, rapes and other abuse in neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo. Rights advocates also point to restrictions on political freedoms and free speech.

Freedom House rates it “Not Free” and cites what it describes as the suppression of political dissent through surveillance, intimidation, arbitrary detention and torture.

“There is a real danger that the Rwanda deal will, with its limited chance for scrutiny, become a cruel black hole for human rights,” Amnesty International said in a statement on Monday.

The United States last year began transferring migrants to Rwanda under an agreement allowing it to deport up to 250 people.

Britain abandoned its own plan to send asylum seekers to Rwanda after it was ruled unlawful by the country’s Supreme Court in 2023. Kigali sought a £50 million ($63.6 million) payment after the UK scheme was scrapped.

During a September visit to Kigali, two European Parliament lawmakers were shown facilities earmarked for Britain’s abandoned scheme that could potentially house migrants transferred from EU countries, including a hotel.

text:
A pregnant U.S. citizen was pepper-sprayed and arrested during a confrontation with federal immigration agents outside a California county jail, according to her attorney and footage (shown above) of the incident.

Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, who is 12 weeks pregnant, was detained Sunday in Modesto as federal agents sought to take into custody another person who had just been released, her attorney Patrick Kolasinski said.

"Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, a pregnant U.S. citizen, was pepper sprayed, thrown to the ground on her stomach, and arrested by ICE agents while participating in a protest outside the Stanislaus County Jail," Kolasinski told Newsweek.

Read More on News

Since President Donald Trump returned to the White House and launched an aggressive mass deportation campaign, immigration authorities have faced mounting scrutiny over allegations of excessive force, racial profiling, unlawful arrests, and due process violations. U.S. citizens have also been questioned and detained during enforcement operations, with a ProPublica investigation published in October identifying over 500 citizens detained by immigration agents since Trump returned to office.

Video obtained by Newsweek shows plainclothes federal agents wearing tactical vests marked "POLICE" and "FEDERAL AGENT" surrounding a silver minivan in a parking lot as bystanders record the encounter.

Behind the minivan, Andrade approaches an agent while recording on her phone. The agent grabs her by the arm, and a second agent moves in to restrain her.

The second agent then pulls out a red canister of pepper spray and points it toward another woman and the person filming as bystanders shout.

Andrade’s husband can be heard behind the camera telling agents that she is pregnant. Two agents then force Andrade facedown onto the pavement beside a black SUV and handcuff her behind her back. An agent rolls her onto her side and into a seated position before later pouring water from a plastic jug over her face as other agents stand nearby.

Newsweek has contacted the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for comment via email.

A news release issued on behalf of Andrade's family said the video was recorded by her husband, Adolfo Talavera.

It remains unclear who immigration agents initially sought to detain or what that person's immigration or criminal history was.

Andrade's husband, Adolfo Talavera Alvarado, said at a Sunday news conference that he, Andrade and his sister, Monica Alvarado, were all pepper-sprayed during the encounter. Monica Alvarado was driving the van stopped by immigration agents. Footage shows the agent briefly pointing the pepper-spray canister toward Monica Alvarado during the confrontation.

Speaking after her release Sunday night, Andrade said she had been monitoring immigration enforcement in the Central Valley and began livestreaming on TikTok after seeing agents outside the jail.

She denied an agent's allegation that she assaulted him, saying they bumped into each other before agents took her to the ground, pepper-sprayed and handcuffed her. Andrade said she hit her stomach during the takedown.

Andrade, 23, of Ceres, said she was taken to an ICE field office in Stockton but was not processed there. Her sister called an ambulance, which took Andrade, who is diabetic, to a hospital, where she said two agents remained with her and denied her access to an attorney. She said neither she nor her pregnancy was harmed.

She was released Sunday night after several hours in federal custody without being charged with a crime, Kolasinski said.

title: ACLU of Wisconsin Files Brief Supporting Milwaukee Ban on ICE Masks Amid DOJ Challenge
description:
In the wake of unprecedented federal immigration enforcement in Chicago and Minneapolis, the Milwaukee Common Council sought to protect Milwaukee residents against ambushes by armed, masked, and unidentified law enforcement agents.
There are numerous instances in Minneapolis, Chicago and elsewhere of ICE agents descending on community members, often in unmarked vehicles, refusing to share any identifying information about themselves.
These ambushes – indistinguishable from kidnappings – escalate the risk of danger to those encountering the agents, bystanders, and law enforcement alike.
The brief also points out that masked and unidentifiable law enforcement raids eviscerate public trust and enable opportunities for impersonators.
This ordinance will bring a measure of transparency and public accountability to all members of law enforcement operating in Milwaukee.”
text:
MILWAUKEE – On behalf of the Wisconsin Council of Churches, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Wisconsin filed a friend-of-the court brief in support of the City of Milwaukee’s ordinance banning ICE agents from wearing masks to hide their identities.

In the wake of unprecedented federal immigration enforcement in Chicago and Minneapolis, the Milwaukee Common Council sought to protect Milwaukee residents against ambushes by armed, masked, and unidentified law enforcement agents.

To that end, the Common Council passed an ordinance prohibiting all law enforcement from wearing face coverings while interacting with the public in the performance of their duties. The ordinance also requires that all law enforcement officers either display on their uniforms the name of their agency and the officer’s last name, badge number, or identification number or verbally provide this information upon request. The US Department of Justice sued the City to prevent the ban from being enforced.

The brief argues that allowing the federal government to continue deploying masked, unidentifiable, heavily-armed officers to Milwaukee would inflict concrete harm on city residents by permitting federal immigration enforcement to proceed under conditions of anonymity, impunity and escalating violence.

There are numerous instances in Minneapolis, Chicago and elsewhere of ICE agents descending on community members, often in unmarked vehicles, refusing to share any identifying information about themselves. These ambushes – indistinguishable from kidnappings – escalate the risk of danger to those encountering the agents, bystanders, and law enforcement alike.

The brief also points out that masked and unidentifiable law enforcement raids eviscerate public trust and enable opportunities for impersonators. Many of these immigration operations have made people afraid to leave their homes, go to work, attend religious gatherings, and make their medical appointments. People are also less likely to come forward and alert authorities when they witness crime. Because law enforcement officials are wearing masks to conceal themselves, it has also enabled individuals who have assaulted and kidnapped others to falsely pose as ICE agents. The FBI reported multiple instances of impersonation in 2025.

The brief also notes that the anonymity of officers makes accountability for misconduct much harder. There are hundreds of reports of constitutional violations by federal agents for which individuals have extreme difficulty seeking relief given the anonymity of the law enforcement personnel. Without knowing officers’ names, badge numbers, or agency affiliation, or remembering their face, victims cannot identify responsible parties or pursue legal remedies when their rights have been violated.

“ICE agents and other law enforcement routinely break the law and have violently harassed, assaulted, abused and even killed multiple people while conducting reckless immigration operations across the country,” said ACLU of Wisconsin Staff Attorney Hannah Schwarz. “Agents have been able to get away with unlawful conduct in part because their use of masks makes them nearly impossible to identify. We cannot have members of law enforcement, who have a duty to serve the public, hiding behind masks, refusing to identify themselves, and operating in secret. No one is above the law – especially not those responsible for enforcing it. This ordinance will bring a measure of transparency and public accountability to all members of law enforcement operating in Milwaukee.”

text:
A federal judge set aside new Trump restrictions on foreign students’ admission to the US.

A Department of Homeland Security rule limiting those students to four years in the country is contrary to statutory authority and failed to consider less burdensome tools available to the government, US District Court for the District of Massachusetts Judge F. Dennis Saylor found in an order Monday.

The DHS regulations sought to end a framework known as “duration of status” that for decades has allowed international students to remain in the US while they make progress toward a degree. The new rule would have required F-1 student visa holders and J-1 exchange visitors to seek extensions from the agency to remain in the US after four years.

The agency hasn’t explained how imposing “an unreviewable, completely discretionary renewal system—after a foreign student has already been in the country for four years—meaningfully enhances the ability of DHS to root out cases of fraud, or how the benefits of such a system outweigh the immense costs of abandoning the existing system,” Saylor wrote.

A coalition of higher education and labor groups, among them the United Auto Workers, argued the rule would create needless disruptions to students’ pursuit of degrees.

Saylor issued an order stopping the regulations from taking effect in September, finding DHS failed to show a rational connection the restrictions and their stated objectives.

Plaintiffs are represented by McDermott Will & Schulte LLP. DHS is represented by the Department of Justice.

name: Litigation
title: Detain and Delay: Does Menocal Change Much for Immigration Detainees? - OnLabor
authors: Martin Konstantinov, Sonia Bastigkeit Ericstam, Sophia Leswing, Luciana Zorzoli, Mia Anastasio, Joel Heller, Benjamin Sachs, Angela Caloia, Sharon Block, Laura Weinrib
description:
In fact, private companies like GEO Group and CoreCivic manage 73% of ICE detention populations, all while making money hand over fist.
On February 25, 2026, in GEO Group v. Menocal, the Supreme Court held that the denial of GEO Group’s defense against plaintiffs was not immediately appealable.
GEO Group again appealed, but the Tenth Circuit affirmed the ruling in 2018.
In 2022, following four years of discovery, the district court ruled on both parties’ motions for summary judgment.
Applying the defense-immunity distinction to the plaintiffs’ case, the Court easily justified denying GEO Group’s appeal.
text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) currently detains around 65,000 people per day, nearly double the number from last year. Although there are over 200 authorized ICE detention centers, most detainees are condensed into a handful of facilities. The government does not run the majority of these centers; private contractors do. In fact, private companies like GEO Group and CoreCivic manage 73% of ICE detention populations, all while making money hand over fist.

Amidst escalating profits and detention numbers, ICE contractors foster center conditions that perpetuate preventable suffering, abuse, and deaths. Private detention facilities have been accused of serious deficiencies in medical care with fatal outcomes, negligence toward their populations, sexual abuse, and draconian punishments. They have also faced allegations of forced unpaid labor in violation of several federal and state laws, including the Trafficking Victims Protection Act (TVPA). In response, contractors have tried to play a near-endless game of delay and deny. And it has worked—for the most part.

On February 25, 2026, in GEO Group v. Menocal, the Supreme Court held that the denial of GEO Group’s defense against plaintiffs was not immediately appealable. In a unanimous 9-0 opinion, Justice Kagan concluded that an immediate appeal under the collateral-order doctrine did not extend to the contractor’s defense.

The case itself originated over a decade earlier. In 2014, a prospective class of over 60,000 people who were at one point detained at GEO Group’s Aurora facility filed a complaint in the District of Colorado and alleged that the contractor violated the TVPA by threatening detainees with punishment, including solitary confinement, unless they worked for the facility without pay or for $1 per day. One year later, GEO Group’s motion to dismiss was denied. For the first time, the contractor requested an interlocutory appeal, which the district court rejected. In 2017, two classes were certified. GEO Group again appealed, but the Tenth Circuit affirmed the ruling in 2018. GEO Group subsequently petitioned the Supreme Court for certiorari, but was denied.

In 2022, following four years of discovery, the district court ruled on both parties’ motions for summary judgment. As part of its decision, the court rejected GEO Group’s argument that it was merely following ICE’s instructions and could not be sued. GEO Group once again filed an interlocutory appeal in the Tenth Circuit. In 2024, ten years after the case’s inception, the Tenth Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of appellate jurisdiction, holding that the district court’s ruling did not qualify for immediate review. GEO once again sought certiorari and was granted certiorari.

The Menocal decision is incredibly technical. The Court began by examining the principal case that establishes the contractor’s defense, Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction. In Yearsley, the Court held that a private contractor may be protected from liability when performing work for the government, provided that the government had the authority to undertake the work and the contractor acted pursuant to valid government authorization. From the outset, the Court drew a clear distinction: “Yearsley provides a defense to liability, not an immunity to suit.”

An immunity from suit protects defendants from litigation itself. Its rejection subsequently qualifies for an immediate appeal under the collateral-order doctrine, a long line of Supreme Court cases that created an exception to the general rule that appellate courts can only review final decisions of district courts. Conversely, a defense to liability is a claim on the merits: a party asserts some reason as to why their conduct was not unlawful. Whereas an immunity makes it such that the defendant does not need to answer for their conduct in court, the Court reasoned that a defense “offers something different, and of lesser value:” an answer to the alleged conduct so as to escape liability.

Unlike a defense from suit, a party’s immunity does not turn on whether its conduct was lawful. When a party’s defense is denied, the Court explained, the right to contest that ruling on the merits can be effectively vindicated after a trial. The Court therefore concluded that any appeal of an order denying the application of the Yearsley defense could only be reviewed after a district court’s final judgment—the resolution of the case on the merits.

Applying the defense-immunity distinction to the plaintiffs’ case, the Court easily justified denying GEO Group’s appeal. The Court concluded that GEO Group was making the argument for a defense on the merits by using Yearsley and saying it complied with the law—the government authorized the contractor’s conduct—while otherwise cloaking it in the language of an immunity from suit so as to justify its appeal. The Court did not allow GEO Group to do so.

Make no mistake about it, the decision is a win—all too rare—for victims of forced labor who seek to hold contractors like GEO Group accountable for their illegal conduct. But the case is also a sobering reminder of just how long plaintiffs must wait for their day in court. In its decision, the Court emphasized that there were good reasons to keep the exception to the collateral-order rule narrow. Doing otherwise would allow for “piecemeal appeals,” whereas finality “promotes the efficient administration of justice and preserves the proper balance between trial and appellate courts.” It is better that contractors will now not be able to immediately appeal the denial of this particular defense in other cases, but that does not foreclose them from taking advantage of the numerous levers of litigation to continuously delay claims from being placed in front of juries and rights from potential vindication. The Court’s decision may promote a more efficient administration of justice, but when the result looks something like shaving off a couple years from cases that themselves routinely take more than a decade, the Court’s promise will certainly ring hollow for those most affected by abuses of power.

text:
Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.

Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.

The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.

Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.

The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024.

Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".

The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.

The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.

In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.

In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".

Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system.

Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants".

He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration".

Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants.

The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.

"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".

With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration.

Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had a major role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries.

Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.

"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."

The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution.

Unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, the agency said.

According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year.

In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands".

text:
VIENNA (AP) — A group of European countries announced on Monday that they aim to set up a “return hub” in Rwanda where rejected asylum-seekers could be sent from next year, a move that they hope will also deter more people from coming.

The European Union has worked for years to tighten migration rules, push down the number of asylum-seekers coming to the 27-nation bloc and increase deportations of migrants who aren’t entitled to stay. Sending people to centers outside Europe has emerged as a central plank of that effort.

The plan by Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands, which have spearheaded negotiations with non-EU countries, drew immediate criticism from human rights groups.

A final agreement is expected within months

The aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said alongside officials from the other European countries and Rwanda's interior minister.

“I think this will be a game changer making us able to confront the massive challenges with illegal migration,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said. “We will break down the business model of human smugglers. We will take back control of our borders and we will remove the incentives for illegal migration.”

She predicted that “many other European countries” would join in. Her immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, said that the plan is to have a fully negotiated agreement with Rwanda “within the next few months.”

European officials point to a deterrent effect

Officials were vague about how many migrants might be sent to Rwanda, but emphasized the plan's deterrent effect.

“The most important number is the number that we will never see because hopefully they will not start their journey to Europe,” Frederiksen said. “So this is a milestone.”

Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said that his country would give a “second chance” to people who have no right to stay in Europe. He said that those who arrive will be offered the opportunity “to voluntarily return to the countries of origin, integrate into Rwandan society or relocate to another destination where they have the legal right to reside, according to their preference.”

Asked how Rwanda would guarantee refugees' human rights, he said that Rwanda would bring on board organizations such as the U.N. refugee agency and “there will be an independent monitoring mechanism.”

Human rights groups criticize plans for facilities in third countries

Human rights groups have criticized plans to deport migrants to facilities in third countries, arguing that European nations can't guarantee that their rights will be respected there. European officials insist that the new hubs would abide by European and international law.

“Offshore deportation centers are the latest cynical expression of the EU’s drive to shift its responsibilities to other countries,” Human Rights Watch researcher Clementine de Montjoye said in a statement. “Paying Kigali to host a deportation program would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad.”

Amnesty International Austria asylum and migration expert Aimée Stuflesser said in a statement that “today’s disgraceful deportation deal between European countries and Rwanda repeats mistakes of the past.”

“Sending people to a country they have never been to is irresponsible and there is a real danger that the Rwanda deal will, with its limited chance for scrutiny, become a cruel black hole for human rights,” Stuflesser said.

The U.N. refugee agency said that it only supports the possible use of return hubs in line with human rights standards, and as a way to help returns of people whose claims for asylum were denied after a full and fair assessment.

UNHCR spokesperson Matthew Saltmarsh said that the agency was involved in “constructive discussions” with the five EU countries “to provide advice on the compliance of the return hub process with international human rights law standards.” No agreement with the countries has been signed.

The United Nations' International Organization for Migration said that it doesn’t take part in or negotiate “state-to-state removal arrangements,” but was providing “technical input on the return hub process.” IOM said that it was prepared to provide help to migrants at the request of the receiving government if “necessary safeguards” are in place.

EU laws have changed in recent years because of persistent public and political pressure for tougher measures against migration.

European lawmakers voted in June to allow member states to set up centers outside the EU on their own or in small coalitions, and send rejected asylum-seekers there instead of to their home countries.

Europeans say plan isn't comparable to scrapped U.K. deal

Rwanda struck a deal with the U.K. in 2022 under which migrants who arrived as stowaways or in boats would be sent to the African nation, where their asylum claims would be processed and, if successful, they would stay. The U.K. Supreme Court ruled that the policy was unlawful because Rwanda isn't a safe third country for migrants sent there.

Then Prime Minister Keir Starmer scrapped that deal immediately after taking office in 2024.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Monday that the European plan for Rwanda isn't comparable. He said that the U.K. had planned to outsource asylum proceedings to third countries, while the European plan involves people who have been through the asylum process and exhausted their appeals.

Geir Moulson reported from Berlin. Jamey Keaten contributed to this report from Geneva.

In May 2025, senators from several states proposed a law based on Trump’s order, creating mandatory death sentences for undocumented immigrants convicted of capital offenses.
text:
Florida is the only state in the country with mandatory death sentences built into its legal system.

Individuals who are unlawfully present in the United States convicted of capital offenses, like first-degree murder or child sexual battery, must be sentenced to death, according to a 2025 Florida statute passed as part of a larger immigration bill sponsored by former state Sen. Joe Gruters and signed into law by Gov. Ron DeSantis.

However, if the person accused of a capital crime agrees to a plea deal before pleading guilty to the crime, they can avoid the death penalty.

Hannah Gorman, the founding director of the Balanced Justice Project at Florida International University, said the statute is unconstitutional in two main ways.

Firstly, it violates the 14th Amendment, which guarantees equal protection regardless of citizenship.

“There is a particular category of people identified and isolated as being treated differently to others, which is discriminatory and certainly not an equal application of the law,” she said.

The second major issue, Gorman said, is the mandatory nature of the statute, which could be categorized as cruel and unusual punishment under the Eighth Amendment because it takes away a jury’s discretion.

In 1976, the Supreme Court ruled mandatory death sentences unconstitutional under the Eighth and 14th Amendments.

Today, the death penalty system operates with two trials. First, there’s a trial to determine if the accused is guilty. Then, there’s a sentencing phase, where a jury determines if the death penalty is warranted after weighing all aggravating and mitigating factors. Gorman said that process narrows the law to include just the worst of the worst cases, ensuring the cases selected for the death penalty are deserving.

Mandatory death sentences make that two-trial process impossible, essentially erasing the sentencing trial for a whole class of people, Gorman said.

“If you deny somebody a trial that constitutionally they should have, and that a large majority of people are having, I would say that’s a huge issue,” she said.

Although those violations are the biggest, Gorman said, there are a host of other issues with the statute, including the vagueness of its “unauthorized alien” definition.

Florida law doesn’t clearly define the term, she said.

“The law is well established that it needs to be clear,” she said. “We need to know what that means, and, certainly on the basis of the statute, we don’t.”

No one has been sentenced to death based on the statute so far, so the issue hasn’t come up within the legal system yet. Gorman said the American Civil Liberties Union is “watching these cases.”

Gorman knows at least six people awaiting trial who could be charged under the statute, she said. One of whom is Akbor Miah, an immigrant from Bangladesh.

Miah was charged with murdering his sister-in-law in Lake County in May 2025, according to a Department of Homeland Security press release. He’s currently in custody.

He first entered the U.S. in 2016 and was deported three years later. According to the press release, Miah illegally re-entered the country in 2022.

Gorman said all the accused people she knows who could face this statute are too early in their trials to predict the outcomes. While the number of people potentially impacted is small, she added, the overall impacts are big.

“One person is too much for a death sentence that’s unconstitutional,” she said.

The statute also has the ability to impact international relationships, she added.

“To kill someone’s citizen is a bold move anyway,” she said. “But to do it with a denial of trial proceedings that you give to your citizens is something else.”

But proponents of the statute argue the law can be a powerful deterrent for illegal immigration and violence.

During a February 2025 Florida Senate Appropriations Committee meeting, Sen. Randy Fine, R-6, said the statute can be used as a tool for prosecutors to negotiate plea deals.

If a defendant takes a plea deal before going to trial, they can avoid the mandatory sentence. Fine said the statute, therefore, incentivizes people to take plea deals and accept more severe punishments than they would have gotten at trial prior to the statute.

He said his support for the measure comes from stories of murder at the hands of undocumented immigrants, citing the 2024 killing of Laken Riley, a 22-year-old Augusta University nursing student.

“I have hundreds of pages … of people who have been murdered by people who shouldn’t even be here,” Fine said. “There could be no greater aggravator than the fact that if you had followed the law, you wouldn’t have been here, and you couldn’t have committed the crime.”

He said that’s what makes the statute constitutional.

During the same meeting, however, Sen. Barbara Sharief, D-35, said the statute violates immigrants’ right to due process.

“I strongly oppose any legislation that applies the death penalty based on immigration status,” she said. “Creating a separate, harsher punishment for immigrants violates the principles of fairness and due process that define our legal system.”

The statute increases the risk of the unequal application of justice, she added.

On his first day in office for his second term, President Donald Trump ordered the U.S. attorney general to sentence people who kill law enforcement officers and undocumented immigrants who commit capital crimes to be automatically sentenced to death, encouraging states to do the same.

Florida wasn’t the only state that listened.

In May 2025, senators from several states proposed a law based on Trump’s order, creating mandatory death sentences for undocumented immigrants convicted of capital offenses.

“This legislation sends a strong message across the globe: We will not tolerate the senseless murder of innocent Americans at the hands of illegal immigrants any longer,” Sen. Steve Daines, R-MT, said in a press release announcing the bill.

Like Fine, supporters of the bill cited Laken Riley’s murder as proving the necessity for a bill like this.

“Republicans in Congress must do our part to ensure no more American blood is shed at the hands of criminals who shouldn’t be here in the first place,” Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-AL, said in the press release.

Juan Carlos Gómez, the director of Florida International University’s Immigration Human Rights Clinic, sees the statute as part of a larger effort against immigrants.

“It’s one more saber-rattling at a very destructive level of the anti-immigration movement,” he said. “You’re playing with human life simply based on the mechanics of immigration.”

He said the statute violates the Fifth and 14th Amendment rights to due process.

“It has nothing to do with citizenship,” he said. “We cannot dehumanize people on one side or another.”

The statute sets the stage for the government to spiral further into more hateful law, he added.

Harper Miller, the president of UF College Democrats, agreed the statute creates a slippery slope.

“I don’t think that anyone’s documentation status should strip them of their right to due process,” she said. “It’s a really dangerous statute.”

She was put off by the statute’s one-size-fits-all approach to the death penalty, she said, which she finds especially concerning given Florida’s high number of death row exonerations, with almost 15% of all exonerations across the country since 1976.

“It’s really disheartening to see any support for this statute,” she said. “This is obviously just part of a larger effort to fearmonger and to create more political polarization surrounding immigrant communities in our state.”

text:
Last year, Elizabeth Lopez moved from El Salvador to pursue a bachelor's degree in political science.

But since a June 30 law prohibited undocumented students from enrolling state colleges and GED programs, the 19-year-old Santa Fe College sophomore felt pressured to prove she belongs. Now, she carries proof of her U.S. citizenship on her at all times.

Even then, Lopez recognizes undocumented students don’t have the same security.

“It almost feels like … they're keeping the undocumented population kind of out of loop in the sense of education,” she said.

Immigrant perspectives

The measure mandates that all 28 Florida College System institutions, including Santa Fe College, stop enrolling undocumented students starting the 2027-28 school year. As the deadline approaches, Santa Fe students like Lopez are concerned about the effect it will have on immigrant students and their access to higher education.

Lopez said the ban is disappointing but isn’t shocking given Florida’s legislative history with undocumented residents. She added that it is only a small step from other anti-immigration regulations already in place.

Last year, Gov. Ron DeSantis passed a Senate bill preventing undocumented students from receiving out-of-state tuition waivers.

Another failed bill proposed blocking undocumented students from enrolling in any public college or university with an acceptance rate lower than 85%.

Lopez said the June 30 ban indicates a shift toward harsher policies targeting undocumented people.

She said colleges like Santa Fe are meant to serve their students, but the bans on higher education limit who can access them.

“It almost feels like the state's nitpicking who they're serving,” she said.

Though international students on F-1 visas are unaffected, Karen Horie, a 21-year-old international Santa Fe nursing freshman from Japan, said the ban isn’t fair to undocumented students. Being of Venezuelan descent, Horie is particularly concerned Hispanic students will be disproportionately affected.

There are more than 400,000 undocumented students in higher education nationwide, and roughly 45% are Hispanic. Roughly three-quarters of those undocumented students come from California, Florida, Texas or New York.

“As an international student, I think it's quite unfair because they deserve the right to have an education,” she said.

Horie said she believes it has been harder for international students to get into universities like UF because of how new regulations affect undocumented students. The ban could complicate financial aid and scholarship procedures for immigrant students regardless of their status, she said, as the benchmark for legality changes.

A Florida Board of Education rule, which went into effect Aug. 5, requires students to prove they are a U.S. citizen or legally present in the country before admission. Prior to the rule change, citizenship or status verification wasn’t necessary.

But the September decision raised concerns about whether the Florida Board of Education will continue to target people’s immigration status, Horie said. Ultimately, she thinks undocumented students will opt for postsecondary education elsewhere in the United States, attempting to avoid legal scrutiny in Florida.

Lisa Brosky, the Santa Fe marketing and communications associate vice president, said the college has no further comment about the decision.

She previously told The Alligator that Santa Fe has no way of predicting how many students can provide proof of citizenship or lawful presence, and the school is working to implement policies in compliance with the Board of Education's ruling.

As of Oct. 19, Santa Fe’s Board of Trustees has yet to rule on the matter.

Beginning Nov. 18, Brosky wrote, incoming Santa Fe students are required to prove lawful presence when applying for admission or readmission.

“It’s really that simple,” she wrote. “Students must provide proof that they are lawfully present in the U.S.”

An outside look

Non-immigrant students further prove they don’t have to be directly affected by public policy to care about it.

Calvin Cisneros, a 19-year-old Santa Fe computer science sophomore, said students shouldn’t have to prove their citizenship to receive an education.

“It's a little bit unfair,” he said. “Whether they're from here or not, or if their family is undocumented, I feel like students should have a right to an education.”

The United Nations recognizes education as a fundamental human right, meaning everyone should have access to education regardless of their immigration status or background, as outlined in Article 26 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

UNESCO, the UN’s educational, scientific and cultural organization, describes education as a basic human right.

Cisneros' friend, Sonia Chaudhari, a 17-year-old dual-enrolled student from Buchholz High School, echoed his sentiment.

She cited a case where a Gainesville High School student was deported with his family even while seeking permanent citizenship. He was just trying to get an education, she said.

Chaudhari said many undocumented students don’t get the chance to pursue higher education. But because a college degree is often essential for landing a stable job, many won’t get far without one, she said.

As a dual-enrolled student, Chaudhari is worried the ban will eliminate a free way for undocumented high school students to earn college credits. Many turn to free community college dual enrollment for credits before being admitted to college.

“It's scary because that's the only way some people can do it, financially,” she said. “It shouldn't be as difficult as it is for dual enrollment students, or honestly anybody.”

title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration 'return hubs' in Rwanda - The Guardian
description:
Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model.
The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.
Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.
The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”.
Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.
text:
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.

In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.

Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.

In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.

Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.

The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.

The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.

Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.

The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”

Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”

Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.

The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”

Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.

“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.

Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.

Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

text:
WASHINGTON—Rep. Lauren Underwood introduced the DHS Funding Accountability Act, legislation that would repeal the $200 billion in funding that Republicans handed to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) through their Big Ugly Bill last year. Underwood serves as a top Democrat on the House Homeland Security Appropriations Subcommittee.

While Republicans cut Medicaid and food assistance for millions of Americans, they poured billions of taxpayer dollars into accelerating the Trump Administration’s mass violation of civil liberties and the rule of law. Underwood’s legislation revokes this funding and prevents ICE and CBP from spending billions in remaining funds.

“Republicans made their priorities clear when they voted to take health care and food off the tables of American families while handing ICE and CBP billions of taxpayer dollars to expand the Trump Administration’s mass deportation agenda,” said Underwood. “Since then, we’ve seen what happens when these agencies are given enormous resources without meaningful accountability. Families are being torn apart, American citizens are being killed and detained, and our communities are being terrorized while the Trump Administration awards lucrative DHS contracts to their unqualified political allies. Congress should not be writing blank checks to agencies that continue to violate the constitutional rights of the people they’re supposed to serve. This legislation is the first step to take that money back.”

ICE and CBP have used this additional funding to violate constitutional rights, brutalize and terrorize our communities, and surveil American citizens.

The DHS Funding Accountability Act would repeal all eight funding provisions of the Big Ugly Bill that directed billions of additional taxpayer dollars to expanding immigration enforcement operations, detention expansion, border wall construction, surveillance technology, and the hiring of thousands of additional insufficiently trained ICE and CBP agents.

The legislation also rescinds dollars that have not yet been committed, making sure these agencies cannot continue drawing on the extraordinary funding provided through the law.

text:
Immigration lawyer Andrew Lattarulo doesn't just work behind the scenes. On his Instagram account—which has more than 57,000 followers—he posts videos explaining to immigrants their rights and warning them about Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operations and tactics. And that, Lattarulo has argued in a federal lawsuit, is why federal agents seized his phone and copied its contents.

Sounds about right, a federal judge held last week.

Granting Lattatrulo's request for a preliminary injunction to stop the Department of Homeland Security from looking though Lattarulo's stored phone data, Judge Allison D. Burroughs of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts wrote that he "is likely to succeed on the merits of this First Amendment retaliation claim."

The case starts with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and its probe of the Georges Cote law firm, where Lattarulo is a partial owner and represents clients in immigration proceedings. HSI alleged that the law firm has employed people who aren't legally allowed to work in the U.S.

In September 2025, Lattarulo and colleague Audai Cote took a weekend trip to Aruba. Upon returning to Boston, Lattarulo was stopped by Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents and an HSI officer as he deplaned. "The agents seized his cell phone without a warrant and then downloaded a complete copy of the data stored on the phone," noted Burroughs in her November 13 memorandum and order.

Warrantless cellphone searches are de rigueur for immigration agents, who claim they aren't required to adhere to the same Fourth Amendment rules as everyone else in the government. CBP policy says agents can conduct warrantless searches of electronic devices at or around the border or its functional equivalents, such as international airports, with or without suspicion. In some cases, they can also retain data from people's phones, laptops, and more.

"Seven federal appeals courts now hold that a warrant is never required to search a phone at the border, while the 4th and 9th Circuits require one in at least some cases," the Pacific Legal Foundation's Amy Peikoff noted at Reason in October. "That means one of your constitutional rights currently depends on which airport you fly into."

After seizing Lattarulo's phone at Logan Airport, officials held onto it for eight days before returning it. They also held onto his phone data—which including privileged attorney-client information, albeit in an unreadable format.

"The government intends to convert the data to an accessible format and search it if the Court permits," Burroughs explained.

Lattarulo sued, saying the search and seizure violated both his First and Fourth Amendment rights.

Lattarulo's suit alleged that he was targeted by immigration officials both because of his public political speech (such as the Instagram videos) and because of his work as an immigration attorney.

The government claimed that he was targeted because of HSI's investigation into the Georges Cote law firm.

But the government "provided no evidence that searches of cell phones are frequently conducted during the kind of employment investigation at issue here, and Lattarulo has directed the Court to sources which suggest otherwise," noted Burroughs. "The fact that the government, after Lattarulo spoke out publicly against it, elected to adopt a highly unusual investigative method that appears designed to inflict a maximal burden on Lattarulo lends substantial support to an inference that its actions were pretextual."

Burroughs pointed out that Audai Cote, who flew back to Boston a day before Lattarulo did and "had the same or greater access to the firm's employment records but did not speak publicly about immigrant rights," was not searched. Furthermore, the search happened just three days after the law firm received notice from HSI, even though the agency says employers who receive such notice have 10 business days to respond. Escalating matters after just three days by seizing an employee's phone "suggests the seizure did not arise from an ordinary investigative motive," Burroughs wrote.

Given all of this, "Lattarulo is likely to establish that he would not have been searched except for his protected speech," the judge concluded.

By granting Lattarulo's request for a preliminary injunction, she blocked the government from looking at his seized data as the case plays out, but stopped short of ordering them to destroy the data entirely.

Because the First Amendment issue was sufficient to warrant a preliminary injunction, the judge did not address the merits of Lattarulo's Fourth Amendment claim.

But she did have thoughts about what happened: "It appears that the government seized on a fortuitous border crossing following a weekend vacation as an opportunity to search for evidence of a domestic crime it was already investigating."

Surely, this can't fall within the scope of the border search exception to the Fourth Amendment—can it?

While refraining "from reaching a firm conclusion on the issue," Burroughs seems skeptical, at least, writing that "the Court is not convinced" that the exception was intended to "to apply to investigations into activity that occurred nowhere near the border and that has no relationship to the border crossing during which the search occurred. Nor is the Court convinced that application of the border search exception to this type of investigation would further the principles underlying the exception."

In the News

A 'single router in southern Arkansas' is supposedly behind the grounding of planes across the U.S. on Friday. Network gear at a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, is what "overloaded the communications system that thousands of air-traffic controllers use to guide pilots through the nation's airspace," The Wall Street Journal reports:

"We saw two places that were actually pinging our network at a very high rate, a thousand connections over every four to five seconds," Rebecca Guy, the FAA's technology chief, said at a Saturday press conference.

These pings traversed a tangle of copper wires and fiber-optic cables that feed into the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure, or FTI. The decades-old system is outdated and undergoing a multibillion-dollar upgrade to move into the fiber-optic age.

The FAA is still investigating what went wrong. But "when the FAA cut off the routers in Arkansas and Texas from the broader network, the communication problems stopped," per the Journal's reporting.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said more disruptions could be in order until it finishes replacing the old copper wires more than two years from now.

A SpaceX rocket successfully circled the Earth more than a dozen times on Friday. But SpaceX saw mixed results overall during Test Flight 15, during which the company tried to catch both the Starship rocket's booster and its upper stage.

"During the first phase of the test flight on Friday, SpaceX failed to catch and recover the booster, instead diverting it to an offshore splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico where it exploded before hitting the water," notes CNBC.

But SpaceX "successfully caught the upper stage, or spacecraft, portion of its massive Starship rocket from orbit on Saturday—a triumphant milestone for the company."

"That was the holy grail of spaceflight," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

Read This Thread

More Sex & Tech

• "Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or 'formally verify,' a number of the Signal protocol's key cryptographic guarantees," reports Wired. The work "serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world's communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp" while also demonstrating "Google DeepMind's formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code."

• Irish politicians are angling for U.K.-style bans on "taboo" porn categories.

• For decades, doctors told Katherine Bindley that nothing was wrong. Artificial intelligence helped figure out what was in fact wrong: endometriosis. "AI ultimately gave me what our siloed medical system couldn't: a look at my health with a zoomed out lens and longitudinal pattern synthesis," she writes.

• The Washington State Human Rights Commission "voted last month to permit businesses to set entry requirements based on genitalia when nudity is a core part of the operation—thus allowing, say, an all-female nude establishment to reject customers with male genitals without having to fear anti-discrimination enforcement from the state," notes Reason's Billy Binion. It's causing complications for "a case concerning a nude spa that has been embroiled in a yearslong, ever-crescendoing fight with the state after it declined to admit a preoperative transgender woman to its location in Lynnwood, Washington."

title: Five EU countries to announce first-ever return hub for migrants in Rwanda - Euronews.com
description:
Rwanda will host the first-ever EU return hub built outside the bloc, in an unprecedented move to send irregular migrants to countries with which they have no connection.
According to the sources, the first hub would be a “pilot project”, set to host a few hundred people deported from the five EU countries, starting in spring or summer 2027.
Rwanda's return hub may face legal challenges Return hubs have raised concerns in Europe over their compatibility with EU law and the protection of human rights.
Costs are unclear The five EU countries will bear the entire financial burden of the deportations and of accommodation in Rwanda.
More EU countries may join Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece in deporting irregular migrants to unrelated countries in the future.
text:
Rwanda will host the first-ever EU return hub built outside the bloc, in an unprecedented move to send irregular migrants to countries with which they have no connection.

The agreement between Kigali’s government and five EU member states is set to be announced on Monday in Vienna, after months of negotiations, two people familiar with the matter told Euronews.

The group of migration hardliners comprises Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece.

Their interior and migration ministers are attending a conference in the Austrian capital, where they will be joined by Rwanda’s Interior Minister Vincent Biruta. A few metres from the venue, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen will hold a press conference in the afternoon to announce the deal.

According to the sources, the first hub would be a “pilot project”, set to host a few hundred people deported from the five EU countries, starting in spring or summer 2027.

It would consist of open facilities housing migrants, who would receive a residence permit and be free to move around the country, with the aim of integrating them into local society and the labour market.

In principle, return hubs are temporary accommodation for migrants awaiting deportation to their countries of origin. However, there is no time limit on stays, and those involved could end up stranded in Rwanda and never be sent home.

The EU border agency Frontex could also be involved in deportations to Rwanda once the European Parliament and member states approve a reform of its mandate, recently proposed by the European Commission.

Rwanda's return hub may face legal challenges

Return hubs have raised concerns in Europe over their compatibility with EU law and the protection of human rights. Critics warn they could lead to violations, particularly when established in countries with limited democratic standards.

The law enabling EU states to set up return hubs outside the bloc establishes that only non-EU countries — “where international human rights standards and principles in accordance with international law are respected” — are eligible.

According to the UN, Rwanda has a questionable track record of respect for human rights.

A similar agreement between Kigali and the United Kingdom, under which Britain would send asylum seekers to Rwanda, was ruled unlawful by the UK Supreme Court in 2023 because of the risk of human rights abuses.

The five governments said the project would comply fully with EU law and international obligations, and would be run in partnership with international organisations such as the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

However, UNHCR and IOM are not directly involved in the negotiations on the procedures and could pull out if certain conditions are not met.

“IOM’s support requires a formal request from the receiving government, and assurances that adequate safeguards are in place,” a spokesperson for the organization told Euronews.

Legal complications may arise when deportations to Rwanda begin next year, as the European Court of Human Rights prohibits countries from transferring individuals to states or situations where they may face violations of fundamental rights.

“With this system, migrants may be subjected to torture and inhuman or degrading treatment,” Eleonora Celoria from Asgi, an Italian association of legal experts specialized in migration, told Euronews.

Costs are unclear

The five EU countries will bear the entire financial burden of the deportations and of accommodation in Rwanda.

There are no current estimates of the total costs, and it is unclear what Kigali will get in return. In 2025, the Rwandan government signed an agreement to accept third-country nationals expelled from the US in exchange for roughly $7.5 million in financial support.

A similar project set up by Italy in Albania sparked controversy over its costs, with a total bill of €670 million over a five-year partnership. According to a study from an Italian university, detaining migrants in these centres is much more expensive for Italy than hosting them on its own territory.

Each available place in Albania costs over €153,000, whereas comparable facilities in Sicily could accommodate migrants for approximately €21,000 per place.

More EU countries may join Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece in deporting irregular migrants to unrelated countries in the future.

Nineteen of the EU’s 27 governments are convinced this is an “innovative solution” for migration management, as a joint letter sent to EU leaders last June made clear.

text:
Citizen journalist Richard Parias was shot by US immigration agents and has been medically neglected in a Los Angeles-area immigration detention centre, where four people have died in the last year alone. Immigration authorities refuse to release him. Sign the petition demanding his immediate release, urgent medical care and protection of his right to freedom of expression.

Carlitos Ricardo Parias, also known as Richard, is a citizen journalist who reports on issues impacting his community in Los Angeles, California. In October 2025, masked immigration agents shot and injured Richard while attempting to arrest him outside his home for immigration purposes. While in hospital he was subsequently charged with assault against a federal agent and taken into US Marshals custody, despite needing ongoing medical care.

A federal judge ultimately dismissed the assault charge against Richard on the grounds that the government failed to uphold Richard’s right to a fair trial. However, while in the custody of the US Marshals, he was transferred into ICE custody where he remains unlawfully and arbitrarily detained – raising concerns that he was targeted for his work as a citizen journalist who is also an immigrant.

Richard continues to suffer severe pain and swelling from his gunshot wound. His lawyers say he has not received adequate medical care, and his family fears he could suffer lasting damage or worse.

Richard is a father of two who loves spending time with his family, whether going for walks or simply watching television together. Instead, Richard has spent a year separated from them. He should be free and receiving urgent medical treatment.

Your action will help increase international pressure on the US authorities to release Richard and ensure his rights are respected.
