title: Hero, villain or victim: why are refugees so rarely seen now as fully human? | Zoe Williams
description:
There was a screening last week of Seize the Summit, which follows four refugees as they try to reach the top of Kilimanjaro.
It was organised by a recent MA graduate from Goldsmiths, with a panel afterwards, which I was set to chair.
So the refugee in the mainstream imagination toggles between hero, villain or victim – except it’s not quite that simple.
Seize the Summit follows Shaqayeq (from Afghanistan), Adnan and Safa (both from Syria) and Tania (from Ukraine).
Safa doesn’t make it to the top of Kilimanjaro: she was the victim of horrific burns injuries that have compromised her breathing.
text:
There was a screening last week of Seize the Summit, which follows four refugees as they try to reach the top of Kilimanjaro. It was organised by a recent MA graduate from Goldsmiths, with a panel afterwards, which I was set to chair. So she and I were spitballing what the film-maker, Arwa Damon, would want to talk about, and Hanya, the graduate, said: “I think her purpose is to mainstream the idea of the refugee as a human being.” It was such a stark statement that we both started laughing.

There are many categories of refugee in current affairs storytelling. There’s the desperate victim; the criminal, or criminal-waiting-to-happen; the hero, battling unimaginable odds, though this tends to be a retrospective narrative, ie second-generation members of a diaspora talking about their parents. There are refugees en masse, shorn of any traits or qualities at all, discussed purely in terms of whether or not the host state can accommodate them, and how long they should be allowed to stay in any given place.

But the refugee as a complex human, a mixture of strength and trauma, motivated variously by wanting to build a new life and return to what was theirs – this is a story I don’t feel I’ve heard much recently. Very few talk a lot about refugees as individuals, with personalities – and yet at the same time, the universalism of the experience, the fact of the status forced upon you and never chosen, is also etched away, or simply ignored.

So the refugee in the mainstream imagination toggles between hero, villain or victim – except it’s not quite that simple. People find it slightly harder to frame the child refugee as anything other than a victim – so instead, the status of “child” is endlessly contested, the tabloids popping up intermittently on a slow news day with rumours of 36-year-olds pretending to be teenagers.

The male refugee, meanwhile, is being steadily erased altogether, as an idea. If you were to get your discussion points from GB News, you would think there was no such thing as a man displaced by war, or hunted down by an authoritarian regime – there are only “fighting age men”, who should be at home, fighting; or predatory men, who arrive here via Europe in order to commit crimes under the cover of their “different culture”. A male refugee can be angry, but only as part of his antisocial, problematic persona, never legitimately. A female refugee can’t be angry at all, even if her home has been destroyed and her children have been killed. She can only be sad.

Seize the Summit follows Shaqayeq (from Afghanistan), Adnan and Safa (both from Syria) and Tania (from Ukraine). Damon said afterwards that the film wasn’t about war and displacement, it was about nature and recovery; but the thing that struck me most forcefully about it was how enragingly life-changing an injury can be. Safa doesn’t make it to the top of Kilimanjaro: she was the victim of horrific burns injuries that have compromised her breathing. Adnan was shot by a sniper and lost the use of his body from his chest down. He doesn’t make it to the top, either; his hero’s journey isn’t really about the mountain, it’s more about his struggle to accept help. He has spent the decade since his injury at age 14 trying to build a life in which he doesn’t need anything, and yet he won’t see any part of a mountain again unless others carry him up it, and his realisation of that is almost unbearably poignant to watch.

Ronan Toal, a human rights barrister speaking on the panel afterwards, said in passing that the Somali word for claiming asylum was “surrender”. That’s another notion that gets lost when the refugee isn’t described as fully human: how exquisitely painful it is to throw oneself on the mercy of anyone; how painful any of us would find it.

If, as a refugee, you’re not allowed a personality, it must be quite hard to feel like a whole, legitimate person in the new society where you’re forced to build a life, right? Yeah, pretty hard, Hanya agreed, being from Gaza. “The one thing you’re definitely not allowed as a refugee,” she said, “is a sense of humour.”

Seize the Summit doesn’t gild the experience of war – it is definitely not fun. Yet the mountaineers spend a lot of time laughing, which is not a heroic, strength-in-the-face-of-adversity story. It’s a human being story.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

On Tuesday 1 December, join Zoe Williams, Lucy Mangan, Jonathan Liew, Heather Stewart, Pippa Crerar, John Crace and host, multi-award-winning comedian Suzi Ruffell, for an evening of candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as we look back on the year-defining stories of 2026.

text:
Muneer Ahmad delivered his inaugural lecture as Sol Goldman Clinical Professor of Law to an audience of his peers, colleagues, friends, and family on Oct. 26.

Cristina Rodríguez ’00, the Sol and Lillian Goldman Dean of Yale Law School, introduced Ahmad and spoke about the trajectory of his career as a lawyer, clinician, and scholar.

“Even before I met you as a person, I knew you by reputation as an innovative and brave young lawyer and clinician in Washington, D.C.,” Rodríguez said, highlighting Ahmad’s representation of Omar Khadr, who had been detained at Guantanamo Bay for 10 years beginning at the age of 15. “At the very outset of his career, Muneer was, much as he is now, a serious, thoughtful, and kind person with an unwavering commitment to justice under law.”

Rodríguez also praised the impact of Ahmad’s work representing immigrants, workers, and other individuals and groups that have been marginalized. “Those on the margins have always been at the center of Muneer’s ambitions and focus,” Rodríguez said. “Muneer has lawyered under the most challenging of circumstances — under political pressure, time pressure, with lives and families at stake. We all stand to learn from his example and his thought.”

Ahmad’s lecture, titled “Lawyering as Accompaniment,” outlined the concept of accompaniment and its applications for practicing law and being in relationship with clients and social movements.

Accompaniment, Ahmad said, is “an alignment with, and commitment to, close personal relationships with poor people, with a goal of systemic change.” He identified and explored four elements of accompaniment: relational intimacy, structural intervention, longitudinal collaboration, and personal transformation.

Ahmad spoke about how this concept has informed the questions that have guided his career: “How can lawyers work most effectively to combat poverty and marginalization? What is the relationship between lawyers and social change movements? And how should we prepare our students to work on behalf of poor and marginalized people?”

Ahmad’s lecture examined how accompaniment has shaped his lawyering and teaching in the face of recent, violent immigration enforcement in the U.S. as well as the longer arc of his career.

“The history of subordination of immigrants sits within a broader marginalization of poor people that is persistent and complex,” he said. “So, while there is an urgency to the work in the current moment, there has been urgency all along.”

Watch the full lecture(link is external)4

Ahmad traced the origins of accompaniment in Catholic social thought through its development into a practice deployed by immigrants’ rights advocates starting in the first Trump administration.

This form of accompaniment, “a means for lay people to support vulnerable immigrants while helping to stop deportations” by personally escorting them to court and appointments with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), serves as a useful prototype for accompaniment in lawyering, he said.

Ahmad shared how he and his students in Yale Law School’s Worker and Immigrant Rights Advocacy Clinic (WIRAC) have applied principles of accompaniment to their work with a recent client, Renso Lino-Ramos, who had been subjected to long-term detention without the opportunity for bond despite having a viable defense against his deportation.

The success of the team’s representation of Lino-Ramos came not only by applying their legal expertise, but by building relationships with his family and establishing sustained physical presence with him while his case worked its way through the court. This approach deepened the team’s understanding of Lino-Ramos’s goals and ambitions, shaped their case theory, and helped to sustain the client’s hope in the face of overwhelming pressure for him to drop his case and accept deportation and permanent separation from his family.

Following this collaborative model of lawyering, the student team successfully litigated Lino-Ramos’s case in habeas corpus proceedings in federal court in Boston. The court ultimately ordered Lino-Ramos released from immigration detention, reuniting with his family after spending two years in detention.

Accompaniment’s focus on human dignity, Ahmad argued, honors the lived experience of the client, informs litigation strategy, and alters both legal and cultural narratives of immigration. And while not every case has a successful outcome — the team has not been able to prevent every client’s deportation — the pastoral aspect of accompaniment has still been valuable, he said.

Ahmad also spoke about accompaniment and its impact on WIRAC’s collaborations with community partners and membership-based organizations, noting how this cooperation enables lawyers to work on both short-term, individual cases and long-term campaigns that support broader legal, cultural, and political change. “While accompaniment centers relational intimacy,” Ahmad said, “it aspires to systemic change.”

Each individual accompaniment holds the potential for personal transformation of the accompanist and the accompanied alike.” —Professor Muneer I. Ahmad

He discussed WIRAC’s work with Hartford Deportation Defense on behalf of a client seeking asylum who had been detained by ICE in a raid on a local car wash, as well as the clinic’s longtime work in defense of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA), including its successful litigation at the Supreme Court. Ahmad highlighted the longitudinal nature of WIRAC’s collaborations with Connecticut Students for a Dream, an organization that advocates for immigrant youth and immigrants’ rights in the state, the national immigrant youth organization United We Dream, and the membership-based organization Make the Road New York.

Ahmad concluded the lecture by emphasizing the transformative potential of accompaniment and exploring its implications for lawyering models, legal mobilization in opposition to extraordinary state violence, and the development of equitable immigration law and policy.

“By creating conditions for deep connection with others, accompaniment enables new understandings of the self and reconceptualized personal and political commitments. Thus, each individual accompaniment holds the potential for personal transformation of the accompanist and the accompanied alike.”

Ahmad joined the Yale Law School faculty in 2009 as a clinical professor of law and was appointed(link is external)5 Sol Goldman Clinical Professor of Law in 2019. He co-directs the Worker and Immigrant Rights Advocacy Clinic6 (WIRAC), in which he and his students represent individuals, groups, and organizations in both litigation and non-litigation matters related to immigration, immigrants’ rights, and labor. His scholarship examines the intersections of immigration, race, and citizenship in both legal theory and legal practice.

Prior to Yale Law School, Ahmad was a professor of law at American University Washington College of Law and a Skadden Fellow and staff attorney at the Asian Pacific American Legal Center in Los Angeles.

Trump Administration also delivers 18 straight months of zero releases at the border

WASHINGTON — Today, the United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) announced that CBP’s October encounters reached the lowest level ever recorded to start a fiscal year. Additionally, October marked the 18th consecutive month of zero releases at the border.

“President Trump unleashed the full strength of DHS to secure the border and enforce the law,” said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “The results speak for themselves. In Fiscal Year 2026, our officers and agents drove illegal crossings to historic lows. DHS carried that momentum into October, when CBP saw its fewest nationwide encounters ever to open a fiscal year. Under President Trump’s leadership, we will continue to deliver the most secure border in American history and save American lives.”

The sustained decline in illegal border crossings and apprehensions—at levels not seen in over three decades—shows the profound impact of robust enforcement policies. With daily Border Patrol apprehensions along the southwest border down 95% over the past year compared with the previous administration, the border remains more secure than at any point in history.

“Under the leadership of President Trump and Secretary Mullin, CBP has been empowered to enforce the law, giving us an unprecedented level of control over our borders,” said CBP Commissioner Rodney S. Scott. “We know more about who and what is entering our homeland than at any time in our nation’s history. America is safer because we are enforcing the rule of law, keeping threats out of our communities, and putting the security of the American people first.”

Below is a snapshot of October’s key figures. Full monthly reporting can be viewed on CBP’s Stats and Summaries webpage.

Border Enforcement at Historic Levels

Illegal crossings remain historically low:

CBP’s nationwide encounters in October were the lowest ever to start a fiscal year

Additionally, CBP’s nationwide encounters in October (27,890) were 7% lower than September, and the lowest for a month since February.

U.S. Border Patrol apprehensions decreased in October

The U.S. Border Patrol’s apprehensions along the southwest border in October (8,288) were 7% lower than September.

Southwest border apprehensions in October were 95% lower than under Biden

The U.S. Border Patrol’s apprehensions along the southwest border in October (8,288) were 95% lower than the monthly average of the Biden administration; 97% below the peak of the Biden administration (December 2023); and less than the number of apprehensions recorded in just 5 days.

Drug Interdictions That Save Lives

CBP remains on the frontline against drug smuggling, seizing dangerous narcotics before they reach American communities.

Nationwide in October, seizures of cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, fentanyl, and marijuana (combined, by weight) increased 44% from September 2026. Total drug seizures in October 2026 (combined, by weight) increased 13% from October 2024 during the Biden administration.

Individual drugs compared to September 2026:

Marijuana seizures increased 29% in October (14,748 pounds seized in October 2026).

Methamphetamine seizures increased 59% in October (14,745 pounds seized in October 2026).

Cocaine seizures increased 60% in October (9,032 pounds seized in October 2026).

Heroin seizures increased 95% in October (246 pounds seized in October 2026).

Trade and Tariff Enforcement

CBP plays a central role in enforcing U.S. trade law and supporting economic security.

$391 billion in imports processed in October 2026.

$26 billion in duties identified for collection in October 2026.

Agriculture Stats/Seizures – Securing American Agriculture

In October, CBP agriculture specialists helped protect America’s agriculture, natural resources, and economic prosperity.

CBP issued 6,020 emergency action notifications for restricted and prohibited plant and animal products.

CBP conducted 96,315 positive passenger inspections and issued 551 civil penalties and/or violations to the traveling public for failing to declare prohibited agriculture items.

text:
HOUSTON, TEXAS— The State of Texas last week filed a Notice of Nonsuit, dismissing its action seeking to terminate the corporate charter of FIEL Houston, Inc., an organization that advocates for and serves immigrant families and students across Texas.

The State’s Notice of Nonsuit, filed last Monday in the 127th Judicial District Court in Harris County, Texas, voluntarily dismisses all claims brought against FIEL with prejudice, meaning the State cannot bring the same claims against the organization again.

MALDEF (Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund) and Carlos R. Soltero, an Austin-based attorney and member of MALDEF’s board of directors, represented FIEL in the litigation.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton filed the lawsuit in July 2024, alleging that FIEL violated rules governing tax-exempt nonprofits through its public statements and advocacy on immigration policies. In August 2024, MALDEF filed court papers opposing the State’s effort to terminate FIEL’s corporate charter. MALDEF argued that Paxton lacked the authority to challenge FIEL’s federal tax-exempt status and that the lawsuit was retaliation for the organization’s advocacy on behalf of immigrants.

FIEL, short for Familias Inmigrantes y Estudiantes en la Lucha, has worked with immigrant families and students in the greater Houston area since 2007, providing community education, disaster relief assistance, higher education resources, and information about individuals’ rights.

MALDEF remains committed to defending the constitutional rights of immigrant-serving nonprofit organizations and the communities they help.

Please attribute the following statement to MALDEF President and General Counsel, Thomas A. Saenz:

“The nonsuit notice brings an early end to one of Paxton’s many shady litigation tactics; this case epitomized Paxton’s overt politicization of his office. Targeting immigrant-serving organizations was biased, improper, and cruel, demonstrating an overarching interest in serving Paxton’s political masters rather than the Texas public.”

Please attribute the following statement to attorney Carlos R. Soltero, Maynard Nexsen, PC:

“As Ken Paxton’s time holding the office and title of Attorney General of Texas comes to an end, his case against FIEL—which should never have been brought and was a waste of taxpayer resources—was dismissed by his office without the courtesy of advance notice or any discussion. This unilateral action ending this case is telling. No prior attorney general had tried to wield the quo warranto power to target nonprofits for political and other legally unwarranted reasons in this manner—not Attorney General Abbott, Cornyn, Mattox, Morales nor any other of his predecessors. It is a relief that FIEL and other nonprofits seeking to help our communities, including immigrants in our communities, can do so without having to respond to the unjustified wielding of the legal power of the state in this manner.”

title: Mayor-elect plans audit of police immigration data sharing - Digital Watch Observatory
description:
Los Angeles mayor-elect Nithya Raman has outlined plans to audit the Los Angeles Police Department’s (LAPD) compliance with restrictions on immigration related data sharing and to review police surveillance practices in the United States of America.
Although the LAPD maintains that it does not participate in civil immigration enforcement, it continues to cooperate with federal authorities on criminal investigations.
Digital Watch has also reported on ICE’s efforts to expand its use of these cameras in immigration enforcement.
Any removal would involve the Board of Police Commissioners or the City Council, as provided by the Los Angeles City Charter.
The proposed audit raises questions about how effectively local restrictions on immigration related data sharing operate across interconnected police databases and surveillance systems.
text:
Los Angeles mayor-elect Nithya Raman has outlined plans to audit the Los Angeles Police Department’s (LAPD) compliance with restrictions on immigration related data sharing and to review police surveillance practices in the United States of America. In a pre-electioninterview, Raman said she would examine the department’s data sharing practices to ensure that information was not being disclosed to United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The proposals were subsequently discussed as part of her incoming administration’s policing priorities.

The proposed audit would examine compliance with Los Angeles’s 2024 sanctuary-city ordinance, which restricts the use of city personnel, resources, property, and data to support federal immigration enforcement. The ordinance builds on the LAPD’s Special Order 40, adopted in 1979, which prohibits officers from initiating police action solely to determine an individual’s immigration status. The 2024 ordinance establishes broader restrictions affecting city agencies and the disclosure of information that could reveal an individual’s immigration status.

Although the LAPD maintains that it does not participate in civil immigration enforcement, it continues to cooperate with federal authorities on criminal investigations. The proposed audit could therefore examine how existing restrictions operate when information is exchanged between local and federal law enforcement agencies, including whether data collected for criminal investigations could subsequently be used for immigration enforcement.

Raman has also indicated that she intends to review the department’s surveillance practices. The debate includes automated licence plate recognition systems, such as those supplied by Flock Safety, and body-worn cameras supplied by Axon. As previously reported by Digital Watch, Los Angeles has faced scrutiny over its use of licence plate recognition technologies, while several US cities have terminated contracts with Flock Safety amid concerns about privacy and potential data sharing. The LAPD reportedly suspended its use of Flock cameras in July 2026, and Raman subsequently called for the city to end its relationship with the company.

The use of body-worn cameras raises related but distinct questions about the collection and management of audiovisual records. Digital Watch has also reported on ICE’s efforts to expand its use of these cameras in immigration enforcement. Although the federal programme is separate from the LAPD’s operations, both developments highlight questions about access to recorded information, retention periods, and safeguards governing its disclosure to other agencies.

The proposals also come amid discussions about the department’s leadership. Raman has expressed her intention to replace LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell, although the mayor cannot unilaterally dismiss the police chief. Any removal would involve the Board of Police Commissioners or the City Council, as provided by the Los Angeles City Charter.

Why does it matter?

The proposed audit raises questions about how effectively local restrictions on immigration related data sharing operate across interconnected police databases and surveillance systems. Information collected through licence plate recognition cameras and other technologies may not explicitly identify immigration status, but can potentially be combined with other records to identify individuals, reconstruct their movements, or support enforcement activities.

This distinction is particularly relevant to Los Angeles’s sanctuary-city protections, which extend beyond information explicitly identifying immigration status. The Los Angeles Administrative Code includes restrictions concerning information that could be used, independently or in combination with other data, to identify or trace a person’s immigration status. Assessing compliance therefore requires examining not only whether police directly disclose immigration information, but also how other categories of personal data are accessed and shared.

The review could also provide an opportunity to assess the accountability mechanisms governing commercial surveillance technologies. Restrictions established through legislation or departmental policies may depend on technical access controls, contractual obligations, retention periods, audit logs, and safeguards against onward disclosure. Where multiple agencies use interconnected platforms, determining who can access information and for what purposes becomes particularly important.

text:
In The Know is your daily briefing on Oklahoma policy-related news. OK Policy encourages the support of Oklahoma’s state and local media, which are vital to an informed citizenry. Inclusion of a story does not necessarily mean endorsement by the Oklahoma Policy Institute. Some stories included here are behind paywall or require subscription. Subscribe to In The Know and see past editions.

Oklahoma News

ICE detainees report exposure to chemicals twice in one week at Watonga: Dozens of people detained while awaiting immigration court dates at the Diamondback Correctional Facility reported exposure to chemical agents twice in one week, resulting in respiratory reactions, fainting and at least one person being taken to a nearby hospital in Watonga. [The Oklahoman]

Protestors against ICE gathered at Oklahoma Department of Corrections (video): [The Oklahoman]

From OK Policy: Corporations in the prison industry exploit communities and cause lasting harm for short-term profit

State Government News

Lawmakers fight regulatory approval of Google data center power plan: A trio of Oklahoma lawmakers known for repeatedly challenging utility rate cases have filed a new lawsuit, this time questioning the approval of an agreement between OG&E and a Google subsidiary to provide electric power to three new data centers. [The Oklahoman]

Amid water supply concerns, new law allows OWRB to tighten usage regulations: As Oklahoma’s water supply faces pressure from increased groundwater use, state regulators are working to track aquifer depletion better and, for the first time, issue violation notices for unreported groundwater use. [NonDoc]

‘Very small law’ may have big impact on foster children: Sen. Chuck Hall and Rep. John Kane have helped to shape major legislation and multibillion-dollar state budgets, but both turned out on the front steps of the Capitol on Thursday to publicly celebrate a “very small law” that they hope will make a big difference in the lives of vulnerable, often overlooked foster children. [Tulsa World]

Oklahoma airports break ground on $24.2M in terminal upgrades: More than $24.2 million in terminal upgrades broke ground this fall at three Oklahoma regional airports as state leaders put money toward modernizing decades-old aviation infrastructure. [The Journal Record]

Political notebook: “Just be nice to people,” Stitt advises Trump: Gov. Kevin Stitt continues to show up in national media as his second term winds down. Most recently, he was interviewed by Politco and offered some advice to President Donald Trump. “President Trump’s policies are amazing, and he does a really good job on a lot of fronts, but … just trying to be nice to people, I think would go a long way.” Some who’ve gotten crosswise with Stitt might raise an eyebrow at that advice, but his year as chairman of the National Governors Association does seem to have softened Stitt’s tone, especially on the national stage. Court Strikes Bill Restricting Initiative Petitions [Oklahoma Watch]

From OK Policy: Oklahoma Supreme Court strikes down SB 1027 that would have excluded millions from initiative petition process

But before he even takes office, T.W. Shannon seems focused on doing the opposite of what his new role entails. The Republican is sharing bigoted and divisive tropes, picking fights with Democrats who lost and attempting to deliver zingers to out–of–state political foes like he’s the head of a dance squad in “Bring It On.” [Janelle Stecklein / Oklahoma Voice]

Almost 50,000 Oklahoma children have lost food assistance after the Big Beautiful Bill [KOSU]

Leaders of the proposed Sooner State Party announced in March that they had fallen just 410 signatures short of the nearly 34,200 needed to become a recognized political party. [Oklahoma Voice]

OU-Tulsa satisfied with TCC relationship, leader says [Tulsa World]

OU-Tulsa leadership: ‘We’re excited to work with TCC’ [Public Radio Tulsa]

Contagious flu cases rise in Oklahoma before Thanksgiving holiday: With holidays approaching, you’ll probably want to avoid spreading a contagious virus to your close family members if possible. Flu cases in Oklahoma are rising above the historical average with two weeks left before the Thanksgiving holiday. [The Oklahoman]

OU diabetes center director brings new research, vision to Oklahoma: A recently published study led by John Kirwan, the new executive director of the University of Oklahoma Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center, identified a protein that may contribute to insulin resistance. Kirwan said the protein, known as Miro1, could be a target for future treatments to help the body regulate blood sugar. [KGOU]

These challenges can be directly reflected in Oklahoma’s health outcomes, especially in counties designated as shortage areas, in communities where recruitment is difficult, and in families that need consistent, physician-led care that is accessible, reliable and relatable. [Dr. Mousumi Som / Tulsa World]

The update by three court-appointed consultants in what is known as the Briggs case says that while the state has made some halting progress in complying with a 2025 consent decree, the wait list for court-ordered competency restoration services is nearly as long as it was two years ago and the services themselves appear just as ineffective. [Tulsa World]

‘Heartbreaking’: Days after election, Pittsburg County Sheriff Frankie McClendon dies: Pittsburg County Sheriff Frankie McClendon died Friday, less than two weeks after he won an election with 60 percent support. He was 60 years old. McClendon spent 37 years in law enforcement, primarily with the McAlester Police Department and then the sheriff’s office. The Pittsburg County Board of Commissioners will have to name an acting sheriff. [NonDoc]

An Oklahoma sheriff says deputy pay is ‘ridiculous.’ Here’s why: Pottawatomie County Sheriff Freeland Wood said his agency ranks among the lowest in pay for the state’s county law enforcement agencies. In a lengthy statement on social media Thursday, Nov. 12, Wood called the pay “unacceptable” and “ridiculous,” admitting that lower salaries make it difficult to retain staff and provide coverage for 653 square miles of unincorporated territory. [The Oklahoman]

5 things to know about death row in Oklahoma after execution last week: James Dwight Pavatt, 73, was executed Thursday at the Oklahoma State Penitentiary. His former girlfriend, 62-year-old Brenda Andrew, is still appealing her murder conviction and remains the only woman on death row in Oklahoma. [Tulsa World]

Prosecutors want more prison time for Sara Polston in drunk-driving case: Prosecutors are asking a judge to order Sara Polston to serve all 15 years of her punishment in prison for a near-fatal drunken driving car crash in 2023. On Nov. 13, Cleveland County District Attorney Jennifer Austin asked the judge to revoke her probation in full because she voted in two statewide elections. [The Oklahoman]

Opinion: Photo shoot at Oklahoma prison gives women back their identity: Photos are a powerful object in prison. They are a way to remember that we were once young. They are tangible proof for friends and family that we exist, but also that we have changed. Photos are framed, hung on walls in cells or secured to refrigerators in kitchens. Loved ones carry them in purses or wallets, and forward them on to distant relatives. Our images hold cherished places in households where our physical bodies cannot travel. [Crystal Avilla / The Oklahoman]

State Farm To Pay $45 Million After Oklahoma Insurance Investigation: State Farm Fire and Casualty Co. will pay a $45 million settlement after a state insurance department investigation found it failed to properly pay roof damage claims by Oklahoma customers. The state’s incoming insurance commissioner, Republican Bob Sullivan, said he was still learning details on Friday but worried the settlement may take some flexibility out of any regulatory approach to State Farm under his administration. Trump Administration Rule Would Take SNAP Away From Millions More Working Families, Seniors, and People With Disabilities: The people who would lose help affording groceries are primarily working families with kids as well as seniors and people with disabilities. text:
Good morning, Helena! In this issue, we look into why city leaders accepted federal funding for security enhancements and why it was controversial. Additionally, the owner of the Lion Building is seeking small-business owners to fill the downtown location, and Blackfoot Brewing Company and other partners will host a celebration of public lands.

But first, a weather preview ☀️

The week starts off a little warmer than usual, with a high around 50 degrees Monday during the day and a slight chance of rain and a low of 32 degrees at night, according to National Weather Service meteorologist Austin McDowell. Tuesday’s high will be in the upper 30s with a chance of rain and snow. Wednesday’s high will be in the upper 30s, also with a chance of snow. Overnight lows will linger in the mid-20s.

The whys and why nots of the DHS grant

After hours of public input and their own deliberations, the Helena City Commission voted last Monday to accept a grant of about $53,300 from the Department of Homeland Security.

The DHS award was coupled with two other federal grants that will support an existing Helena Police Department detective and replace some emergency equipment. The three grants combined total about $258,000 and garnered over two hours of public comments, mostly from those who pleaded with city leaders to reject the money or find alternatives.

The main argument from residents and some commissioners concerned the grant agreement, which many said left unclear what conditions the city would be held to if it accepted the federal money, including fears of local involvement in federal immigration operations.

In the end, Helena Mayor Emily Dean and commissioners Sean Logan and Ben Rigby voted to accept the grants; commissioners Julia Gustafson and Melinda Reed were opposed.

For Dean, accepting federal money to improve Helena’s law enforcement efforts demonstrates fiscal responsibility.

“I also want to address the implication that supporting these grants somehow reflects a lack of concern for Helena and our residents,” Dean said in her closing remarks Monday night. “Nothing could be further from the truth.”

Dean said that it’s the commission’s job to evaluate facts while keeping in mind the financial and legal impacts that will have long-term effects in Helena, and to lean heavily on the city attorney’s guidance that accepting the grants wouldn’t mean entering into any federal agreements with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“By accepting these grants, there will be no change in how the city of Helena or the HPD operate,” Dean added. “As noted in our city attorney’s legal analysis, the language questioned in our last meeting is negated and do not impact the current city policies.”

Commissioner Logan agreed that accepting the money was the responsible course of action for the city.

“The truth is, and the responsible path forward is, that we need to accept this funding,” Logan said. “…We simply don’t have the resources to otherwise fund these activities that are proposed in the grants, and without them, the work doesn’t get done, and the public safety services aren’t provided.”

Reed was not convinced by the city attorney’s report, adding that the analysis of the agreement doesn’t answer key questions about whether accepting the grants requires the city to comply with federal immigration law.

“We’ve heard it multiple times, and I’ve seen it with my own eyes, multiple attorneys have multiple interpretations of what this contract means, and that is deeply problematic,” Reed said. “We have given no assurances to this community, and for that, I am sorry; you deserve better.”

Reed proposed an amendment to accept the grants on the condition that a portion of the contract language be stricken.

City Attorney Rebecca Dockter responded that DHS does not enforce the grant requirements. That’s handled by the Montana Department of Disaster and Emergency Services, which she said doesn’t require the city to agree to comply with federal immigration requirements. Additionally, she said the city can’t strike any provisions of the grant agreement.

“While they’re called grant agreements, because we sign on the dotted line, they aren’t an agreement that you can negotiate between two parties,” Dockter said. “You either take the language and the monies, and then you take the conditions, or you don’t take the money, and you don’t take the conditions.”

Reed’s proposal failed on a 3-2 vote, and the commissioner was not pleased.

“It has become clear to me that the majority of the members of this commission are comfortable with cooperation with ICE on immigration enforcement,” she said. “To accept any other explanation is a false narrative.”

Public Notice 🧐City chamber of commerce changes location

ℹ️ The Helena Area Chamber of Commerce last week moved from its location off of Sixth Avenue. But the agency didn’t move too far and is still located in the downtown area at 27 Neill Ave. The chamber’s Facebook page posted a video showing workers putting up its sign at the new spot.

“While our address may have changed, our mission remains the same: connecting businesses, developing leaders, strengthening partnerships, and creating opportunities for our community to thrive,” the post states.

Holter gets money for new roof

ℹ️ The Holter Museum of Art announced last week that it was awarded a $315,000 grant from the Montana Department of Commerce to replace the museum’s roof. In addition to the grant, Holter raised $150,000 for the work from more than 180 donors.

text:
The Briefing:

A federal judge in Boston is scheduled to hear arguments November 20 on whether to impose a longer statutory freeze on a DHS rule that cut refugees' deadline to contest status termination from 30 days to 10 — a two-thirds reduction enacted overnight on October 14 without public comment.

That same day, a 14-day Ninth Circuit administrative stay shielding an estimated 600,000 Venezuelan TPS holders — which began running November 6 — is set to expire, leaving protections in limbo without further court action.

Neither proceeding guarantees a favorable outcome: the Boston court has not ruled on the refugee rule's legality, and the Ninth Circuit has not committed to extending the Venezuelan TPS pause.

A Rule That Gave Refugees Almost No Time to Fight Back

On the morning of October 14, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security published an interim final rule in the Federal Register — effective immediately — compressing the window for refugees to respond to a Notice of Intent to Terminate their status from 30 calendar days to just 10. The change, documented at 91 FR 65077, applied to refugees who arrived under CHNV-related programs in the last decade and have not yet secured permanent resident status. For Venezuelans, Cubans, Nicaraguans, and Colombians in that category, it meant that upon receiving a government termination notice, they would now have roughly one working week — including weekends — to hire an attorney, compile documents, and file a formal legal defense.

DHS bypassed the standard notice-and-comment process by invoking the Administrative Procedure Act's "good cause" exception, arguing that advance warning would allow individuals it claimed were improperly admitted to evade termination proceedings. The rule retained existing grounds for termination and preserved the right to submit evidence or request a USCIS interview — but collapsed the timeline in which all of that must occur. Immigration legal aid providers have long argued that even the previous 30-day window was insufficient given language barriers, limited access to counsel, and the procedural complexity of refugee status cases. The original deadline had remained unchanged for 45 years.

Lawsuit Filed Within Days, Court Steps In

Twelve days after the rule took effect, a coalition of refugee advocacy groups — including the Partnership for the Advancement of New Americans, HIAS, African Communities Together, the International Institute of New England, Jewish Family Service of Western Massachusetts, and Refugee Council USA — filed a class action challenge in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts. The coalition argued that DHS had no legitimate "good cause" to skip public comment, that the compressed deadline violated due process, and that refugees currently caught mid-process deserved protection from retroactive enforcement.

A federal judge granted an emergency administrative stay on October 27, initially blocking the rule through November 6. On November 2, Judge Myong J. Joun extended that freeze through December 4, 2026, barring DHS and USCIS from issuing new 10-day termination notices and from taking action against anyone who failed to respond within 10 days to notices already issued since October 14. The court has not evaluated whether the rule itself is lawful — both orders are procedural holds, not verdicts on the merits.

What the November 20 Hearing Could Decide

The PANA et al. v. Edlow, No. 1:26-cv-14817 hearing scheduled for November 20 addresses a specific request: whether Judge Joun will impose a statutory stay under 5 U.S.C. § 705 of the APA, suspending the rule for the duration of full merits litigation rather than just through the existing December 4 deadline. Under the court's briefing schedule, the government submitted its opposition on November 13; plaintiffs' reply is due November 19; and Judge Joun is set to hear arguments in person on November 20.

The stakes are concrete. If the § 705 stay is granted, the 10-day termination rule would remain on ice well past December 4 — potentially for months — while the court examines whether DHS had legal authority to skip public notice and whether the compressed timeline violates due process rights of the affected refugee class. If the motion is denied and the court issues no further order before December 5, DHS could immediately resume issuing 10-day termination notices, placing refugees with pending cases in an abrupt race against an almost unworkable deadline.

The Venezuelan TPS Clock Runs Out the Same Day

November 20 carries a second, parallel urgency. In National TPS Alliance v. Mullin, No. 25-5724, the Ninth Circuit on November 3 granted the federal government a 14-day administrative stay beginning November 6 — the day the Supreme Court's own stay in the case expired. That pause temporarily blocked the reinstatement of Temporary Protected Status for an estimated 600,000 Venezuelan nationals while the appeals court considers the case's posture following the Supreme Court's October 5 remand order in light of Mullin v. Doe.

The 14-day clock means the administrative stay runs until approximately November 20. Without a further extension, a new order, or a merits ruling before that date, those Venezuelans lose the procedural protection the stay had provided — meaning active TPS designations would not be formally restored, leaving them without deportation protection and unable to renew work permits through that program. Court filings from both parties in the Northern District of California, submitted November 10, confirmed the November 20 expiration date; a district court case management conference is also scheduled for November 17, three days before the stay runs out.

Why These Two Deadlines Matter Together

The convergence is not a coincidence — it reflects how the administration's immigration enforcement strategy has moved simultaneously across multiple legal tracks, targeting different categories of Latino immigrants through separate regulatory and executive actions. CHNV-program parolees admitted as refugees face the 10-day termination rule; Venezuelans who registered under TPS face the ongoing fight over whether that designation was lawfully vacated. Many of the same communities — Venezuelans especially — are caught in both proceedings simultaneously.

What happens inside those two courtrooms on Thursday will not resolve either case. What it will determine is the legal footing hundreds of thousands of people stand on while the litigation plays out — whether they retain formal protections against removal, whether they can renew work authorization, and whether the government faces a durable judicial check on its ability to accelerate the pace of status terminations faster than the affected communities can mount a defense.

What to Watch After November 20

Judge Joun's ruling on the § 705 refugee stay will signal whether federal courts are prepared to impose long-term injunctive limits on the administration's refugee termination agenda or leave that fight to the full merits trial on a compressed clock. For the Venezuelan TPS track, the question is whether the Ninth Circuit extends, replaces, or simply allows its administrative stay to lapse — and what posture the court takes when it reconsiders the case under the Mullin v. Doe framework the Supreme Court directed it to apply. Both communities are watching the same Thursday with no guaranteed answer waiting for them on the other side.

text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

November 16, 2026

media@adc.org

Washington, D.C. | The American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC) filed an amicus brief before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit on November 13, challenging a ruling that could effectively allow the federal government to detain noncitizens in retaliation for their protected political speech without timely judicial intervention. The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE), PEN America, the Rutherford Institute, and the National Coalition Against Censorship (NCAC), all signed on.

Mahdawi, a Palestine-born, U.S. permanent resident and Columbia University student, co-founded the university’s Palestinian Student Union and helped organize campus protests opposing Israel’s genocide in Gaza. On April 14, 2025, federal immigration agents arrested him during an appointment to complete the process of becoming a U.S. citizen. He spent 16 days in detention before a federal judge ordered his release.

A federal district court concluded that Mahdawi had raised a substantial First Amendment retaliation claim. However, on appeal, the Second Circuit panel held that the district court lacked jurisdiction to review his challenge to the detention before the conclusion of his immigration proceedings.

The brief argues that this reasoning fundamentally misunderstands the nature of the constitutional injury. Retaliatory detention and removal proceedings violate First Amendment rights, regardless of the ultimate outcome in immigration court. By postponing judicial review until the immigration process concludes, the government is permitted to inflict constitutional and psychological harm while simultaneously sending a chilling message to millions of noncitizens that their political expression may carry devastating consequences.

“The First Amendment was intentionally framed as a restraint on government. Its plain text is unconcerned with the citizenship status of the speaker, and for good reason. The Framers understood that free speech is a human right, and that societies flourish when all those living within them may speak their minds without retribution from government,” said Jenin Younes, ADC President and Legal Director. “Non-citizens do not forfeit their freedom of expression merely because they are subject to the government’s immigration authority. As another federal court recently reaffirmed, ‘Stated plainly, in the United States, freedom of speech belongs to the people. It is not the government’s to take.'”

The brief further warns that the consequences of retaliatory immigration enforcement extend far beyond any single individual. Citing federal court findings, it points to evidence that noncitizen journalists and contributors have withdrawn articles, refused assignments, requested anonymity, and refrained from speaking publicly out of fear of immigration consequences. This chilling effect begins when individuals are targeted for their protected expression, whether through detention, investigations, or removal proceedings, not merely when deportation ultimately occurs.

“The government cannot be permitted to imprison people for exercising their First Amendment rights and then tell them they must wait months or years for a federal court to hear their challenge,” said Malak Afaneh, ADC Staff Attorney and Counsel of Record for the amici. “Mohsen Mahdawi was confined in a 7-by-12-foot solitary cell for expressing political views protected by the Constitution. No court ruling months or years later can give him back that time, undo the suppression of his speech, or erase the fear instilled in millions of noncitizens who watched what happened to him. The First Amendment means little if the government can punish people for exercising it while denying them timely access to an independent federal court.”

The brief also challenges the notion that immigration proceedings can provide an adequate substitute for independent federal judicial review. Immigration courts operate under the Department of Justice, which is part of the same executive branch responsible for enforcing immigration law. Unlike independent federal judges, immigration judges and members of the Board of Immigration Appeals operate under the authority of the Attorney General, who has the power to remove immigration judges and review their decisions.

In Mahdawi’s own case, the Board of Immigration Appeals declined to consider his constitutional arguments or the lawfulness of his detention, deferring those issues until a potential appeal from a final removal order. The immigration judge who initially terminated his removal proceedings after finding that the government had failed to establish grounds for deportation was subsequently fired by the Department of Justice.

These circumstances, the brief argues, expose a fundamental flaw in requiring noncitizens to spend months or even years fighting their deportation through immigration hearings and appeals overseen by the federal government before they can bring their constitutional claims before an independent federal judge. During that time, the same government accused of punishing individuals for their protected speech can continue pursuing their detention and removal without a federal court determining whether those actions violate the First Amendment.

As the Supreme Court has long recognized, the loss of First Amendment freedoms, even for minimal periods, constitutes irreparable injury. A ruling issued months or years after an unlawful detention cannot restore the period during which political expression was suppressed, nor can it erase the fear inflicted on others who witnessed the government’s actions.

ADC and its co-signatories urge the full Second Circuit to affirm the district court’s authority to review Mahdawi’s independent First Amendment retaliation claim and reject an interpretation of federal immigration law that would leave constitutional violations without timely judicial redress.

The brief concludes by invoking the Supreme Court’s landmark declaration in West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette:

“If there is any fixed star in our constitutional constellation, it is that no official… can prescribe what shall be orthodox in politics.”

VIENNA (AP) — A group of European countries announced on Monday that it aims to set up a “migrant hub” in Rwanda where rejected asylum-seekers could be sent from next year.

The European Union has worked for years to tighten migration rules, push down the number of asylum-seekers coming to the 27-nation bloc and increase deportations of migrants who aren’t entitled to stay. Sending people to centers outside Europe has emerged as a central plank of that effort.

Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands have spearheaded negotiations.

Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, speaking alongside officials from the other European countries and Rwanda's interior minister, said the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.

“I think this will be a game changer making us able to confront the massive challenges with illegal migration,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said of the accord the Europeans hope to finalize. “We will break down the business model of human smugglers. We will take back control of our borders and we will remove the incentives for illegal migration."

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Monday laid the blame for the nationwide grounding of all planes last week on old technology as well as his Democratic predecessor Joe Biden.

“What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,” Trump said Monday outside the White House ahead of his trip to Asia.

Trump's comments came after a rare nationwide grounding of airplanes Friday because of a router issue in the aging air traffic control system. The Republican president hadn't spoken publicly or commented on the flight grounding until Sunday, when he posted on social media blasting his Democratic predecessor and asking for more money to cover the cost of system improvements.

Trump's blame-shifting and congressional Democratic finger-pointing underscore political divisions that could widen when Democrats take control of Congress in January, with scrutiny of his administration accelerating.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who made the decision Friday to ground the planes, also pushed Congress for billions more dollars to upgrade a system he said had been neglected for decades.

Duffy said the problem began when a federal contractor was replacing a section of old copper wire with new fiber wire, causing the system to overload.

The Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement that “excessive data” was flooding the system “at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds.” That deluge created instability with “aircraft communications and radar feeds,” the agency said.

Duffy said on Sunday that billions of dollars are needed to build new architecture for the network and said companies — including AT&T, Verizon and Lumen — are ready to deploy it as soon as the money is there.

Under Trump's immediate predecessor, President Joe Biden, Congress approved a massive infrastructure bill that included $25 billion over five years for airport and air traffic control infrastructure improvements. Much of that money went to airport projects like new runways and taxiways and updated terminals.

The Trump administration said the money would provide critical updates to outdated radar systems and traffic control centers, some dating back to the 1960s. Republicans used the same bill to allocate $170 billion for Trump’s immigration crackdown, for more border security and immigration enforcement.

text:
Each week on The Newsfeed, host Paris Jackson and a team of veteran journalists dive deep into one topic and provide impactful reporting, interviews and community insights from sources you can trust. Each day this week, this post will be updated with a new story from the team.

Hundreds of WA children face immigration enforcement

By Jaelynn Grisso, story published 11/16/2026

Six-year-old Victoria went to downtown Seattle earlier this year after being called in for an immigration court hearing. Officials had marked her as an “unaccompanied minor” - despite the fact she came to the U.S. with her parents - and separated her case from her parents’ case.

Advocates working closely with families told Cascade PBS they frequently see this process of separating kids' cases from their parents and believe it’s a tactic to sow confusion.

“In the last year we've really seen an escalation in the attacks by ICE on migrant families, migrant children, migrant women," said Anna Beyette, an organizer with International Women’s Alliance. “What we've actually seen, since the start of the year, is the escalation of particularly children's courts into something that they're referring to as ‘mega master’ hearings.”

Those hearings often saw dockets with a hundred cases or more per day. Beyette says the mega master hearings have slowed since this summer, but the number of cases in a regular court day has still gone up. She estimates that dockets had about a dozen cases a day before the mega master hearings began, and now they have an average of 50 60 cases in a regular court day.

In the first half of this year, more than 300 children were arrested as part of immigration enforcement in Washington. But that is only a fraction of the kids who have ongoing cases and could be called into court. Beyette estimates the number of children with hearings this year to be over a thousand.

“It's terrifying for the children. Many of them are young,” Beyette said. “When you go in there, you see families with babies and toddlers who are there for their toddlers' appointments. And so to ask children to advocate for themselves oftentimes in like not their native language, without proper information to them about what's happening, is just really a violation of their human rights.”

Many of those arrested are between 10 and 14 years old. But some arrests are for kids much younger, including a handful that were under a year old.

As for 6-year-old Victoria, Beyette and many others successfully rallied to push for her case to be reconnected to her mom’s case. She says she sees that as a win not just for Victoria, but for every family encountering this situation.

“One thing that I really want to make very clear is that even as there are these heightened attacks on migrant families and our communities, we're seeing people fighting back,” she said. “Even as they're afraid for their families, they're fighting back because migrants always are at the forefront of fighting not just for their families, but to end a system that is forcing them from their homelands and then targeting them when they come here to the U.S.”

text:
The Justice Department’s immigration courts are moving forward with the core of a regulation making it harder for immigrants to challenge orders against them.

The Executive Office for Immigration Review on Monday released a final regulation that overhauls the Board of Immigration Appeals, giving its members broader discretion over which cases to review while swiftly dismissing others.

The rule took effect on an interim basis earlier this year, drawing complaints and litigation from immigrants’ rights advocates who said individuals were robbed of due process when the board could simply choose not to review their challenge to an immigration court order. DOJ has said the changes are necessary to address a ballooning backlog of cases on the Board of Immigration Appeals.

The final version, set to publish Tuesday in the Federal Register, makes some changes to the regulation but rejects the due process concerns.

“Importantly, the rule’s summary dismissal procedures affect only the Board’s review process, which exists only as an exercise of the Attorney General’s discretion, not as a result of any constitutional requirement,” the regulation said. “Put more directly, there is no constitutional due process right entitling an alien to an administrative appeal before the Board.”

The rule also notes that immigrants have other options for challenging orders, including litigation in federal court.

The final rule revises the interim version by standardizing the language of summary dismissal orders to clarify their impacts, and to specify that a new 10-day appeal deadline, down from 30 days, applies to practitioner discipline cases.

Donald Trump’s efforts to blame Friday’s four-hour nationwide flight stoppage – and the resulting travel chaos – on Democrats are “absurd”, an incoming Democratic member of Congress said on Sunday.

The president remained largely silent and out of public view as air travel shut down on Friday, but on Sunday he emerged to issue a series of posts blaming the incident on the Biden administration.

“The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster,” he said in one post on Truth Social. “Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began. We have the knowledge and plan for the Flight Control Systems, we need Congress to give the money, FAST! Our FAA is doing a great job, and is ready to go.”

In another post, Trump said: “If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently. It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old – RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve. The Biden Administration set it back years!”

Dan Koh, a US House representative-elect from Massachusetts and former Biden administration official, blasted the effort to cast aside blame on Sunday.

“It’s kind of revisionist history – you might as well start blaming Ronald Reagan for the FAA strike in the 80s as part of this, too,” he said on Sunday during an appearance on MS NOW’s The Weekend. “It’s absurd.”

Koh said Joe Biden secured “historic funding not only to the FAA but over a trillion dollars of infrastructure money” between Trump’s two presidencies. But, Koh added, “a lot of it … Donald Trump has reversed on the grounds of it being too woke”, invoking a term that those on the political right use to refer to things they perceive to be overly leftist.

The congressman-elect said he talks frequently with mayors and city council members in his district about “all this money that would help them with upgrades to transportation including flights” – but “they don’t even know if they’re going to get any more because the [Trump] administration has not even gotten back to them on the status.”

“This is the reality: Donald Trump likes to say it’s Biden’s fault, but it’s actually his policies that are stopping the funding from hitting the towns and cities,” Koh said.

Biden’s signature legislative achievement, the bipartisan infrastructure law, allocated $25bn to the FAA to improve air traffic control. The Republican controlled-Congress also approved $12.5bn to modernize air traffic control in July 2025, months into Trump’s second presidency.

Trump’s transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, has said the FAA needs $50bn for improvements and has blamed Democrats for the stoppage – which evidently resulted from botched maintenance work upgrading telecommunication lines from old copper wire to fiber optic cables in at least one remote location, leading to the delay or cancellation of thousands of US flights mostly on Friday and Saturday.

“The Congress was very specific in how I spend that money,” Duffy said during an interview on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday. “I have a certain allotment for radar, a certain allotment for radios, a certain allotment for building new infrastructure for centers for air traffic controllers. They didn’t give me money for telecom. They didn’t give me money for new software.

“We’re going to spend that $12.5[bn] by the end of 2028. But I need to rest of the money for software and a new telecom architecture that will be way more resilient.”

US senator Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, noted in his own interview on Sunday that Republicans had spent only a third of the $12.5bn allocated.

text:
Fewer international students are studying at US universities as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education, data released on Monday show.

Overall, US campuses saw a 9% decrease in international enrollment this fall compared with last year, according to a survey from the Institute of International Education. And the number of new students entering the United States for the first time fell by 15%.

“No one aspires to send their kids to get educated in the US,” said Veena Dubal, general counsel for the American Association of University Professors, whose father traveled from India to attend Tuskegee University, then the Tuskegee Institute, in the late 1960s on a student visa.

“It feels like an unsafe place. That’s the message that the Trump administration has been sending to families all over the world and they’re listening.”

Last year, the enrollment decreases were partially offset by large numbers of students who stayed in the US for temporary work after graduating. But after months of speculation, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposed requiring schools to pay a $70,000 fee for every student who participates in the optional practice training program.

Although the rule hasn’t been finalized, participation in the program, known as OPT for short, dropped 6% this fall, according to the survey.

The proposed rule, which is expected to face legal challenges, is part of wider DHS efforts that include terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, along with detaining and deporting many of them.

And this summer, the administration finalized a rule that will prevent international students from staying in the US for more than four years without approval from the federal government, although a judge has temporarily blocked it.

DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the changes were intended to crack down on loopholes that international students were exploiting by extending their studies.

Although the US remains the top destination for international students globally, the changes are having an effect, college leaders told the IIE.

Among more than 800 US colleges and universities surveyed this fall, 88% blamed the visa application process and 70% blamed travel restrictions for the enrollment drops. And if OPT options are limited, 95% of schools predicted that international students would probably look to another country, according to the survey, which offers an early look at trends before full data is released next year.

Politics aren’t the only reason students are looking elsewhere, said Mirka Martel, head of research, evaluation and learning for the institute. Its survey found more global competition for international students and the rising cost of a US degree also contributed.

Fanta Aw, the executive director and CEO of Nafsa, an association that represents international education, said students also are worried about research funding. Last year, the Trump administration began dismantling the federal grant-giving process and attempting to exert more political influence over what projects get funded.

“They’re saying to themselves: ‘Too much uncertainty in the United States. It’s too difficult, and you know, more importantly, we have many more choices today than we did 10 years ago. Why subject ourselves to this?’” Aw said, noting that students are going to places like China.

Nafsa, in partnership with the international education technology company JB International, found that amid the enrollment decline, international students’ contributions to the US economy dropped by $2.4bn this fall.

US colleges and universities heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue. So the drops have punched big holes in tuition revenue at some schools.

At Cleveland State University, international enrollment has dropped by 46% in two years, from 1,542 in fall 2025 to 828 this fall. And fewer than 50 new international students started this fall, said provost Nigamanth Sridhar, who estimated that the budgetary impact ranges from $2m to $4m.

Decades ago, he arrived in the US on an F1 student visa and participated in OPT. Eventually, he went through the process to become a naturalized citizen.

“I am here in this position, in this job, because I had the opportunity to come to the United States as an international graduate student and then decided to stay here and build a career,” said Sridhar, who is from India. “So international education is personal to me.”

The biggest drops were at the graduate level. This fall’s data shows a 15% drop in international graduate enrollment, compared to a 3% decrease at the undergraduate level. The report also found declines in international students from India, which sends more students to the US to study than any other country.

Sarah Spreitzer, vice-president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents, said substantial immigration bills are unlikely while Donald Trump remains president. But she said congressional oversight after Trump’s Republican party suffered big losses in the 3 November midterms might halt new policies targeted at international students.

“Those types of things could provide more certainty for our international students that there’s not just going to be these sudden or unexplainable changes,” Spreitzer said.

text:
At the end of July, the Trump administration terminated a contract with a nationwide network of legal service providers that represented thousands of unaccompanied minors in immigration court. In response, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul announced state funding to help maintain services for the roughly 1,400 New York children who were directly

affected.

The funding has allowed some organizations to continue representing children whose cases were already underway. But advocates say it has not resolved the broader problem: Children are still appearing in immigration court without lawyers, leaving some of the most vulnerable people in the immigration system to navigate complex proceedings on their own, often with little understanding of what is at stake.

New York has the third-largest unaccompanied minors caseload in the nation, with more than 9,800 cases that make up just under 10% of the state's immigration backlog, according to data through Aug. 31 analyzed by the Acacia Center for Justice, which had the federal contract that ended this summer.

The state was the first to adopt a funding measure that would support children previously served under the federal contract. The money can also support immigration-related legal services for unaccompanied minors and immigrant youth as needed, a spokesperson for Hochul's office said.

"No child should have to navigate complex immigration proceedings alone," the spokesperson said. "As New York's first mom governor, she will continue fighting to protect these children against Trump's cruel deportation agenda."

The governor's office did not directly address reports that immigrant children are still showing up in courts without legal representation.

The state's $7.25 million in funding includes $6.5 million for the Hispanic Federation, which has assembled a coalition of legal service providers, and $750,000 awarded to Prisoners' Legal Services of New York, an Albany-based firm that provides legal services to unaccompanied minors.

Kristin Brown, president and CEO of Empire Justice Center, which is part of the coalition assembled by the Hispanic Federation, said the money has enabled the organization to continue working on the 125 cases it had pending when the Acacia contract lapsed.

Brown said the group is continually assessing its capacity but is confident it will be able to continue serving the children for whom it has already signed retainers.

"I feel so incredibly grateful for New York's action because other states have not been so fortunate," she said. "In other parts of the country, there has been no funding flowing to either represent the kids or help them transition. As attorneys, we feel ethical obligations to continue to represent our clients, but a loss of funding puts organizations in a terrible, heartbreaking position."

Even as the funding has allowed some legal work to continue, Brown said there are growing concerns about the increasingly strained immigration system and shifting policies that are leaving unaccompanied children with fewer protections.

In general, Brown said there has been a significant increase in the number of children appearing in court without counsel and being asked directly by federally appointed judges about their fear of returning to their home countries.

Nationally, the Acacia Center for Justice found that more than three-fourths of completed unaccompanied children's cases that never had legal representation ended with a removal order. The Vera Institute found that as of August, at least 702,220 children are facing deportation in immigration court, more than half of whom have never had legal representation.

"A 10-year-old kid being asked questions by a judge, that's really intimidating," Brown said. "These kids may not have the presence of mind or understanding of what fear of returning to their country would be."

Brown said the process is accelerating the removal of unaccompanied minors. If a child does not express a credible fear of returning to their home country, they are often issued a removal order. If they do express fear, they are given an asylum application, often in English, that they must fill out themselves.

As the removal process moves more quickly, children also face greater limitations on the types of legal support available to them beyond direct representation.

A February 2025 directive reinstated a policy from the first Trump administration that significantly limits the information friend-of-the-court attorneys can provide. Previously, these attorneys served as advocates for children in immigration court. Under the reinstated policy, however, they are prohibited from taking certain actions, including filing or accepting legal documents and informing the court when an individual intends to exercise certain rights.

The Trump administration has also moved to reduce the advance notice period for asylum interviews for unaccompanied children from 21 to 14 days, prompting a lawsuit from national advocacy organizations. These changes follow the administration's broader overhaul of the asylum interview process over the summer, as well as its increased use of pretermission, where decisions are made on asylum applications without a full hearing.

"These are systemic techniques that are being used to speed up the moving of unaccompanied minors out of the country at this moment in time," Brown said. "The limitations on the ability of attorneys to serve, to support, or even just provide simple legal advice - it's devastating."

Jennifer Connor, executive director of the Buffalo-based Justice for Migrant Families, said volunteers with the organization have also noticed that unaccompanied minors are being placed into removal proceedings at an accelerated pace. The group leads a court accompaniment program for those attending the Buffalo Immigration Court, which hears cases for individuals living in the Capital Region.

Connor said unaccompanied minors appeared in court without counsel even before the Acacia contract was terminated, but the increase since then has been significant.

She added that the western New York immigration court has had new judges holding hearings in recent weeks, particularly since the abrupt closure of the Batavia Immigration Court in July. Connor described several of these judges as being impatient with young children appearing for proceedings.

Children who enter the United States without a parent or legal guardian are legally classified as unaccompanied minors and transferred to the Office of Refugee Resettlement, which places them in shelters or foster homes until they turn 18 or are reunited with a sponsor.

In recent years, the majority of unaccompanied minors came from Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, according to federal data that has not been updated to include fiscal year 2026. There was a significant decrease in the number of children in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement between 2024 and 2025, dropping from 98,356 to 22,833.

That decline in the number of unaccompanied children has led the nonprofits previously responsible for providing shelter and foster family placement to lose federal contracts and lay off workers. Just last month, the Children's Home of Poughkeepsie laid off 39 workers and suspended its programs for unaccompanied minors. In New York City and Westchester County, at least five nonprofits housing this population faced funding cuts earlier this year, forcing them to lay off about 1,000 people in total, according to reporting by New York Focus.

Under the second Trump administration, advocates have called for increased support and protections for this vulnerable population. But some, like Connor, worry these legal proceedings are just the beginning. She raised concerns about another emerging population of children she said have been "made unaccompanied" as the Trump administration carries out its deportation agenda.

"As the aggressive enforcement tactics continue on the streets and in courts, I think there are going to be questions about the future of unaccompanied kids," Connor said. "There are kids being orphaned and then they'll have to go to court without lawyers after their parents, who were working or paying lawyers, are removed. That category is different from how people have previously thought of unaccompanied minors."

text:
“You have been weighed in the balance and found wanting” (Daniel 5:27). So concluded many voters about President Donald Trump and his immigration policies.

Few places suffered from such policies more than South Texas, where Department of Public Safety officers — at the behest of Gov. Greg Abbott — acted as immigration deputies, arresting many noncitizens on pretextual traffic stops and turning them over to ICE. We in the immigration bar represented fathers, mothers, grandpas and grandmas who had lived many years in the United States with U.S. citizen spouses and children.

Many of our clients had no ability to seek release from custody, despite not being dangers to the community or flight risks. These realities were in the minds of many voters, particularly Hispanic voters, as they cast their votes for Democrats in Texas during the midterm elections.
