I have written about the exceptionally harsh Trump administration policies since his inauguration in 2025. What can we hope for in these next two years?

Democrats now have majorities in the House and the Senate, although not veto-proof majorities. They can pass bills that eliminate many of the unduly harsh penalties and bars that prohibit deserving noncitizens from obtaining lawful status in the United States through their U.S. citizen spouses, parents and children.

Congress doesn’t need to pass a new, broad legalization bill to do this. It simply needs to change a few words to allow for waivers and modifications for some of the unjust procedural bars to obtaining lawful status, such as the unlawful presence grounds of inadmissibility in the Immigration and Nationality Act.

This would be consistent with recognizing the value in U.S. citizens living with their noncitizen parents, children and spouses. A child having his father present in his life justifies a path for that father to overcome past immigration violations. Congress should eliminate outright prohibitions to green cards based on technical violations of the immigration law and enact broader discretionary waivers for such violations.

These sorts of moderate improvements could attract enough Republican votes to override a presidential veto. Or perhaps Trump might even agree with such changes or even sign a broader bill. As a fellow immigration lawyer quipped, “Democrats should draft and pass the Donald J. Trump Immigration Reform and Control Act of 2027. He will sign it.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Congress should also (finally!) create a pathway to lawful status to those who have lived in the United States for decades under the DACA program. Congress should also place the burden on the government to justify detention during a noncitizen’s removal proceedings. As Justice William Rehnquist stated, “in our society, liberty is the norm, and detention prior to trial or without trial is the carefully limited exception.”

ICE needs to return to the exercise of reasonable enforcement discretion. For years, many others in ICE and I focused on the removal of noncitizens who recently entered the United States or who were dangers to our country and communities. But we also knew our job was to enforce the provisions of the immigration law that allowed deserving noncitizens to obtain lawful immigration status.

At present, many deserving persons could obtain their lawful status, such as a noncitizen married to a U.S. citizen who received a removal order when she was a child, if ICE would exercise such discretion. This discretion was exercised under every prior administration I worked under, including Trump 45.

ICE also needs to have its authority restored to make reasonable custody decisions for noncitizens it apprehends. Right now, it is “once detained, always detained.” People who pose a danger should remain detained. But I have represented many noncitizens detained in ICE custody who are clearly not dangers to the community or flight risks.

I think of one client who was allowed into the United States 20 years ago to care for her ailing husband. She did so for 19 years. Her child, a drug addict, physically assaulted her. She had a pending petition to obtain a green card on account of that abuse, but she was stopped for a traffic infraction, turned over to ICE and deported. I think the local ICE officers would have released her if they could, but their hands were tied by the Trump administration policy.

ICE should focus its enforcement on dangerous noncitizens, not quotas set by the administration.

So much of change in ICE is dependent on leadership. Such leaders need to be empowered to faithfully apply the law and exercise reasonable and humanitarian discretion. ICE has gone almost 10 years without a Senate-confirmed director, the last was Sarah Saldaña, formerly the U.S. Attorney in Dallas and North Texas.

True advice and consent from the Senate regarding the next ICE director could go a long way to restore ICE.

Paul Hunker is an adjunct professor of law at the SMU Dedman School of Law; a partner in the immigration law firm of De Mott, Curtright, & Armendariz; and the former chief counsel of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Dallas.

text:
Four days. That’s all the notice that the New Orleans immigration court gave attorney Corinne Beth to get a family of six ready to defend their asylum case to stay in the US, an intensive process that lawyers estimate requires at least 50 to 75 hours of dedicated preparation.

The court had already brought forward the family’s next hearing once, from a date in July 2028, saying that it was “a priority case” and must be completed by the end of November without explaining why.

Then, on a Thursday in late October, Beth learned that officials had switched her clients’ judge to one in Cleveland, Ohio, without their permission and they now had a virtual hearing come Monday.

A government attorney arguing for the family’s deportation acknowledged the circumstances were strange. But instead of agreeing to give them more time, the Trump administration’s lawyer proposed “pretermitting” their asylum application, jargon for denying their request and deporting them without ever holding a full evidentiary hearing.

“It just doesn’t make sense why we’re behaving this way as a human race,” Beth said.

Beth was able to convince the judge to move her clients to a different hearing date, later this month, the same week it had been rescheduled the first time. Yet even the new court date – so much sooner than in the past, when she would at least get six months’ notice – would not give the family enough time to prepare, she said.

The family’s struggle is an extreme example of what migrants and asylum seekers across the United States are enduring, as federal officials rapidly expedite hearings, send cases to far-flung judges and use every tool in their legal toolbox to prioritize mass deportations without, immigration attorneys protest, any semblance of due process.

“It’s like: ‘Your hearing’s been moved up. Oh, now your hearing’s cancelled. Oh, now you have a new judge. Oh, that judge just quit, so now here’s another one. Oh, we’re randomly going to move it to this other judge just because,’” said Genevra Alberti, a lawyer in Kansas City. “It doesn’t make any sense. There’s no rhyme or reason to it.”

Immigrants without attorneys are faring just as poorly, if not worse, with hearing dates set for next year suddenly pulled forward to just a few weeks’ time, giving them almost no notice to seek legal representation or prepare, according to a source with knowledge of the situation, who could not be named for fear of government retribution.

In this hostile environment for applicants, the rate of US immigration judges granting asylum has already plummeted, with 94% of cases denied in June, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, in stark contrast with the Biden administration, when at certain times asylum grants eclipsed denials. Children and some nationalities targeted by the second Trump administration, including Somali immigrants whom as a group Donald Trump has called “garbage” in past xenophobic rants, have been harmed even more than others, a number of attorneys said.

Meanwhile, the administration’s aggressive tactics have plunged immigration courts into chaos as they collide with the reality of large-scale personnel departures, after a whopping 279 judges – 38% of the bench – resigned or were fired between October 2024 and the end of September 2026.

Those experienced officials are now being replaced by the administration’s “deportation judges”, as the government refers to the role in some of its recruitment literature – often former military lawyers, immigration enforcement attorneys or prosecutors whose tenure has predictably coincided with an abundance of removal orders.

“The job has become so non-neutral that they can’t find anybody that wants to keep the job unless it’s these judges that they’re appointing to the ‘Somali rocket docket’ or to the kids’ dockets,” said Hannah Sullivan, an attorney outside St Louis, referring to expedited proceedings for Somalis and in many children’s cases, in front of a small number of chosen judges. “They’re known to deny and move cases as quickly as possible. So those guys are still on the bench. The ones that were good and wanted to, you know, be a neutral arbiter have not stayed around,” she added.

Sullivan said that the court where she practices in Kansas City lost two veteran judges back-to-back in recent months. And even newer ones – Scott Ison who was appointed in April and Katherine Estes who was appointed in March – left almost as soon as they arrived.

“It’s been very difficult to get information from the court because nobody’s available to answer phones or emails,” Alberti said. Sometimes she receives an answer to her urgent questions weeks later, and other times she never hears back, she said.

As short-staffed courts nevertheless contend with the administration’s pressure to rush immigrants on to deportation flights, many people are being ping-ponged to judges across the country, often nowhere near where they live, and sometimes outside the court circuits with specific case law that should apply to their situations.

That includes children. A new plan has those who came to the US unaccompanied by a parent or legal guardian appearing before a select bench of judges who are not necessarily even hearing juvenile cases in their own courts, but instead adjudicating remotely across time zones and state lines.

“I don’t understand why they’re messing with the kids. Like, why go after children? It doesn’t make any sense to me. But that’s what’s happening,” Alberti said.

Children will still have to show up in-person to their home courts, despite judges being virtual and based elsewhere, and adjudicators are being double-booked to funnel through two courts’ full caseloads at once, said a source familiar with the situation who could not be named for fear of government retaliation.

“It’s insane. Just insane,” the source said.

The latest onslaught comes amid a barrage of legal attacks against these children, even as a growing army of lawyers rallies to try to protect them.

The children are being denied the time they need to access pathways to citizenship for which, a number of advocates stressed, they qualify, as the administration sets what appear to be arbitrary deadlines for judges to end their cases – while also defunding many of their attorneys.

All this can mean immigration lawyers having to rush to the point where children are being pulled out of class at school so that they can practice describing some of their greatest life traumas that are at the heart of their asylum cases. Sometimes, lawyers recounted, they may not have processed the effects of what happened to them yet but still have to confront those memories in preparation for an accelerated court hearing that could change their whole life.

“[Government officials] are not giving us the chance to build the record. They’re not giving us time to prepare the cases. They’re saying, you know, basically, without [actually] saying it: ‘We’re going to speed up these cases for kids because we don’t believe them,’” Sullivan said.

The courts’ new policies – which make it harder to submit evidence, ask for more time, pause proceedings while applying for a legal status through other agencies, and otherwise receive meaningful due process – have rendered it nearly impossible to successfully fight for a client to stay.

“If somebody wins a case at all at trial, it is considered a unicorn,” Alberti said. “It really is becoming a deportation machine … just hiring deportation judges, right? To help fuel this deportation machine.”

text:
One of Concord’s newest immigration judges is a former police officer with a history of allegations of excessive force.

Michael Rapiejko, who was accused of using excessive force as a police officer in Arizona in 2005 and New York in 2015, has been hearing cases since July at the Concord Immigration Court.

He is based in Florence, Arizona, at a detention center complex, and hears cases remotely.

Before becoming a judge, the 2018 graduate of Quinnipiac University School of Law worked as a police officer in Arizona and New York, as a tax attorney, and most recently as an attorney for Immigration and Customs Enforcement from July 2025 to his court appointment in July 2026.

Rapiejko is one of the hundreds of recent hires to replace immigration judges fired by the Department of Justice in the last two years. Many, like Rapiejko, have little experience in immigration law, according to the 257 judges’ biographies reviewed by Mission Local.

Nevertheless, they heeded the call this spring, responding to the Justice Department’s advertising campaign calling for “deportation judges” and promising between $159,951 and $207,500 a year.

Take Ryan Beyers, another newly appointed judge in Concord, who had only a year under his belt working for ICE. He had otherwise worked as a prosecutor in Florida and at a private firm. Another newly appointed judge, Lucas Abbott, was hired with just four months of immigration experience working for ICE. Prior to that, he ran his own private law firm for about five years.

Rapiejko is not the only judge with an allegedly storied past as a police officer.

Brett Rogers, now an immigration judge in West Los Angeles, spent 18 years with the Seattle Police Department, and in 2002 he was one of two officers placed on administrative leave after the fatal shooting of a man brandishing a sword, the Everett Herald reported at the time.

Seattle’s police chief later praised the officers’ actions, the Seattle Times reported, and he was cleared of any wrongdoing in 2002.

In the biographies of the over 200 new hires across the nation, however, 45-year-old Rapiejko stood out.

In 2005, while Rapiejko was an officer with the New York Police Department, he arrested a man who later sued him, accusing Rapiejko of pointing his gun at him, ordering him back into his car, and then choking him.

Rapiejko’s lawyer acknowledged in court records that Rapiejko pointed his gun and ordered the man into the car, but denied threatening or choking him, according to court records.

Records show the city of New York settled the lawsuit and paid $20,000 to settle the case.

Years later, while working as a police officer in Marana, Arizona, in 2015, dashcam video shows Rapiejko using his cruiser to jump a curb and ram into an armed suspect who had threatened to kill himself. The dashcam video released by media outlets shows the incident.

Fox News reported that Rapiejko was placed on administrative leave for three days before rejoining the force. The police chief at the time told NBC that Rapiejko “took a very bold action” against a threat to the community, and the Marana police internal review board cleared him of wrongdoing the same year, arguing that his use of force was “appropriate, reasonable and timely,” according to the report.

A civil lawsuit filed by the suspect was dismissed in 2016.

The Executive Office for Immigration Review, the administrative body that oversees the immigration court system, declined to comment on Mission Local’s questions about Rapiejko’s background or qualifications, saying it does not comment on personnel matters.

Mission Local also tried contacting Rapiejko multiple times through a listed phone number and through the Concord and Florence, Arizona courts where he works. A legal assistant at the Arizona court told Mission Local she would pass along the message to Rapiejko, but he never responded.

Experience in immigration law is not required to be an immigration judge. The main requirements are a law degree, an active bar license, and at least seven years of experience practicing law. Rapiejko fulfills those requirements.

Rapiejko worked for one year as an attorney for ICE in Arizona, according to the Department of Justice. Before that, he spent most of his legal career doing tax law, including a seven-year stint as an attorney for the Internal Revenue Service. He is an active member of the District of Columbia Bar.

Since starting as an immigration judge, Rapiejko has yet to grant asylum to any immigrants in the 65 cases he has heard since he began in July, according to “Inmigreat,” which analyzes immigration court data. This is in line with the asylum grant rate of other judges at the court during the same time frame, which is far lower than the 32% nationwide rate of asylum approval the year before the Trump administration took office in 2025.

Maddie Boyd, an attorney with an immigration nonprofit providing legal advice to immigrants, called Rapiejko’s appointment another example “of the administration prioritizing fast-tracked deportation over a system that is neutral.”

Jeremiah Johnson, the vice president of the National Association of Immigration Judges and a former San Francisco immigration judge, said that under the Trump administration, the hiring and backgrounding standards have been weakened.

“The process is not as robust as it used to be, and that is concerning because of how important the job is,” said Johnson.

title: The Right Way to Do Congressional Oversight | Washington Monthly
authors: Elizabeth Wydra and Praveen Fernandes, Bruno V. Manno, Jon Marcus, Michael T. Nietzel, Elizabeth Wydra, Praveen Fernandes
description:
The Trump administration will almost certainly resist accountability, but that should not deter Congress from exercising its oversight duty.
Oversight requests to private corporations have historically yielded rich information that supported strong investigations.
Understand the Power of Narrative As Congress performs oversight on behalf of the American people, it should remember the importance of narrative.
They want Congress to provide a check against Trump administration abuses that are making their lives more difficult and less secure.
The Constitution provides the legislative branch with broad oversight powers, and the incoming Congress should use them.
text:
The November midterm election results taught us a lot. Exit polling shows Americans are fed up with the corruption and self-dealing by President Trump, his administration, and his allies. In fact, 90 percent of voters surveyed in an NBC exit poll identified corruption as a “crucial or significant factor” in their votes. The cost of living, the brutal immigration crackdowns, and concerns about AI also loomed large in the minds of voters. And the American people aren’t only upset with this administration; they’re upset with the current Congress as well. Importantly, a majority of Americans polled disapproved of the job Congress has been doing. Voters clearly want elected leaders to tackle affordability, but they also want a legislative branch that checks the Trump administration’s abuses and corruption. The incoming Congress should provide Americans with the accountability they demand. Here are three things Congress can consider as it approaches the task.

Be Bold and Broad in Conducting Oversight

The Supreme Court has recognized that Congress’s broad power to investigate is “co-extensive with its power to legislate.” Congress cannot legislate wisely without good information, and when it lacks it, it must obtain it from other sources, including the executive branch.

The Trump administration will almost certainly resist accountability, but that should not deter Congress from exercising its oversight duty. Congress should investigate issues that require investigation, full stop. It should expect pushback and plan accordingly. This means not only considering criminal enforcement of subpoenas, but also anticipating resistance to such criminal referrals by a Department of Justice headed by Todd Blanche, President Trump’s former personal criminal defense lawyer. Committee leadership should be prepared to move promptly for civil enforcement of its subpoenas in federal court when parties refuse to testify or provide requested information. And Congress can and should ask the courts for expedited consideration to prevent the administration from running out the clock, as it tried to do during Trump’s first term.

Breadth will be important as well. For instance, if investigating how no-bid contracts led to the botched restoration of the Lincoln Reflecting Pool, and why taxpayers ended up footing the $14.7 million bill, it will be important not only to request testimony and information from executive branch officials, but also from the private companies and non-governmental actors involved. A broad approach acts as a safeguard. Courts can move quickly, but sometimes they don’t. If litigation to enforce subpoenas against executive branch sources proceeds too slowly, private companies and non-governmental actors can at least provide the other half of the communications that led to the Reflecting Pool fiasco. Remember that the Supreme Court recently reaffirmed Congress’s power to investigate the executive branch—including the president—and acknowledged that such investigations can involve information held by private third parties. Oversight requests to private corporations have historically yielded rich information that supported strong investigations. For example, congressional investigations of banking industry abuses that led to the 2008 financial crisis informed the crafting and passage of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act. More recently, investigations and hearings involving social media companies informed the drafting and introduction of multiple bills aimed at strengthening protections for children.

Use All The Tools In The Toolbox

If Congress finds it is being thwarted by an administration trying to run out the clock on oversight requests, it can create an expedited pathway for federal courts to review oversight disputes. In the past, Republicans and Democrats alike have proposed such a judicial fast track. Congress can also use its power of the purse when faced with stonewalling. For example, if Congress does not get prompt answers about the atrocious killings by ICE and CBP agents, or the federal government’s continuing failure to cooperate with state and local officials to investigate this violence properly, it should make its Department of Homeland Security appropriations decisions accordingly. And this does not simply apply to future appropriations. Congress can also rescind appropriations.

Understand the Power of Narrative

As Congress performs oversight on behalf of the American people, it should remember the importance of narrative. Americans must understand that these investigations are about accountability and making things better for them, not about political retribution. Hearings can help Congress explain. But given a limited legislative calendar—and the reality that most busy Americans don’t follow congressional hearings closely—clear, well-structured hearings with strong witnesses will be necessary, but not sufficient. Congressional leaders should proactively communicate the connections between the problems they are investigating and the very real pain points in people’s lives. Some leaders and committees have already begun to do this, producing materials that explain the costs of unchecked corruption and self-dealing, with glaring examples of how these abuses have led to higher prices and fewer protections for everyday Americans. Finally, in our fractured, siloed media landscape, congressional leaders need to use the full array of new media and enlist interested content creators to get their message out as widely as possible. Even a clear narrative will be of little value if it doesn’t reach its audience.

The American people spoke at the ballot box. They want Congress to provide a check against Trump administration abuses that are making their lives more difficult and less secure. The Constitution provides the legislative branch with broad oversight powers, and the incoming Congress should use them.

text:
At the end of July, the Trump administration terminated a contract with a nationwide network of legal service providers that represented thousands of unaccompanied minors in immigration court. In response, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul announced state funding to help maintain services for the roughly 1,400 New York children who were directly affected.

The funding has allowed some organizations to continue representing children whose cases were already underway. But advocates say it has not resolved the broader problem: Children are still appearing in immigration court without lawyers, leaving some of the most vulnerable people in the immigration system to navigate complex proceedings on their own, often with little understanding of what is at stake.

New York has the third-largest unaccompanied minors caseload in the nation, with more than 9,800 cases that make up just under 10% of the state’s immigration backlog, according to data through Aug. 31 analyzed by the Acacia Center for Justice, which had the federal contract that ended this summer.

The state was the first to adopt a funding measure that would support children previously served under the federal contract. The money can also support immigration-related legal services for unaccompanied minors and immigrant youth as needed, a spokesperson for Hochul’s office said.

“No child should have to navigate complex immigration proceedings alone,” the spokesperson said. “As New York’s first mom governor, she will continue fighting to protect these children against Trump’s cruel deportation agenda.”

The governor’s office did not directly address reports that immigrant children are still showing up in courts without legal representation.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The state’s $7.25 million in funding includes $6.5 million for the Hispanic Federation, which has assembled a coalition of legal service providers, and $750,000 awarded to Prisoners’ Legal Services of New York, an Albany-based firm that provides legal services to unaccompanied minors.

Kristin Brown, president and CEO of Empire Justice Center, which is part of the coalition assembled by the Hispanic Federation, said the money has enabled the organization to continue working on the 125 cases it had pending when the Acacia contract lapsed.

Brown said the group is continually assessing its capacity but is confident it will be able to continue serving the children for whom it has already signed retainers.

“I feel so incredibly grateful for New York’s action because other states have not been so fortunate,” she said. “In other parts of the country, there has been no funding flowing to either represent the kids or help them transition. As attorneys, we feel ethical obligations to continue to represent our clients, but a loss of funding puts organizations in a terrible, heartbreaking position.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Even as the funding has allowed some legal work to continue, Brown said there are growing concerns about the increasingly strained immigration system and shifting policies that are leaving unaccompanied children with fewer protections.

In general, Brown said there has been a significant increase in the number of children appearing in court without counsel and being asked directly by federally appointed judges about their fear of returning to their home countries.

Nationally, the Acacia Center for Justice found that more than three-fourths of completed unaccompanied children’s cases that never had legal representation ended with a removal order. The Vera Institute found that as of August, at least 702,220 children are facing deportation in immigration court, more than half of whom have never had legal representation.

“A 10-year-old kid being asked questions by a judge, that’s really intimidating,” Brown said. “These kids may not have the presence of mind or understanding of what fear of returning to their country would be.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Brown said the process is accelerating the removal of unaccompanied minors. If a child does not express a credible fear of returning to their home country, they are often issued a removal order. If they do express fear, they are given an asylum application, often in English, that they must fill out themselves.

As the removal process moves more quickly, children also face greater limitations on the types of legal support available to them beyond direct representation.

A February 2025 directive reinstated a policy from the first Trump administration that significantly limits the information friend-of-the-court attorneys can provide. Previously, these attorneys served as advocates for children in immigration court. Under the reinstated policy, however, they are prohibited from taking certain actions, including filing or accepting legal documents and informing the court when an individual intends to exercise certain rights.

The Trump administration has also moved to reduce the advance notice period for asylum interviews for unaccompanied children from 21 to 14 days, prompting a lawsuit from national advocacy organizations. These changes follow the administration’s broader overhaul of the asylum interview process over the summer, as well as its increased use of pretermission, where decisions are made on asylum applications without a full hearing.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“These are systemic techniques that are being used to speed up the moving of unaccompanied minors out of the country at this moment in time,” Brown said. “The limitations on the ability of attorneys to serve, to support, or even just provide simple legal advice — it’s devastating.”

Jennifer Connor, executive director of the Buffalo-based Justice for Migrant Families, said volunteers with the organization have also noticed that unaccompanied minors are being placed into removal proceedings at an accelerated pace. The group leads a court accompaniment program for those attending the Buffalo Immigration Court, which hears cases for individuals living in the Capital Region.

Connor said unaccompanied minors appeared in court without counsel even before the Acacia contract was terminated, but the increase since then has been significant.

She added that the western New York immigration court has had new judges holding hearings in recent weeks, particularly since the abrupt closure of the Batavia Immigration Court in July. Connor described several of these judges as being impatient with young children appearing for proceedings.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Children who enter the United States without a parent or legal guardian are legally classified as unaccompanied minors and transferred to the Office of Refugee Resettlement, which places them in shelters or foster homes until they turn 18 or are reunited with a sponsor.

In recent years, the majority of unaccompanied minors came from Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, according to federal data that has not been updated to include fiscal year 2026. There was a significant decrease in the number of children in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement between 2024 and 2025, dropping from 98,356 to 22,833.

That decline in the number of unaccompanied children has led the nonprofits previously responsible for providing shelter and foster family placement to lose federal contracts and lay off workers. Just last month, the Children’s Home of Poughkeepsie laid off 39 workers and suspended its programs for unaccompanied minors. In New York City and Westchester County, at least five nonprofits housing this population faced funding cuts earlier this year, forcing them to lay off about 1,000 people in total, according to reporting by New York Focus.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Under the second Trump administration, advocates have called for increased support and protections for this vulnerable population. But some, like Connor, worry these legal proceedings are just the beginning. She raised concerns about another emerging population of children she said have been “made unaccompanied” as the Trump administration carries out its deportation agenda.

“As the aggressive enforcement tactics continue on the streets and in courts, I think there are going to be questions about the future of unaccompanied kids,” Connor said. “There are kids being orphaned and then they’ll have to go to court without lawyers after their parents, who were working or paying lawyers, are removed. That category is different from how people have previously thought of unaccompanied minors.”

title: Briefly Speaking: How the Constitution covers undocumented immigrants
description:
A common misconception in the United States is that only citizens have constitutional protections, not undocumented immigrants.
So, the question arises: What constitutional rights do undocumented immigrants actually have?
Case by case In several cases dating back to the late 1800s, the Supreme Court has established constitutional rights aren’t off-limits to undocumented immigrants.
It ruled that denying children of undocumented immigrants education punishes them for their parents' actions and creates a permanent underclass.
The letter of the law Based on precedent, the Supreme Court has recognized undocumented immigrants have legal rights and are protected by the Constitution.
text:
A common misconception in the United States is that only citizens have constitutional protections, not undocumented immigrants.

In reality, the Constitution’s language typically uses the words “people” or “person,” extending baseline rights based on physical presence within U.S. jurisdiction rather than citizenship. So, undocumented immigrants have certain constitutional rights because they’re on U.S. soil.

There are some rights, such as the right to vote and run for public office, reserved only for citizens. But many basic rights, like the right to a fair trial and due process, are still applicable.

So, the question arises: What constitutional rights do undocumented immigrants actually have?

Case by case

In several cases dating back to the late 1800s, the Supreme Court has established constitutional rights aren’t off-limits to undocumented immigrants.

The 1896 case Wong Wing v. United States ruled that even though the U.S. government has the right to expel undocumented immigrants from its borders, they still have a right to due process and a fair trial before being sentenced to criminal punishments such as hard labor.

Another is the 1982 Plyler v. Doe case, which challenged a Texas law allowing public school districts to deny enrollment or state funding to the children of undocumented immigrants.

The Supreme Court struck down the law. It ruled that denying children of undocumented immigrants education punishes them for their parents' actions and creates a permanent underclass. Ultimately, the court found no legally valid reason for the state to discriminate based on immigration status because doing so would not serve any substantial state interest.

The Supreme Court’s finding in Plyler established that the children of undocumented immigrants are protected by the 14th Amendment's Equal Protection Clause.

The Court further examined government action against undocumented immigrants in the 1975 United States v. Brignoni-Ponce. In this case, U.S. Border Patrol agents in California stopped a car only because those inside appeared to be Mexican. The Court ruled that, under the Fourth Amendment, which protects against unreasonable searches and seizures, people can’t be stopped based solely on their race.

A more modern example was seen in the 2025 Noem v. Vasquez Perdomo case.

In this case, a federal district court issued an order restricting immigration enforcement stops based on a combination of race, location, speaking Spanish or a person's line of work. In response, the federal government appealed, resulting in the Supreme Court granting an emergency stay pending further litigation. The court found that these factors could be considered a "totality of the circumstances" and therefore permissible. However, this ruling served as a temporary interim stay and did not establish a final majority holding.

Because of this, the current standing of the case does not broadly permit Border Patrol to employ racial profiling. However, the litigation is still ongoing, so this finding could change.

However, even if Border Patrol identifies an undocumented immigrant, the 2001 Zadvydas v. Davis case establishes that the government can’t detain them indefinitely.

In this case, two non-citizens were to be deported but couldn’t be removed, leaving them in U.S. immigration custody indefinitely. The non-citizens were essentially stateless, meaning they had no country that would take them in. The Supreme Court stepped in, establishing a six-month limit before action must be taken to avoid indefinite detention, which violates Fifth Amendment protections against government overreach during criminal and legal proceedings.

While that limit doesn’t guarantee release after six months, it aims to ensure people aren’t detained for an unreasonable length.

The letter of the law

Based on precedent, the Supreme Court has recognized undocumented immigrants have legal rights and are protected by the Constitution.

While this doesn’t grant undocumented immigrants the constitutional right to remain in the country without lawful immigration status, it does limit the government’s ability to act. Immigrants are protected by elements such as due process, equal protection and restrictions against unreasonable searches and seizures.

In practice, this means the government can’t bypass established legal safeguards to enforce immigration laws. The Fourth Amendment ensures immigration officers need to have reasonable suspicion to conduct investigative stops and probable cause or a warrant to enter someone’s home.

The Fifth and 14th Amendments establish undocumented immigrants have the right to the actions of due process, including a fair hearing with a judge before they’re deported. This means they are protected from arbitrary discrimination in the law.

Taking shortcuts

However, the law allows some fast-track “expedited removal” procedures that never go before an immigration judge, and they’re frequently employed by the government.

The Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 allows undocumented immigrants deemed inadmissible by an immigration officer to be deported without further hearings.

These circumstances are described as when an immigrant has been apprehended when arriving at an official point of entry, has arrived by sea and physically been in the U.S. without papers or was found in the U.S. within 100 miles of the border less than 14 days after entering without documentation.

While this process has been protested as unconstitutional, the courts have allowed it on the grounds that immigrants seeking entry to the U.S. do not have the same protections as those who have been established on U.S. soil for sufficient time.

Children are exempt from this practice; adults have the option to petition for an administrative review of their case, but a substantial number of deportations are still completed through this expedited process, according to Congress. Expedited removals accounted for 190,000 deportations in 2024, according to the American Immigration Council.

The government is allowed to take substantial steps to enforce immigration laws. The law offers several advantages to the government, allowing it to further those actions.

However, the government doesn’t have unrestrained authority over how undocumented immigrants are treated and what rights they have as a person on U.S. soil.

text:
This story was first published at Colorado Newsline.

WASHINGTON | Colorado Democratic Rep. Jason Crow, a military veteran, is making an attempt during Congress’ lame-duck session to provide legal protections for Afghanistan immigrants who aided the U.S. military for years, but now face swift deportations.

Earlier this week, Crow filed a discharge petition. If he gains 218 signatures, he can force a House vote on his measure, H.R. 9899, which would allow certain Afghan nationals to qualify for Temporary Protected Status until July 2029.

So far, the discharge petition has 114 backers, with two Republicans, Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Don Bacon of Nebraska, on board. There are 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats and one independent in the House.

“After more than two decades of war, we made a promise that we’d look after them. It’s both a moral and national security imperative that we keep that promise,” Crow said in a statement. “I’m working to force a vote that will protect Afghans already in the United States because I won’t let our nation leave these brave Afghans behind.”

The Trump administration has moved to effectively end the TPS program that Congress created in the 1990s to temporarily grant relief for nationals hailing from countries deemed too unsafe for return. The administration also has sought to revoke humanitarian protections, including TPS, for Afghans initially given under the Biden administration.

The Department of Homeland Security initially moved to deport hundreds of Afghan allies to Pakistan, where they would likely then be removed to Afghanistan, but paused those efforts, which Bloomberg Law first reported.

The practice of removing a noncitizen to a country with which they have no ties and then back to a home country where they will face harm is known as refoulement and it’s prohibited under international law.

The Taliban currently controls the government in Afghanistan and the State Department’s travel advisory for the country is at the highest level, which means it advises against traveling.

DHS estimated that there were roughly 11,000 Afghan nationals with TPS before then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem revoked protections in May 2025.

Legal protections sought

Crow is a former paratrooper and Army Ranger who was deployed to Afghanistan and has long petitioned for thousands of Afghan allies to receive legal protections after the chaotic 2021 U.S. withdrawal from the country that resulted in the Taliban taking over. Many of those Afghan allies and their families had to flee because of likely harm from the Taliban, a terrorist organization, for aiding the United States.

“Our Afghan partners put their lives on the line to help protect American servicemembers like me,” Crow said.

While Crow’s discharge petition might reach the 218-vote threshold for a vote, it will likely not move in the Senate, which Republicans control, or reach the 60 votes needed to advance.

But in the 120th Congress, Democrats and independents who caucus with them will have 55 votes in the Senate, potentially 56 if Democrat Mary Peltola wins the Alaska race against GOP incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan.

Passing any legal protections for immigrants, especially nationals from Afghanistan, will likely face a veto from President Donald Trump, and need a two-thirds majority to override.

During his second administration, Trump instituted a ban on nationals from Afghanistan, and directed the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to stop processing legal immigration paperwork for Afghans after last year’s National Guard shooting in Washington, D.C.

A federal judge in June ordered the Trump administration to continue processing that paperwork.

The person charged with killing West Virginia U.S. Army Spc. Sarah Beckstrom, 20, and injuring another, came to the U.S. under the humanitarian program for Afghan allies and was granted asylum.

A federal judge in August, allowed the Trump administration to force-feed Rahmanullah Lakanwal, the man charged in the National Guard shooting, because he has refused to eat while incarcerated.

text:
Operation of Direction 110

The High Court ruled that the delegate:

did not misunderstand or misapply para 5.2(2) of Direction 110

considered each of the matters in paras 8.1–8.5 of the direction, as required

assigned the greatest weight to the considerations reflecting the terms of para 5.2(2), properly construed

Upon considering the plaintiff’s submissions, the court found that they did not align with the operation of Direction 110.

The court explained that para 5.2(2):

addressed the Australian community’s safety from the risk of physical or other harm from a non-citizen’s criminal or other serious conduct, which was the federal government’s “highest priority” and which was part of the decision-makers’ framework when approaching “their task of deciding whether to refuse or cancel a non-citizen's visa under section 501” of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth)

aimed to help the decision-maker assign weight to the potentially competing primary considerations in paras 8.1–8.5

did not require the decision-maker to consider each possibly competing primary consideration in those paragraphs, except in line with its own terms

Reasonableness of the decision

The High Court disagreed with the plaintiff’s assertion that the delegate’s decision was legally unreasonable. The court held that the plaintiff based his argument on the same misinterpretation of Direction 110’s requirements.

According to Direction 110’s requirements, the court decided that the delegate had logically and reasonably determined that granting the plaintiff a visa and letting him return to Australia would amount to an unacceptable risk of harm to the Australian community, specifically the risk that he would harm his own family through criminal conduct involving family violence.

Child’s best interests

Given the best interests of the plaintiff’s daughter, the High Court could not infer that the delegate failed to consider that the plaintiff's continued absence from Australia would negatively impact his wife’s capacity to care for their family.

The court pointed out that the delegate had found that the daughter’s best interests strongly favoured family reunification.

More High Court cases

On 10 June 2026, the High Court of Australia ruled that the Commonwealth and its officers had no defence against liability for the tort of false imprisonment relating to a plaintiff’s immigration detention between 28 July 2022 and 8 November 2023.

On 22 April 2026, a High Court justice granted leave for Maddocks to withdraw as the applicant’s solicitors and for the respondent minister for immigration, citizenship, migrant services, and multicultural affairs to file a bill of costs in this proceeding.

title: Pregnant U.S. citizen pepper-sprayed, detained by ICE in Modesto, lawyer says
description:
Modesto immigration attorney Patrick Kolasinski identified the woman who was arrested as 23-year-old Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, a U.S. citizen and resident of Ceres (Stanislaus County) who is pregnant.
During the press conference, Andrade said an ICE agent accused her of assaulting him, which she denied.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents pepper-sprayed and arrested a woman who was protesting an immigration detention Sunday outside the Stanislaus County jail in Modesto, according to a lawyer and video of the incident.

Modesto immigration attorney Patrick Kolasinski identified the woman who was arrested as 23-year-old Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, a U.S. citizen and resident of Ceres (Stanislaus County) who is pregnant. He said the arrest happened when Andrade and other community members gathered to protest as ICE agents attempted to arrest a person who had just been released from the jail.

In a press conference Sunday night after her release, Andrade said she is among a group of hundreds of community members who monitor ICE activity in the Central Valley, where immigration enforcement has surged in roughly the past month. She noticed ICE outside the jail Sunday and began recording live on TikTok, she said, as agents stopped a minivan and forced open its doors.

“We’re not going to stop helping the community, even though this happened. We want our immigrants to feel safe here,” Andrade said, wearing the same sweatshirt she had been wearing upon her arrest. “The stores are empty… we’re trying to bring people back out.”

Video of the encounter shows two men who appear to be ICE agents, one masked and both wearing vests labeled “POLICE,” attempting to pull a person from a parked car. A woman can be heard saying, “I have my papers.”

A handful of protesters record the scene on their phones and shout, “Oh my God,” “Get away,” and “Leave him,” according to the video, as four other ICE agents tell them to stay back.

In the video, an ICE agent grabs Andrade by the arm after she follows him around the back of the car, saying “Alright, that’s it.” The video shows a second ICE agent grab her and deploy pepper spray.

Andrade’s husband, who was recording video of the arrest, said to the agents: “She’s pregnant with child.”

Two agents then throw Andrade to the ground and handcuff her as she lies facedown, her abdomen against the ground, according to the video. An agent then rolls her to her side and places her in a sitting position, standing guard over her.

During the press conference, Andrade said an ICE agent accused her of assaulting him, which she denied. “We kind of bumped into each other, and then he was like, 'She hit me,’” Andrade said. “They threw me to the ground, they Maced me, and then they handcuffed me. When they threw me to the ground, that’s when I hit my stomach area pretty hard.”

Andrade was brought to the ICE field office in Stockton after her arrest, although she said she was not processed there. From outside the facility, she said, her sister called for an ambulance, which responded to the ICE office and transported Andrade, who is diabetic, to the hospital. She said she remained under the supervision of two ICE agents, who denied her access to an attorney, as she was medically evaluated.

She said an ICE agent eventually received a phone call and told her she was being released from custody.

The incident did not harm Andrade or her pregnancy, she said. “Thanks to God, everything is good, and nothing worse came from this situation,” she said.

Kolasinski said the arrest follows a recent pattern of ICE arresting people outside the Stanislaus County jail. He said community members have previously raised concerns about the presence of immigration agents in the jail parking lot and the potential for confrontations.

“Those concerns now appear especially significant,” Kolasinski said. “The video raises serious questions about whether ICE agents maintained control of the situation or instead escalated a confrontation into a dangerous use-of-force incident.”

Erich Layton, a spokesperson for the Stanislaus County Sheriff’s Office, said he was aware of the incident in his agency’s parking lot but referred questions about what happened to ICE, saying deputies “had no involvement in the arrest of Ms. Vargas Andrade.”

text:
When a Georgia man tried to sponsor his wife for a green card, federal immigration officials demanded he clear the same steep legal hurdle prosecutors face to put someone behind bars: proof beyond a reasonable doubt. A federal judge in Washington, D.C., just ruled that the government broke its own rules by setting the bar that high.

U.S. District Judge Royce C. Lamberth Thursday threw out U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ denial of Ryan Castaneira’s spousal visa petition in a Nov. 7 opinion, ordering the agency to take a fresh look at the case. While the Department of Homeland Security holds sweeping power over family immigration waivers, Lamberth found that officials cannot simply ignore their own binding legal precedents.

The legal battle stretches back to 2019, when Castaneira filed a Form I-130 petition so his wife, a Mexican national, could apply for lawful permanent residency. Instead of an approval, immigration officials sent a warning that they planned to reject the request because of Castaneira’s criminal history in Georgia.

Castaneira had been convicted of attempted child molestation, attempted enticement of a child for indecent purposes, computer pornography and child exploitation, and obscene internet contact. Court records show those convictions stemmed from online chats on an adult-only website with someone he thought was a 15-year-old girl, though he was actually messaging an adult undercover police officer.

Under the 2006 Adam Walsh Act, U.S. citizens convicted of certain sex offenses involving minors are barred from sponsoring relatives for visas. Congress carved out a narrow exception, allowing a petition to move forward only if the Secretary of Homeland Security decides, in the secretary’s “sole and unreviewable discretion,” that the citizen poses “no risk” to the relative.

Relying on an internal 2007 agency memo, USCIS told Castaneira he had to prove “beyond any reasonable doubt” that he posed no danger to his wife. Castaneira turned over rehabilitation records, but officials rejected the petition anyway, pointing to his active probation and ongoing need for monitoring and treatment.

Acting as his own attorney, Castaneira sued in 2022. He argued that his crimes did not qualify under the Adam Walsh Act because no actual child was involved, and he accused the agency of violating federal law by ignoring its own 2010 precedential ruling, Matter of Chawathe. That 2010 decision established that unless Congress explicitly requires something stricter, immigration applicants only have to prove their case by a “preponderance of the evidence”—essentially showing their claims are more likely true than not.

Judge Lamberth initially tossed the lawsuit in 2023, ruling that federal courts had no authority to second-guess the agency’s discretionary calls. Last year, however, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit breathed new life into the fight. While the appeals court agreed that an undercover sting still counts as an offense against a minor under the law, it ruled that judges can step in if an agency violates its own self-imposed rules.

Back before Lamberth, government lawyers argued that the 2010 Chawathe precedent never applied to Adam Walsh Act waivers and claimed a recent U.S. Supreme Court decision stripped the court of jurisdiction. Lamberth disagreed, noting that immigration officials had quietly used the lower preponderance standard in similar visa cases back in 2012.

Citing the Accardi doctrine—a foundational administrative law rule forcing government agencies to follow their own binding policies—Lamberth declared that the lower preponderance standard must govern Adam Walsh Act no-risk reviews.

“The immense amount of daylight between those burdens makes the Agency’s adjudication substantially defective and likely to prejudice Plaintiff,” Lamberth wrote, contrasting the most lenient standard of proof in American law with the strictest.

The ruling is a partial victory for Castaneira. While he won on the procedural violation, Lamberth dismissed his separate claim under the Administrative Procedure Act, finding that federal law still shields the agency’s original 2007 policy memo from direct judicial challenge.

Still, the decision forces USCIS back to the drawing board, requiring officials to re-evaluate whether Castaneira poses a risk to his wife under a much lower burden of proof.

text:
A Doral councilwoman says city officials blocked her attempt to publicly discuss the city's agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, warning that even debating the issue could put the entire City Council at risk of removal from office.

Councilwoman Maureen Porras raised concerns about Doral's participation in the federal 287(g) program, which allows designated local law enforcement officers to perform certain immigration enforcement duties under ICE supervision.

But according to Porras, the city's attorney prevented the proposed discussion from appearing on the council's agenda, citing concerns that it could be interpreted as an attempt to violate Florida law.

The controversy comes as Doral, a Miami-Dade County city with a large Venezuelan population that overwhelmingly supported President Donald Trump in the 2024 election, grapples with the effects of his administration's immigration policies.

The administration's decision to end Temporary Protected Status for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans, combined with increased ICE enforcement, has fueled fear among residents and contributed to business closures in the community.

Doral councilwoman says residents deserve public discussion about ICE

During an interview with Jim DeFede on CBS Miami's Facing South Florida, Porras said her proposal was motivated by concerns she had heard from residents about the city's cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

"I think we are facing a very big issue in the city of Doral," Porras said.

"I know that our residents want to have this discussion in a public forum as well, and unfortunately that is being blocked … before we have it."

Watch the full episode of CBS Miami's Facing South Florida with Jim DeFede in the video below.

Porras said she was not seeking to take immediate action against the agreement but wanted council members to have an opportunity to discuss its impact on the community.

"All I wanted to do was bring this up to the council, be able to discuss it with my colleagues … and unfortunately, we are getting blocked from being able to do that," she said.

City attorney warns discussion could put council members at risk

The city's attorney warned in a memo that discussing Doral's 287(g) agreement could be viewed as signaling an intent to violate state law.

According to the memo as described on Facing South Florida, such a discussion could prompt Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier to pursue the removal of the entire council from office.

Florida law requires local law enforcement agencies to cooperate with federal immigration authorities, and state officials have taken an aggressive approach toward enforcing those requirements.

The dispute raises questions about how much authority local elected officials have to publicly debate immigration enforcement policies affecting their communities.

For Porras, the issue is whether Doral residents and their elected representatives should be able to discuss an agreement that has become increasingly controversial amid heightened immigration enforcement.

The architect of the controversial ICE operations was promoted days after sweeping mid-term losses. Immigration attorneys say ICE activity has been ramping back up in Minnesota. And video of an ICE arrest in Robbinsdale last week sparked memories from Operation Metro Surge.

"Thin I.C.E." – a new series from FOX 9 Documentaries– details how immigration operations have escalated during Trump's second term.

"And in each state, it just got worse and worse and worse," said Jose Alvillar, with Unidos Minnesota.

By the time thousands of ICE and Border Patrol agents flooded the Twin Cities metro area last January, a pattern of aggressive tactics and dragnet immigration enforcement had already emerged in other major cities across the country.

From Chicago to Minneapolis

Why you should care:

The Trump Administration has repeatedly claimed they are targeting the "worst of the worst" during immigration operations.

But during Operation Midway Blitz in Chicago last year, they also wrongfully detained immigrants, falsely accused observers of interfering with federal law enforcement and shot at least two people.

The operation in Chicago resulted in numerous legal challenges that revealed federal agents provided misinformation, tampered with evidence and bragged about deadly force.

It foreshadowed what would happen in Minnesota months later.

"I do have very close, very close friends in Minneapolis, one of whom works in immigration, and I did warn them right away, 'they're really coming in hot, they're really coming in aggressive,'" said Theresa Kleinhaus, a civil rights attorney in Chicago.

And yet those warning signs still could not fully prepare Minnesota for the impact of Operation Metro Surge.

More ICE than police

By the numbers:

"Midway Blitz at its height had 500 (agents)," said Gov. Tim Walz. "And we had, by most accounts, I mean, it's hard to get true numbers… above 3,000."

At one point, there were more federal immigration agents in Minneapolis and St. Paul than local police officers.

"In Minneapolis, they could fully saturate and occupy," Kleinhaus said.

The feds deployed four or five times as many agents in a metro area with a much smaller footprint.

"You put 3,000 agents in a very tiny Twin Cities, you’re going to bump into an agent," said Luis Argueta Jr. with Unidos Minnesota.

Unidos Minnesota, which ultimately trained thousands of legal observers, started preparing for a surge in June 2025 after seeing the aggressive tactics being utilized in Los Angeles.

"And so by the time they got to Minnesota, we knew that things were gonna be really bad," Alvillar said.

DHS defended the arrest and claimed the man threw a bird feeder at agents while trying to flee.

text:
Houston — The siblings of a Mexican construction worker run over last month by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in an unmarked SUV allege the incident that left their brother with severe injuries was "intentional."

"It was not an accident," Miguel Parra Hernandez's sister, Carmen Parra, told CBS News in an exclusive interview. "The videos show everything."

Rodolfo Parra said he cried when he saw videos depicting the Oct. 10 incident that left his brother with a broken leg and hip injuries.

"You can hear all my brother say, 'Ah, you broke my leg. Ah, you're breaking my leg,'" Rodolfo Parra said.

The siblings described 48-year-old Parra Hernandez as a "hardworking" family man who has lived in the U.S. for 34 years, since leaving Mexico in the 1990s as a teenager.

"My brother is not a criminal," Carmen Parra said.

Mario Alberto Morales, the ICE officer who struck Parra Hernandez with his vehicle, was indicted in late October by a Texas grand jury on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Morales' attorney has called the incident an "accident," while ICE has denounced the prosecution as a "political stunt."

"He says he's done"

While Parra Hernandez does not have a criminal history and was not the target of the ICE operation the day he was hit and detained, he remains in the agency's custody, recovering from his injuries. ICE has not disputed that Parra Hernandez lacks a criminal record, but says the Mexican national is in the U.S. illegally and subject to deportation.

Parra Hernandez's siblings claim their brother's mental and physical health has deteriorated while in ICE custody, so much so that he's suffered from suicidal ideation.

"He says he's done," Carmen Parra said. "He wants to just go to sleep and not wake up because he says, 'I'm done in this life.' But we love him."

In a letter to acting ICE Director David Venturella and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Friday, a group of Democratic lawmakers led by Rep. Lizzie Fletcher accused ICE of obstructing efforts from Parra Hernandez's family and counsel to talk to him and rejecting food brought by relatives.

"The treatment of a long-time community member is unacceptable and a violation of his constitutional rights," the lawmakers said, demanding Parra Hernandez's release.

Representatives for ICE did not respond to questions about Parra Hernandez's health and treatment, and the allegations in the lawmakers' letter.

Parra Hernandez's siblings said he was on his way to work on Oct. 10 when he and a co-worker were approached by ICE agents. Surveillance video shows the two men running out of a white truck and attempting to flee, before an ICE vehicle appears to strike Parra Hernandez from behind.

In a statement following the incident, ICE claims Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle. But Sean Teare, the Harris County district attorney, alleges the ICE agent "aggressively steered his vehicle into Parra Hernandez."

Houston limits cooperation with ICE

Parra Hernandez's hospitalization is one of several ICE-related controversies that Houston Mayor John Whitmire said have spread fear in the Houston area and prompted him to take action.

Following the stunning Republican losses in Texas and across the country on Election Day, Whitmire blocked Houston police officers from contacting ICE when they stop someone who may be in the U.S. without a valid immigration status.

"We do not collaborate unless the person is a really bad person. We're not concerned about someone that got pulled over for a traffic violation, or someone over a noise ordinance," Whitmire told CBS News. "We are going after the bad guys that have committed a new offense, a new danger to our community."

Whitmire said local officials can still work with ICE when someone in the U.S. illegally is booked in jail for criminal conduct.

He argued his executive order is designed to lower "fear and anxiety" in the community, referencing the fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican immigrant killed by an ICE agent over the summer during an attempted vehicle stop. The deadly shooting remains under investigation.

Since the policy change in Houston, officials in Austin and San Antonio have announced similar proposals.

Whitmire said he's taking a risk with his directive, citing the threat that Republican Gov. Greg Abbott's administration could sue Houston. But Abbott will soon be replaced by Gina Hinojosa, the first Democrat to be elected Texas governor in decades, and Whitmire said he can "guarantee" she will not force him to work with ICE.

He also acknowledged the move may prompt the Trump administration to withhold federal funds from Houston.

"Of course, I'm concerned about the Trump administration every day, but you have to use your good judgment," he said.

Protesters at a Contra Costa County courthouse in Martinez rallied against Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who are using a county parking lot to stage operations.

ICE has been using the lot adjacent to the A.F. Bray Courthouse and Martinez Detention Facility, and multiple people have been detained there, said Hernan Soto, an organizer with the Contra Costa Immigrant Rights Alliance, speaking at the protest on Thursday.

“We’re here to let the people and the county know that we know what’s going on,” he said.

ICE’s use of county property is “unacceptable,” he said, but Contra Costa doesn’t prohibit county cooperation with ICE — though immigrant rights activities have called for it for more than a year.

“While other counties are strengthening their policies and issuing cease-and-desist orders to ICE, Contra Costa remains silent,” Soto said.

At a County Board meeting in September, supervisors Shanelle Scales-Preston and John Gioia voted to put forward an ordinance that would require its staff to adhere to rules around interacting with ICE and the agency’s use of county-run facilities.

But Preston and Gioia were outvoted by Candace Andersen, Diane Burgis and Ken Carlson, who opted for a policy — a non-binding guideline — rather than an ordinance, which is a legally binding local law.

The board will vote Tuesday on the proposed policy for responding to Immigration Issues, which is intended to guide county staff on their rights interacting with immigration officers.

In recent weeks, ICE has made itself known in several parts of the county, particularly in an area of Concord known as Monument Corridor, according to Julia Quintero of Monument Impact, a nonprofit organization that serves low-income families.

“The Monument is the holder of most of the immigrant community,” Quintero said at the protest

“We’ve seen a huge increase in the last two weeks,” she said, referring to ICE activity in the neighborhood.

“Monument is a really bustling part of the city, but right now, nobody’s out,” she said. “It automatically puts fear in people’s minds.”

Most of the ICE arrests have targeted men — typically fathers — on their way to work in the morning, Quintero said.

text:
The Trump administration's expanded deportation campaign is delaying home building in New Mexico by creating widespread fear among workers and their families.

Starting in June, arrests of undocumented immigrants and those in the multistep process of becoming U.S.-naturalized citizens have soared to record highs.

Miles Conway, executive vice president and CEO of the New Mexico Home Builders Association, said agents have descended on construction sites, often in unmarked SUVs, to arrest multiple workers.

"The quotes I have heard from my contractors are that job sites are just simply ghost towns. That means at the end of the day, housing prices go up," Conway explained.

An analysis by the New Mexico Office of Housing found the state lacks at least 50,000 affordable housing units for low- and moderate-income households. ICE arrests reached historic highs in the past year, as the second Trump administration narrowed pathways to legal status and expanded the pool of individuals targeted for removal. More than 90,000 arrests were made in June and July, with an additional 50,000 in August.

New Mexico has the highest percentage of Hispanic or Latino residents of any U.S. state. The Trump administration originally said its primary immigration focus would be removing violent criminals, but is now pursuing broader mass deportations, including nonviolent undocumented workers, relying on technical loopholes to evade previous legal limits.

Conway noted one of his largest subcontractors is operating with only 10% of his usual crew and others have reported similar situations. For many in the industry, it is also a human dignity issue.

"A lot of tradespeople absolutely have their documentation in order, and they're being swept up in these administrative warrant raid-like situations. When that happens, that atmosphere of fear really takes hold," Conway observed.

The raids have mostly occurred at large, multifamily developments in New Mexico's largest cities, such as Albuquerque and Santa Fe. Earlier this month, ICE agents arrived in an Albuquerque neighborhood where single-family homes were being built by the global nonprofit Habitat for Humanity.

text:
Hundreds of demonstrators gathered at Rockaway Mall on Saturday to protest plans for a proposed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility in neighboring Roxbury.

The demonstration was sparked by a warehouse property in Roxbury that the Department of Homeland Security purchased earlier this year, with plans to convert the site into an ICE detention center.

The project remains tied up in court after a judge issued an order temporarily that prevents DHS from moving forward until an environmental impact study is completed. However, Roxbury Township officials said DHS reportedly signed a contract worth more than $30 million for renovations recently.

"It was a successful delay tactic, but I don't think it was a permanent solution and we have to keep working harder to stop this for good," said Roxbury resident Sierra Winters about the court order.

More than 300 protesters marched through the mall Saturday, voicing concerns about the potential impact the facility could have on immigrant communities across Morris County.

"The Rockaway Mall being so close to Dover, that's the heart of where they're taking our neighbors from," Winters said. "Dover, Hackettstown, Morristown. We've seen ICE raids in all of these local communities and this is where they're going to be planning to bring those folks if this facility is able to be changed into more of a detention center."

Residents also expressed concerns about a potential increased ICE presence in the area with a detention center nearby.

"We're a small community here. We love our neighbors, we love our community and we don't want them to be harassed," said Ronnie Bauman, of Netcong.

Others questioned whether local resources could handle a mass detention facility.

"Water issues, the Highlands Act with the protected land - this would definitely take a toll on our environmental issues as well as, of course, sewage," said Roxbury resident Nicole Maguire.

According to court filings, the Department of Homeland Security, Roxbury Township and the State of New Jersey are required to submit a joint status report to the New Jersey District Court by Tuesday that details actions taken since the court's order was issued in May.

text:
WASHINGTON – The Supreme Court agreed on Nov. 13 to con­sider the leg­al­ity of Pres­id­ent Don­ald Trump’s restric­tions on access to asylum at the U.S.-Mex­ico bor­der, a hard-line immig­ra­tion policy his admin­is­tra­tion has cred­ited with help­ing reduce bor­der cross­ings.

The justices took up Trump’s appeal of a lower court’s rul­ing that found he exceeded his author­ity by deny­ing migrants caught enter­ing the coun­try illeg­ally the chance to apply for asylum.

The court is expec­ted to hear argu­ments in the case in the com­ing months and rule by the end of June.

Trump, who has described the influx of migrants as an inva­sion, announced the new curbs just hours into his second pres­id­en­tial term on Jan. 20, 2025. His policy sweeps more broadly than sim­ilar curbs put in place by his pre­de­cessor, Joe Biden, who lim­ited asylum eli­gib­il­ity at the south­ern bor­der in a bid to reduce illegal cross­ings.

Trump’s asylum policy is one of a num­ber of meas­ures his admin­is­tra­tion has taken as part of his crack­down on immig­ra­tion pur­sued since return­ing to office last year. Top offi­cials have also sought to per­suade other nations to join in a global cam­paign to roll back asylum pro­tec­tions in an effort to reshape the post-World War II frame­work around human­it­arian migra­tion.

Under Trump’s policy, migrants caught cross­ing the south­ern bor­der illeg­ally are barred from pur­su­ing asylum claims. The pro­hib­i­tion also applies to migrants who arrive at offi­cial bor­der cross­ings and lack cer­tain med­ical or crim­inal his­tory inform­a­tion, a require­ment that advoc­ates say is often impossible to meet for people flee­ing viol­ence.

Trump’s pro­clam­a­tion announ­cing the asylum restric­tions – and the fasttrack deport­a­tion pro­ced­ures they are meant to enable – said the policy would remain in effect until the Repub­lican pres­id­ent determ­ines that the “inva­sion at the south­ern bor­der” has ended.

Immig­rant rights groups filed a class-action law­suit chal­len­ging the policy on behalf of would-be asylum­seekers who say they were denied a “cred­ible fear” inter­view by U.S. immig­ra­tion offi­cials before facing deport­a­tion. Such inter­views are meant to determ­ine whether migrants seek­ing asylum would face per­se­cu­tion in their home coun­try based on race, reli­gion, nation­al­ity, mem­ber­ship in a par­tic­u­lar social group or polit­ical opin­ion.

A fed­eral judge in Wash­ing­ton, DC, ruled in favor of the immig­rant rights groups in July 2025. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Dis­trict of Columbia Cir­cuit in April upheld the judge’s rul­ing but largely agreed to block the decision from tak­ing effect to let the admin­is­tra­tion appeal to the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court, which has a 6-3 con­ser­vat­ive major­ity, has been largely defer­en­tial to Trump in his second pres­id­en­tial term in chal­lenges to his immig­ra­tion policies.

In June, the court handed Trump a vic­tory by back­ing the fed­eral gov­ern­ment’s author­ity to turn away asylum­seekers when offi­cials deem U.S.-Mex­ico bor­der cross­ings too over­burdened to handle addi­tional claims.

In Septem­ber, the court let the admin­is­tra­tion resume deport­ing migrants to coun­tries other than their own without offer­ing them the chance to show the harms they may face. The justices are due to hear argu­ments over the leg­al­ity of that policy on Dec. 9.
