text:
In August 2018, Stephen Miller’s uncle, a retired neuropsychologist who had been affiliated with the Boston University School of Medicine, published an opinion piece in Politico. “I have watched with dismay and increasing horror as my nephew, an educated man who is well aware of his heritage, has become the architect of immigration policies that repudiate the very foundation of our family’s life in this country.” The Trump administration was implementing its family separation policy during Donald Trump’s first administration, a policy that Miller’s political mentor and ticket into the Trump administration, Jeff Sessions, ardently supported, as did Miller.

Miller’s Jewish ancestors fled from what was then called the Russian Empire, modern-day Belarus, shortly after the start of the 20th century. Their story parallels my own family history. I have always been acutely aware that because my great-grandmother, Rose Rubenstein, had the courage to demand that the family immigrate, I am here. Had she not, it’s uncertain they would have survived the violence in the shtetl they lived in, in the Pale. And if they had, they would likely have perished in the Holocaust. As Miller’s uncle writes, “The Glossers [Their ancestors] came to the U.S. just a few years before the fear and prejudice of the ‘America first’ nativists of the day closed U.S. borders to Jewish refugees. Had Wolf-Leib [their ancestor] waited, his family likely would have been murdered by the Nazis along with all but seven of the 2,000 Jews who remained in Antopol.”

Now Stephen Miller is going to be Donald Trump’s chief of staff in the waning days of his administration, when Trump is likely to become ever more dangerous as his power seeps away. Glosser, Miller’s uncle, objected to his immigration policies, writing that Miller and Trump had become “numb to the resultant human tragedy and blind to the hypocrisy of their policy decisions.” He points out that Trump, too, has an immigrant family story, one from Germany, where his grandfather reportedly fled conscription into the army.

Stephen Miller is not a lawyer. I suppose that makes it easy to ignore the law and to misrepresent how it works and what it requires of this administration, like all others. But Miller has never hesitated to espouse views suggesting that the law, far from protecting immigrants, permits the administration to treat them like damaged goods that inflict further harm.

Here are just a few of the times he’s been willing to bypass the rule of law to do Trump’s bidding, or, when it comes to immigration, it’s his own. Earlier this year, Forbes called him “the primary architect, strategist, and enforcer of the Trump administration's immigration agenda, operating with Donald Trump's backing rather than independently or in contradiction to him.”

Miller has suggested that Trump could suspend habeas corpus, the fundamental mechanism people in government custody use to challenge the legality of their detention. Miller has publicly discussed suspending it in connection with immigration enforcement, but the Suspension Clause (Article I, Section 9 of the Constitution) provides that habeas cannot be suspended except during rebellion or invasion when public safety requires it. In May 2025, he said that habeas “can be suspended in a time of invasion. So I would say that's an option we're actively looking at.” What invasion? The faux one used to justify sending people to a torture prison in El Salvador and killing people on boats in the Caribbean and the Pacific. Suspension is up to Congress, not the president; Trump and Miller’s assessment was that an invasion was happening notwithstanding. Yet these are the lengths Miller is willing to stoop to back Trump’s immigration policy, suggesting habeas could be suspended to permit the administration to deport migrants.

Miller has supported Trump’s view that federal judges should be impeached if he doesn’t like their decisions. In February 2025, we discussed the early trend among Trump influencers to seek impeachment of judges who didn’t bend the knee to the administration’s moves. More recently, in this piece, Judges Aren’t Supposed to Please Presidents, we took the topic up again. I noted that “Judicial independence is at the heart of American democracy. It’s what’s keeping us afloat right now.” That independence has made the judiciary a target of Miller and other Trump allies, including in February 2025, when Miller joined others in attacking federal judges with a tweet.

Miller continued to advance the administration’s position on birthright citizenship as the correct one, even after the Supreme Court rejected it. On June 30, 2026, the Supreme Court decided Trump v. Barbara, and held that the Fourteenth Amendment conveys citizenship at birth to children born in the United States, even when their parents are unlawfully present. But Miller made remarks on August 6, 2026, in which he continued to discuss excluding categories of people from birthright citizenship through new executive orders issued by Trump, even though the Supreme Court had firmly rejected the constitutionality of doing so.

These examples barely scratch the surface of Miller’s contempt for the law and the judges who administer it. But they demonstrate his determination to bend the law to his and the administration’s will, instead of following it, which the oath that both he and Trump took requires.

Miller’s uncle ended his Politico piece with the following words:

“Most damning is the administration's evident intent to make policy that specifically disadvantages people based on their ethnicity, country of origin and religion. No matter what opinion is held about immigration, any government that specifically enacts law or policy on that basis must be recognized as a threat to all of us. Laws bereft of justice are the gateway to tyranny. Today others may be the target, but tomorrow it might just as easily be you or me.”

It is so much worse now than it was in 2018. We watched as Renee Good and Alex Pretti, and now still more people, have been shot dead on American streets by American law enforcement officers, supposedly public servants who are sworn to serve and protect, during the second Trump administration. We know of the horrors of places like Alligator Alcatraz and other “detention centers” and have read recent stories about people who have disappeared in them. It is inhumane and intolerable to treat people like this. It is unconstitutional. And Stephen Miller shows no signs of caring.

You can support Civil Discourse by signing up for a paid subscription if you don’t already have one. That helps keep the newsletter available to anyone who wants to read it. People who seemed to have their minds made up before the election are now more open to shifting their views, and I’m committed to helping that along by giving them access to the quality of information and analysis that empowers them to change their minds.

We’re in this together,

Joyce

OREGON, Ohio (WTVG) - William Midubo, a full-time engineer for the city of Oregon, was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement after flying to Seattle, according to the city’s law director.

Law Director Chynna Fifer sent a letter to Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine on Friday asking for his help in the case. The letter is dated Nov. 13.

The full letter is available at the end of this story.

Midubo is from the Democratic Republic of Congo and attended the University of Toledo. He interned with the city before becoming a full-time engineer in 2022.

Detention after flight

Fifer said Midubo took time off to attend a friend’s wedding in Washington. He flew from Detroit to Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, where he was met by ICE, she said.

Midubo is being held at an ICE detention facility on a $75,000 bond. Fifer said she believes he is being wrongfully detained based on the documentation the city has.

“We do have his work authorization, it’s till 2030 it looks like it was just renewed in 2025,” Fifer said. “So from what I can see he does have authorization to be here. He is authorized to work in the United States.”

City asks governor for assistance

In the letter, Fifer wrote on behalf of the city of Oregon and described Midubo as “a valued employee of the city.” The letter states that Midubo held a valid work visa and was authorized to work in the United States when he was detained.

The letter states the city has relied on Midubo’s skills, experience and service, and that his continued employment is important to the community and the operation of city services.

Fifer asked DeWine for help in seeking a timely review of the circumstances of the detention. She also asked for support for Midubo’s release “or any other appropriate resolution” that would allow him to return to his job with the city.

Family working to post bond

Midubo’s brother, Elie Midubo, said he has spoken with him only a handful of times by phone at the ICE processing center. Elie said authorities took his brother’s phone at the airport and denied him an opportunity to call his lawyer.

Elie said he has worked to get an attorney, and the family is trying to post bond to bring William back to Toledo.

“They asked him for his papers, he showed everything, work permit, ID, flight tickets, so why do they send him to a facility when there is no grounds, no criminal record?” Elie said. “They didn’t even give him a chance.”

“We are short on cash, we are short on money,” Elie said. “All of our plans got thrown away. We are praying he can be released today.”

text:
Sixteen Ecuadorian fishers are suing the US government over “catastrophic” harm resulting from a drone strike in the eastern Pacific Ocean earlier this year, and what they say was their subsequent abduction and torture, as part of the Trump administration’s boat-bombing spree supposedly targeting drug smugglers.

The Guardian reported Saturday that the lawsuit is set to be filed Monday in the US District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania. The suit concerns a March 17 drone strike on the fishing vessel La Negra Francesca Duarte II, which the fishers said was returning from a two-week expedition when it was bombed approximately 385 nautical miles off Ecuador’s coast.

According to the filing, Ecuadorian authorities had inspected the vessel shortly before the attack and concluded it was carrying no drugs and that its crew had no affiliation with drug cartels.

However, two drones bombed the vessel, setting it ablaze and seriously burning two crew members. The fishers jumped into the water and escaped aboard smaller emergency boats before being intercepted by US military personnel, who allegedly restrained them with zip ties and covered their heads with plastic hoods.

The survivors say they were subsequently taken to a detention center in El Salvador, where they were held for several weeks before being returned to Ecuador. Their lawsuit seeks unspecified financial compensation for what it describes as a “manifestly unlawful” attack and the subsequent “kidnapping and torture.”

Other survivors of US boat strikes have also said they were abducted and tortured by American forces.

“There is no actual armed conflict that could justify the use of military force against the boats, nor was there one on March 17 when the attack took place,” the lawsuit states. “The US’ campaign of bombings against defenseless vessels and individuals violates long-standing and well-accepted international law.”

Dan Kovalik, the attorney filing the lawsuit, told The Guardian that the men “go out fishing, they don’t come home for a month, they’re... in a migrant detention center in El Salvador, and as we know those centers are not so nice.”

“So there’s a lot of trauma there,” he continued. “It was catastrophic for them. They are home now, but they are struggling financially, and the two guys who were hurt bad are still dealing with that.”

“They would also like the US to stop these boat strikes,” Kovalik added. “That’s another goal of all this, and I think the US public and the media have been, honestly, not outraged enough about these strikes.”

The suit is the latest legal challenge to President Donald Trump’s Operation Southern Spear, which the administration launched in September 2025, ostensibly to combat drug trafficking. But US officials have provided scant evidence to support claims that targeted vessels were engaged in narcotrafficking.

The Washington Office on Latin America, a human rights NGO, estimates that as many as 250 people have been killed in the campaign.

In January, relatives of two Trinidadian fishers killed by a US boat strike last year filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the Trump administration in a Massachusetts court. The men were among six people killed in an October 14, 2025 missile strike while traveling from Venezuela to Trinidad. Their families, represented by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and the Center for Constitutional Rights (CCR), are seeking damages under the Death on the High Seas Act and the Alien Tort Statute.

The ACLU, CCR, and New York Civil Liberties Union also filed a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit last December demanding the release of a secret Justice Department Office of Legal Counsel opinion purportedly providing the legal framework for the strikes.

Relatives of a Colombian man killed during Operation Southern Spear also lodged a complaint with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights last December, accusing US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth—who earlier this week survived an attempt to impeach him, in part over the boat strikes—of ordering murder.

Meanwhile, The Washington Post reported in August that strikes on Ecuadorian fishing boats near the Galápagos Islands earlier this year were carried out by the Central Intelligence Agency.

Eight crew members of one vessel, the Fiorella, also disappeared after an apparent attack in January and remain missing.

The Former Judge Advocates General Working Group, which includes former officials who served as legal advisers for the US military, said last year that Hegseth’s alleged order to “kill everybody” in one September 2025 boat strike—which resulted in a follow-up attack on two survivors—suggested that the defense secretary committed “war crimes, murder, or both.”

Kovalik said he looks forward to the incoming Democrat-controlled Congress holding Trump administration officials accountable for the strikes.

“Some of the Democrats that we met with are very interested in doing hearings on these boat strikes,” he said. “We hope this case will encourage the Democrats when they get sworn in in January to start some hearings. I think it will have that impact.”

text:
Protesters descended on the Rockaway Townsquare mall on Saturday afternoon to demonstrate against plans for a proposed Immigration and Customs Enforcement warehouse in nearby Roxbury.

Between 250 and 300 people attended the No More Cages protest organized by the Sussex Visibility Brigade at the Rockaway Township mall. The chants of “What do we want? ICE out! When do we want it? Now!” and “Money for jobs & education! Not for war & deportation!” echoed throughout the shopping center during the two-hour protest.

The protest was scheduled after new reports that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security is moving forward with plans to convert the Route 46 warehouse into a detention facility.

Jenny Garcia, an immigration activist from Morris County with the American Friends Service Committee, was in attendance and recounted the deaths and poor conditions at the ICE detention centers at Delaney Hall in Newark and Elizabeth.

Two retired Franciscans with St. Anthony’s Fraternity in Butler, Michael Barrett and Christopher Keenan, attended the protest, holding a sign that said "Love melts ICE."

"We are here because of our respect for human rights and the cause of our children, who should not be in prison," said Keenan. "As Pope Francis said 'We should not be afraid of immigrants.’ We are all immigrants in this country.”

Barrett said he was attended because he was an American but he also believed in the "gospel of Jesus Christ.

"And both of those stand up for human dignity,” Barrett said.

Aatish Gupta, co-chair of the Skyland branch of the Northern NJ Democratic Socialists of America, helped organize the protest.

He said the state should demand an inspection of the Roxbury warehouse to ensure DHS complies with a court agreement prohibiting use of the property until an environmental assessment is completed. He also said state and local police should do more to enforce traffic laws and other rules that he claimed ICE was violating in its immigration sweeps.

Holiday shoppers and merchants watched the protesters go by, mostly without comment and there didn't appear to be any confrontations.

The proposed detention center has created intense controversy and has resulted in the state and Roxbury filing a lawsuit against DHS.

Shortly after rumors began spreading late last year that ICE planned to purchase the 470,000-square-foot warehouse on a narrow stretch of Route 46 – the actual purchase was confirmed in February – the all-Republican Roxbury Township Council passed a resolution opposing the use of the warehouse for detaining immigrants.

In May, a court order barred DHS from undertaking "any activities" at the site to turn it into the detention center, with limited exceptions, until after an environmental assessment and a chance for the state to challenge the results of the assessment.

On June 29, it announced that it would not move forward with its plans to convert the warehouse. However, just two weeks later, on July 11, the department reversed its decision and informed township officials and the court that it intended to proceed with its plans to retrofit the warehouse for detention use.

In the most recent federal court filing by the state, it informed a judge that DHS entered into a $31.8 million contract with a private company to convert the warehouse into a detention facility.

Protesters showed up to the Nov. 10 Roxbury Council meeting, which was shut down by the mayor. Mayor Shawn Potilllo stated after the meeting that he called for an adjournment "out of an abundance of caution" after "escalating disruptions involving protesters whose conduct created significant concerns for public safety and the orderly conduct of township business."

Bill Angus of Project NINJA, a Warren County-based, volunteer-led civil liberties initiative opposing the conversion of the warehouse, gave a statement following Portillo's.

"Normally, when there is some noteworthy development, Mayor Potillo makes such a statement at the opening before any other town business is handled. For whatever reason he did not do this and very quickly launched into the first public speaking session," said Angus. "His failure to do so at the onset gave the impression that he was ignoring the matter, since that has been his protocol to do so right at the start."

"The idea that we prevented him from making the statement is a flat-out lie," Angus said. "He chose to do things differently for reasons known only to him, and he could've called for a moment to address this when things escalated. He chose to walk out of the room. That choice was his."

Staff writer William Westhoven contributed to this story.

text:
Part of the Series

The War That Was Never Meant to End: 25 Years of the War on Terror

Guantánamo Bay has repeatedly made headlines in recent months. In August, the Trump administration sent 12 Somali men to the remote prison, several of them from Minnesota, where the community has faced relentless harassment. Some of the men have since been deported to Somalia, while others remain in detention.

Dr. Maha Hilal, a scholar of institutionalized Islamophobia and the “war on terror,” told Truthout that the recent transfers have brought “renewed attention to Guantánamo and the prison as a site of carceral violence.” But, she added, “this isn’t the first time migrants have been held at Guantánamo. There’s a historical component.”

Guantánamo’s Long History of Migrant Detention

Guantánamo’s use for migrant detention predates its role in the war on terror. Following Haiti’s 1991 coup, the U.S. detained thousands of Haitian asylum seekers intercepted at sea. In the mid- to late-1990s, tens of thousands of people fleeing Cuba on makeshift rafts were also detained there. The offshore location allowed the government to circumvent its humanitarian and legal protections to asylum seekers.

The Guantánamo Migrant Operations Center, operated by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Department of State with support from private contractors, has continued to detain migrants intercepted at sea. During Donald Trump’s first term, DHS proposed housing migrant children at the base as a solution to overcrowded immigration jails on the U.S. mainland. At the start of his second term, Trump signed an executive order directing the expansion of the Migrant Operations Center to hold up to 30,000 “high-priority criminal aliens.” For the first time, immigrants arrested within the United States were being transferred to Guantánamo for detention.

An August 2026 congressional oversight visit found that 852 immigrants had been flown to the facility since January 2025. Sen. Dick Durbin of Illinois condemned the administration’s policy as “cruel, immoral, and an abuse of taxpayer funding.”

Although Guantánamo’s newest arrivals are being held under a different legal pretext than their predecessors, the instrumentalization of national security and racialized suspicion remains unchanged.

Guantánamo Bay and the War on Terror

Two months after the September 11 attacks, President George W. Bush issued a military order authorizing the detention and military trial of certain noncitizens suspected of terrorism. The first 20 detainees arrived at Guantánamo Bay on January 11, 2002, as “unlawful enemy combatants,” a label that limited their ability to challenge their detention and placed them beyond the reach of habeas corpus protections. The Bush administration capitalized on the fear and national trauma that followed 9/11 to not only suspend the rule of law, but to create a geographic and legal space that existed entirely outside of it.

Since opening, Guantánamo has held approximately 780 Muslim men and boys, the youngest of whom, Omar Khadr, was just 15 years old at the time of his detention. The vast majority of the prison’s detainees have never been charged with a crime. Many were kidnapped and captured abroad, transferred from CIA black sites, or sold to U.S. forces by bounty hunters for sums ranging from $3,000 to $25,000.

In the context of the U.S. prison system where a staggering 2 million people are incarcerated, 780 men seems like a relatively small number, but as Hilal argues, “Guantánamo’s significance is not in its size or scope, but in what it represents — the right to place people outside of the law. In that sense, it’s a problem of great magnitude.”

Guantánamo Bay quickly became synonymous with human rights abuses during the Bush administration. The Department of Justice authorized the use of “enhanced interrogation techniques,” a euphemism that described practices like waterboarding, sleep deprivation, and prolonged isolation, despite longstanding prohibitions against torture under international law.

In 2006, a UN report found that the United States had violated its international human rights obligations, and called for Guantánamo’s closure and the trial or release of detainees. In December 2008, the Senate Armed Services Committee concluded an 18-month investigation into the abuse of detainees in military custody. The committee’s final report refuted the Bush administration’s claim that the abuse was the result of a “few bad apples.” Following the report’s release, Sen. Carl Levin released a statement: “How did it come about that American military personnel stripped detainees naked, put them in stress positions, used dogs to scare them, put leashes around their necks to humiliate them, hooded them, deprived them of sleep, and blasted music at them?”

The answer was damning: what had been allowed to happen at Guantánamo directly influenced the abusive treatment of prisoners in Iraq and Afghanistan. In February 2003, a U.S. military task force preparing for the invasion of Iraq adopted an interrogation policy previously developed in Afghanistan, changing little more than the letterhead. In July, an interrogation officer at Abu Ghraib submitted a nearly identical policy for approval. Just over a year later, photographs exposing the physical torture, psychological humiliation, and sexual abuse of detainees at Abu Ghraib sparked international outrage. But Abu Ghraib was not an aberration. The Department of Defense’s failure to hold senior officials accountable for their role in authorizing torture at Guantánamo had institutionalized a system of brutality and a culture of impunity.

The Long Struggle to Close the Prison

Guantánamo was meant to be a temporary solution to what the Bush administration deemed an extraordinary threat. Instead, it became one of the most enduring legacies of the war on terror.

Barack Obama campaigned on closing the prison in 2008. Two days after taking office, he signed an executive order directing its closure within a year. The order was met with fierce opposition in Congress. By the end of his presidency, he reduced Guantánamo’s prison population from 242 to 41, but failed to deliver on his campaign promise.

In 2018, Donald Trump revoked Obama’s order and reaffirmed the government’s authority to detain future “enemy combatants” at the facility. Joe Biden also campaigned on closing the prison. In 2021, seven former detainees who had been held without charge or trial made a personal appeal to the president: “Many of us were abducted from our homes, in front of our families … Some of us had children who were born in our absence and grew up without fathers … waiting in vain for news of our return.”

At the end of Biden’s presidency, he had only managed to secure the transfer of 11 Yemeni detainees to Oman, reducing the number of prisoners at Guantánamo to 15. These 15 men remain imprisoned: three have been approved for transfer, and three others have been dubbed “forever prisoners” — men who are allegedly too dangerous to be released but have not been brought to trial. Human rights groups criticized the Obama and Biden administrations, arguing that the failure to close the prison was not due to a lack of political power, but a lack of political will.

The struggle to close Guantánamo has not been confined to courtrooms, campaign trails, and congressional hearings. It has been sustained by movements in Cuba, the U.S., and within the prison itself. Those imprisoned there have routinely resisted their indefinite detention and the physical and psychological abuse that they endure.

Since its opening, hunger strikes have been a regular occurrence within the prison, happening on a large-scale and coordinated level. Tariq Ba Odah of Yemen undertook the longest hunger strike in Guantánamo’s history, lasting for eight years. In retaliation, he was force-fed twice a day, a practice condemned by medical professionals and human rights groups. Upon his release to Saudi Arabia in 2016, he weighed 75 pounds.

In Cuba, opposition to the prison is inseparable from the broader struggle for national sovereignty and an end to the U.S. occupation. Following the Spanish-American War, the Platt Amendment imposed conditions on Cuban independence, granting the United States the right to intervene in national affairs and lease naval bases on the island. Although the amendment was repealed in 1934, the lease on Guantánamo Bay remains in place despite the Cuban government’s demands for the territory’s return.

In February 2025, the Cuban Institute of Friendship with the Peoples condemned Trump’s plan to send immigrants to Guantánamo, calling it “a flagrant violation of human rights and an affront to human dignity.” Thousands of people also rallied in Guantánamo City to oppose both Trump’s plan and the U.S military presence on the island.

Onyesonwu Chatoyer, an organizer with the Venceremos Brigade and the National Network on Cuba, told Truthout that the impact of the U.S. military base on the residents of Guantánamo Province is often overlooked by those who don’t live on the island. The naval base has economic and environmental consequences for the communities who live there under a “high degree of surveillance.”

“The base blocks fishermen from accessing marine resources. It causes pollution. It’s a drain on the countryside,” Chatoyer said.

She invites people to visit the island so that they can see the truth for themselves: “The U.S. is constantly accusing Cuba of being a dictatorship, of persecuting its own people, and yet they are the ones torturing people and holding them indefinitely without charge on illegally occupied Cuban land.”

From the Mirador de Malones observation point, Chatoyer says visitors can see the “full scale of the occupation.” Through a telescope “cookie-cutter suburban houses” come into view and form a dystopian picture, replete with white picket fences, American flags, and the only McDonald’s on the island.

“It’s a scar on the land,” Chatoyer said.

For Chatoyer, the prison is emblematic of the new world order imposed across much of the Global South: “The places that are under the boot of U.S. imperialism are building massive mega-prisons, are massacring land defenders and poor working-class people, are building huge police forces, and are going all-in on AI for military technology.”

The stakes of the struggle to end the occupation and uphold national sovereignty are clear: “Guantánamo is the vision of the world that these people want,” she said.

As Above, So Below

Dr. Hilal has long warned that the government’s expansive and malleable definition of terrorism would eventually extend beyond its original targets. Guantánamo can no longer be seen as an anomaly, but as a model for U.S. detention at home and abroad.

“The construction of parts of Guantánamo was modeled after a supermax prison in the United States,” Hilal told Truthout. Federal communication management units (or CMUs) are restrictive prison units established in the post-9/11 counterterrorism era that isolate certain prisoners deemed “high-risk” and restrict their communications. CMUs are often referred to as “Little Gitmo” or “Guantánamo North” by those detained there and their advocates. While these units have disproportionately been used to hold Muslim prisoners, they have increasingly held people with “unpopular” political views, including environmental and animal rights activists.

As the boundaries between military and civilian systems of control grow increasingly porous, portraying entire populations as threats to national security has helped normalize state violence and shield it from accountability. A war without clear geographic limits or defined rules of engagement blurs the line between combatant and civilian, extending the battlefield into everyday life.

When Hilal first saw images of Venezuelan men being sent to Guantánamo, she was struck by their resemblance to photographs of Muslim detainees taken by the Department of Defense two decades earlier: “They look exactly the same. The same posture. The same forms of control,” she said.

The resemblance underscores Guantánamo’s enduring symbolic power and the ease with which its logic can be imposed on new targets. “The government can convince us that we are dealing with a different manifestation of the same threat. And that threat must be dealt with in the exact same way,” Hilal told Truthout.

Although several of the Somali men recently sent to Guantánamo had no criminal records, a DHS spokesperson described them as the “worst of the worst.” The phrase echoes former Vice President Dick Cheney’s description of the prison’s first detainees as “the worst of a very bad lot.” While previous presidents may have reduced the prison’s population, they did little to dismantle the legal and political architecture that sustained it. Arguably, their failure to take meaningful action to close Guantánamo facilitated the Trump administration’s ability to expand its use to detain immigrants. Across five administrations, Guantánamo’s legacy, and the narratives that fuel it, have only become more deeply entrenched.

Whether in the war on terror or Trump’s war on immigrants, what was sold to the American public as an exception has become the rule. The detention of immigrants at Guantánamo is the latest chapter in a familiar playbook. Dehumanize, detain, disappear. All that has changed is the enemy du jour.

description:
The Supreme Court said Friday that it will rule on whether President Trump may close off asylum to migrants who cross the southern border, taking up a policy that a federal judge and an appeals court in Washington both found unlawful.
In April the federal appeals court in Washington ruled against the administration in a split decision.
In July the full appeals court declined to rehear the case.
In its filings, the administration called the appeals court decision "judicial interference in one of the administration's most important policy initiatives."

text:
The Supreme Court said Friday that it will rule on whether President Trump may close off asylum to migrants who cross the southern border, taking up a policy that a federal judge and an appeals court in Washington both found unlawful.

The justices granted the administration's petition in the case, Mullin v. RAICES, which is named for Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, in an order list released after their private conference. They narrowed the case to two questions. The first is whether the proclamation and the Homeland Security guidance that carries it out are legal. The second is whether a provision of federal immigration law, 8 U.S.C. 1252(f)(1), prevented the district court from granting relief to an entire class of migrants. The court declined to hear a third question the government raised about whether the class itself was properly defined.

The dispute traces to Jan. 20, 2025, Trump's first day back in office. That day he issued a proclamation that said an invasion was under way on the border with Mexico and halted entry for the people he said were part of it. Under the order, migrants who cross between ports of entry or without the required papers may not seek asylum or a related protection called withholding of removal. Homeland Security Department guidance went further, directing that such migrants be removed quickly and without some of the procedural safeguards in federal law.

Thirteen individuals who say they suffered persecution or torture in their home countries brought the suit along with three groups that provide legal help to immigrants. The groups are RAICES, the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project, and Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center. The American Civil Liberties Union and other advocacy organizations represent them.

Randolph Moss, the federal district judge hearing the case, certified a class made up of everyone who is or would be covered by the proclamation. He threw out the Homeland Security guidance and barred officials from enforcing those measures.

In April the federal appeals court in Washington ruled against the administration in a split decision. Writing for herself and Judge Cornelia Pillard, Judge J. Michelle Childs said that Congress, in letting presidents suspend entry by proclamation, never handed the executive the sweeping power to remove people that the administration claimed. Judge Walker, the third member of the panel, dissented in part. In July the full appeals court declined to rehear the case. It then paused its own ruling while the government sought review, so the asylum restrictions have stayed in force throughout the litigation.

In its filings, the administration called the appeals court decision "judicial interference in one of the administration's most important policy initiatives." The administration's top Supreme Court lawyer, Solicitor General D. John Sauer, argued that the proclamation "rests on a commonsense understanding of the President's inherent and delegated powers to exclude aliens." His petition told the justices that border encounters have dropped 93% since the proclamation took effect, to levels unseen since the 1960s. Iowa and 21 other states filed a brief urging the court to take the case.

Lawyers for the migrants said they would defend the lower court rulings. "The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger," said Lee Gelernt, the ACLU lawyer leading the case. "We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court."

The case adds to an already crowded immigration docket for the term. The justices are also weighing the administration's practice of deporting people to countries not named in their removal orders and its policy of holding immigrants arrested inside the United States without a bond hearing.

Arguments in the asylum case are expected in the spring. In a separate order Friday, the justices added Robinhood Markets v. Sodha, a securities case over what a company must tell investors before a public offering.

text:
Welcome back, Deadline: Legal newsletter readers. When the Supreme Court decided Louisiana v. Callais in April, Justice Elena Kagan said in dissent that the case marked the “latest chapter in the majority’s now-completed demolition of the Voting Rights Act.” The ruling bolstered Republican efforts to reshape electoral maps in their quest to further cement political power.

Yet it also helped to galvanize Democrats in the midterm elections. It certainly motivated one of the most notable Democrats riding the “blue tsunami” to Washington: Mississippi’s Scott Colom. He cited Callais in an interview with MS NOW’s Symone Sanders Townsend after he defeated GOP incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith for a Senate seat.

To understand the significance of Colom’s victory, consider my colleague Jarvis DeBerry’s observation that it was historic partly because “every Democrat the state previously sent to the Senate was some combination of slave owner, Confederate soldier or segregationist,” but even more so because Colom “is Black, and for the first time, voters in the Blackest state in the country have elected a Black person to a statewide office.”

In his interview with Sanders Townsend, Colom said that when Callais came out and Republicans started gerrymandering in Tennessee and threatening to do so in his state, he “knew that that was a threat to go backwards in a way that’s going to hurt a state like Mississippi.” Colom said that the threat prompted him to “start focusing and giving everything I got, being as creative as I could be, listening to the right people, staying in prayer, and just working hard.”

Another GOP action that backfired in this remarkable race is that Hyde-Smith previously used her power as a senator to block Colom from being considered for a federal judgeship. Had she backed his nomination, Colom might have become a federal judge instead of challenging her for the Senate seat.

More articles

Now it’s Colom who will have a vote on federal judges, including any Supreme Court justices nominated while he’s in the Senate. Much of the high court retirement speculation lately has been over whether the author of Callais, Justice Samuel Alito, or Justice Clarence Thomas, who joined Alito’s opinion, would step down this year to give President Donald Trump and the outgoing Republican-controlled Senate a chance to confirm their replacements.

But both justices are reportedly sticking around, raising the possibility that Colom and his Democratic colleagues in the incoming Senate majority will have a chance to consider their replacements. If those two justices were to leave the court before Trump leaves office in 2029, the Democratic-controlled Senate could reject any nominee the Republican president puts forward.

And if a Democratic president wins the next election and those seats become vacant, Colom could help swing the court back to a Democratic-appointed majority. The Callais decision may continue to motivate him as he considers what sorts of judges and justices he is willing to confirm.

Meanwhile, the court just finished its second two-week hearing session of the term. The justices will be back on the bench later this month to start the December session, which features arguments over AR-15s, voting and deportations. Adding to the term’s immigration-related caseload, the court on Friday agreed to review Trump’s bid to ban asylum claims at the southern border.

title: Europe Relies on Illegal Pushbacks to Deter Migrants - Jacobin
description:

Civil and humanitarian groups, of national and international composition, fight for the application of international but also national maritime assistance and asylum law.
The cases can halt and frustrate rescue operations for years but rarely make it to court, spurious as they are.)
And this monolith, this Castle, this “Fortress Europe” is getting more formidable each year as the death rate rises.
Right-wingers accuse migrants of exploiting this danger in order to claim rescue and asylum.
text:
Pushback is illegal. It violates the individual’s right to claim asylum under international law and constitutes a deportation without trial. Pushbacks at sea also seem to contravene the universal duty to render assistance to those in distress, enshrined in the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea and the 1974 International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea. Given the typical state of repair of the vessels that irregular migrants use to cross, for example, the Mediterranean, their capacity, and the typical condition of the individuals concerned (Akehurst reports multiple instances of pregnant or unconscious passengers), one would think that this duty would kick in automatically for any state agent in a seaworthy boat coming to meet them.

These conventions are only the latest legal formulation of a nautical norm probably as old as seafaring itself. Xenophon’s Hellenica records that it was the failure of the six Athenian generals to rescue shipwrecked soldiers after the Battle of Arginusae in 406 BCE that prompted their trial and execution by the Athenian democracy. In Roman Law, the Lex Rhodia, codified by Justinian I but likely already over a thousand years old by that point, protects the duty to rescue by establishing the principle that any damages from jettison must be compensated by contributions from all those saved (the law of the general average). Similar conventions are present in the medieval pan-Mediterranean compendium the Consolato del Mare and were brought into the new “maritime law” of various states in the seventeenth century. As the concept of “international law” developed in the eighteenth century, influential Swiss jurist Emer de Vattel argued that there was a right of entry into port for a vessel in distress, and that this right existed notwithstanding the opposition of the coastal state. So universally established was the duty to render assistance, so ingrained in the psyche of European sailors, that Nazi Admiral Karl Dönitz felt obliged to issue an order forbidding such rescue after German U-boats repeatedly went to the aid of sunk Allied vessels and most famously attempted to rescue British and Italian survivors of the ocean liner Laconia (when they were attacked by American aircraft).

One can also tell different stories of Europeans’ behavior at sea. The same Rhodian law of the general average was relied upon by the owners of the slave ship Zong when they filed an insurance claim for the loss of 132 enslaved Africans thrown overboard when the ship ran low on drinking water. The same Vattel published an opinion justifying settlement of North America by Europeans who, “finding land of which the savages stood in no particular need, and of which they made no actual and constant use, were lawfully entitled to take possession of it and settle it with colonies.” The development of maritime and international law in the early modern period is inseparable from the development of European colonialism. European states established laws for their mutual conduct and the rights of their people, and in the same sweep drew the physical and ideological lines beyond which they would not apply: the persons who would not be legal subjects and the peoples who did not meet the criteria for statehood, and who could therefore be brutalized. The law was a technology concurrent to military force, economic extraction, and administrative imposition by which Europeans established sovereignty over distant land, in a process Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari would call “territorialization.”

At Europe’s borders today, exceptions to its “universal” human rights are still being made. The border as Akehurst describes it has become a bitter, one-sided contest between rival regimes of law. Civil and humanitarian groups, of national and international composition, fight for the application of international but also national maritime assistance and asylum law. They are obstructed by international lawfare. (Akehurst cites cases of search-and-rescue volunteers being charged with offenses such as smuggling and espionage. The cases can halt and frustrate rescue operations for years but rarely make it to court, spurious as they are.) Meanwhile, European governments cooperate to maintain states of exception for persons they deem deserving and outsource their lawmaking violence to foreign state and non-state actors. This is not a conflict between state sovereignty and international law but rather between different transnational agents attempting to undermine each other’s governance over social relations in a geographical area — in Deleuze and Guattari’s language, territorializing and deterritorializing actors.

Parallel to post hoc legal justification runs a tradition of European thought, from Diogenes to Franz Kafka, which examines the law not from the perspective of its writer but from the perspective of its sufferer. For the woman experiencing her twentieth pushback at the hands of men with guns in EU-funded patrol vehicles or the teenager in his second year in an offshore detention center waiting to hear whether his asylum claim will be successful, or whether it is even still “under review” at all, what good would be an invocation of the European origins of humanitarian law? The monolith they encounter just is the law. And this monolith, this Castle, this “Fortress Europe” is getting more formidable each year as the death rate rises. How did we get here?

Along the Watchtower contains a fascinating and timely history of European politics since the millennium, one that turns received wisdom on its head. The familiar story is the competition between liberal Europeanists, who favor increased powers for pan-European institutions, perhaps with the end goal of a supranational European state, and Euroskeptics, who want to maintain nation-state sovereignty as they see it. But Akehurst argues that what characterizes recent developments in Europe is a strategic accord, or at least a confluence of interests and convergence of policy, between these two factions.

In the economic and political crisis in Europe after 2007, amid mildly rising levels of irregular migration, the Europeanists sensed an opportunity to consolidate the European project with two key material tools of statehood: an army and a border. A minor agency, based in Warsaw as a favor to new EU member Poland, proved to be the answer. This was Frontex, and it quickly grew from a budget of €6 million in 2004 to €90 million in 2014. After the “migrant crisis” of 2015, it was supercharged, and its 2025 budget was over €1 billion of taxpayer money. It is now the EU’s largest agency. The number of its Standing Corps, the EU’s first uniformed service, is set to reach ten thousand next year. They have been increasingly equipped like a military force. Meanwhile, Europeanist politicians such as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen have toured borders from Poland to Greece and claimed them as “European borders,” capable of being “defended” only by diverting money and power toward the coordinators in Brussels.

In this project, the Europeanists found strange bedfellows in the European far right, on an upward trajectory since 2007. They traditionally opposed European centralization and what they saw as the resulting importation of liberal values into the national body politic. They too spotted an opportunity, and one they too were able to escalate after 2015: to reframe economic downturn and national decline as the fault of immigrants and an overly permissive immigration system. As they started to gain power in countries like Austria and Italy, they worked with European institutions to bring about their desired treatment of migrants. It turned out that Brussels’s liberal values were up for sale, and not for a high price. Through bilateral state agreements, partnerships with illiberal external regimes like in Tunisia and Turkey, and victories for the border lobby within the EU, the far right secured the militarized “hot spot” system that Frontex was only too happy to enforce. This system, in turn, funnels irregular migrants into certain dangerous pinch points, from which emerge the spectacles of large groups of people pushing at fences or overcrowded dinghies making landings, which the far right then uses to campaign on.

And so, von der Leyen and far-right Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni will come together for a photo op on Lampedusa, and both have endorsed the EU’s New Pact on Migration and Asylum that took effect this year. The far right get their ritual violence and their spectacle, and the Europeanists consolidate their transnational power. Whether each side believes they are strategically outmaneuvering the other is by the by: the result is washing up at the shores of the Mediterranean every day. (British pro-Europeans optimistic about Andy Burnham’s recent interventions on reversing Brexit ought to be cognizant that this is the EU to which they would be returning.)

So we are stuck in a vicious cycle of immiseration. Every migrant that fails to get through the border proves that Fortress Europe is working: every migrant that succeeds only proves that more resources, more surveillance, more emergency powers are required. Deeply unpleasant regimes and warlords pocket their fees for maintaining Europe’s external border, which they then use to conduct their own internal repressions, producing more refugees. The arms and surveillance technology companies, often in a revolving-door relationship with European agencies, enrich themselves to the tune of billions of dollars, which they use to lobby for more investment in arms and surveillance technology. The far right surges in Germany, France, Britain, and all over Europe as voters choose the real thing over the milquetoast versions of migrant demonization offered by liberal and social democratic politicians unable to resist the trap their enemies have set for them. Historic landscapes of Europe, Africa, and the Near East, gateways of ancient exchange and adventure, mountain passes, river valleys, and coastlines get covered in barbed-wire fences, tents, and patrolling soldiers. And the Mediterranean continues to groan with blood: the latest count is over thirty five thousand lives lost since 2014.

And still people move. It shouldn’t be unfamiliar to Europeans that people move: after all, they’ve always done it. The stories of the European imagination are littered with travelers, voyagers, and migrants: from Homer’s Odyssey to the skaldic poets, from Sadko in the byliny to the Celtic immrama. Without naively imagining this movement as always benevolent, and whatever its rationale, we can recognize that the arduous journeys have been respected; their human cost commemorated; the miracle of rescue honored. In Greek myth, the Aegean Sea is named for the life lost in it. We don’t know all the names of the people who have died in the Mediterranean in the last twelve years. The ones we do know are thanks to the tireless work of legal advocates, humanitarian campaigners, and migrant self-organizations. Akehurst interviews volunteers from I Have Rights in Samos, Mission Wings in Bulgaria, Medical Volunteers International in Serbia, Sea-Eye in the Mediterranean, and many more. We can situate their work in the legacies of civil and socialist opposition to the state, given their utilization of those material concessions won by previous struggles and inscribed within bourgeois law to defend and enact visions of human life beyond capitalist systems of violence. What Akehurst doesn’t give as much detail on is the relation — actual or optimal — between these groups and socialist parties working within national contexts. Nor is his book a theoretical account of the political economy of contemporary migration — a new left-wing popular introduction to which would be welcome. Nonetheless, the stories of these campaigners and the author’s sometimes joyous, normally mad encounters with them and the people seeking safety resonate long after the final chapter.

There are more traditions in Europe than just the imperial, and they include the civil organization of lifesaving at sea, kept alive today by search-and-rescue groups in the Mediterranean. The sea, that “howling infinite,” is not an easy place to territorialize. There is a natural disrule, and everything is more dangerous. This is why it lends itself more to the mythic mode than the juridical. Right-wingers accuse migrants of exploiting this danger in order to claim rescue and asylum. But the reverse is true: it is the European authorities that exploit the remoteness, lack of oversight, and hazard of the water in order to prevent legitimate asylum claims. It should concern us all whether what prevails on the Mediterranean, in the English Channel, and around the world is the law of assistance to those in distress or the law of the pushback.

While we have much to thank these first responders for, they won’t be enough on their own. As migration increases with climate breakdown and capitalism at war, it behooves us all to defend human movement and facilitate its safety. The alternative is becoming increasingly clear: the Mediterranean as mass grave, from the bloody outcrop of Ceuta to Trump hotels on the ethnically cleansed beaches of Gaza; a Europe without enough firefighters to tackle its wildfires, relying on the water cannons of border guards; and a thousand Daniel Thomases in brown shirts patrolling the Channel.

Against such a future, and the present powers who would midwife it, we must build a politics capable of pushing back.

name: Human Rights
title: Residents in CA Agricultural Town Face Down ICE Facility and Amazon Data Center
authors: Blanca Missé, Austin C. McCoy, Derek Seidman, Kelly Hayes, Amy Goodman, Nathalie Levey, Mike Ludwig, Ashley Smith, Finley Williams, Nolan Higdon
description:
South of San Jose, California, residents of the city of Gilroy are fighting a proposed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility and an Amazon data center.
The proposed ICE facility would menace workers and their families, while Amazon’s project would turn agricultural land into space for cloud infrastructure.
A Federal Facility, a Private Landlord The proposed ICE facility in Gilroy would generate rent and construction payments for a private landlord, Elmwood Capital Group, which is based in Beverly Hills.
Armendáriz, ICE Out of Gilroy’s chair, was among those elected and campaigned on protecting residents from ICE.
Kim sees the proposed Gilroy facility and the former Dublin federal prison as parts of one regional system, with Gilroy processing people and Dublin detaining them.
text:
South of San Jose, California, residents of the city of Gilroy are fighting a proposed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility and an Amazon data center. Organizers with ICE Out of Gilroy, a coalition that launched in May of this year, have linked the two fights in a united struggle against detention and Big Tech surveillance. The coalitionincludes Community Agency for Resources, Advocacy, and Services (CARAS), a Gilroy-based immigrant-rights group; Services, Immigrant Rights & Education Network (SIREN), based in San Jose; and Bay Resistance, a Bay Area coalition for racial and economic justice which formed after Trump’s 2016 election and reactivated in 2025.

Gilroy’s farms and service economy depend on immigrant labor. The proposed ICE facility would menace workers and their families, while Amazon’s project would turn agricultural land into space for cloud infrastructure. The projects have distinct origins, but both raise the same question: Who gets to use Gilroy’s land, labor and infrastructure — and who gets to decide how?

On August 23, 2026, local residents joined the “Dump Big Tech” march opposing the ICE facility on Holsclaw Road, Amazon’s data center on Camino Arroyo, and the 54 automated license plate readers (ALPRs) owned by Flock throughout Gilroy. Mateo, an organizer with CARAS and the rapid-response network who asked to use a pseudonym due to concerns about potential repression, summed up why the coalition has linked the fights: “The data centers take our resources; the detention center takes our people.”

Kim Woo, a community organizer with SIREN, traced the connection in another direction: “Flock cameras lead us to the data center, and then to detention facilities.” Kim is concerned with how surveillance data moves across agencies to circumvent sanctuary policies. Records show out-of-state police searched the San Francisco Police Department (SFPD) Flock data for ICE-related purposes. Separately, an SFPD audit found a regional fusion-center network routed 299 federal and out-of-state queries; none were marked immigration-related. Kim calls these indirect channels “side-door sharing.” Rebeca Armendáriz, chair of the ICE Out of Gilroy Coalition and now a council-member-elect, says Flock data are being used to identify local rapid-response activists and monitor journalists. She calls all these technologies part of “the authoritarian state machine.”

A WIRED investigation found that, since 2023, ICE and Customs and Border Protection have spent at least $515 million on services from Palantir, Microsoft, Amazon and Google. Palantir supplies investigative and case-management software; the others provide cloud and computing services. ICE’s Palantir case-management system runs on Amazon Web Services (AWS), and the companies also have a technology partnership. The government contracts are separate: ICE committed $86.3 million to Palantir on April 30, 2026, for case-management modernization; on September 8, the Department of Homeland Security committed $18.3 million to AWS for cloud infrastructure supporting ICE. All together, these figures exceed $619 million today.

A Federal Facility, a Private Landlord

The proposed ICE facility in Gilroy would generate rent and construction payments for a private landlord, Elmwood Capital Group, which is based in Beverly Hills. On January 8, 2025, the Trump administration awarded Elmwood a 20-year lease for up to $26,551,532 in rent. A March 2026 amendment authorized up to $8.66 million in construction reimbursements, bringing potential federal payments to the Elmwood Capital Group subsidiary ECG6 to $35.2 million over 20 years, according to the court order. Rent begins when General Services Administration (GSA) accepts the completed site, under a 20-year lease with a 15-year firm term. This arrangement uses public money to prepare private property for detention and then lease it to the government for profit.

On May 14, residents and immigrant-rights advocates rallied with county officials, who pledged to fight the project and said they were coordinating with Attorney General Rob Bonta, which led organizers to hold a community briefing and a mass organizing call on May 22. In response, the state of California and Santa Clara County sued after federal agencies began construction without the environmental review required by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). Gilroy’s then at-large city council, which had no Latino members, declined to join the lawsuit.

The complaint alleges Elmwood described the project to county planners as “office and operations space,” without disclosing its holding rooms or the scale of construction. ICE’s court filing estimates about 10 detainees on a normal day; the state and county say plans show rooms for up to 150. A judge found the state and county likely to prevail on their NEPA claim and halted construction; the court later extended the pause.

The Detention-Industrial Complex

The Gilroy lease is part of a national detention buildout. An internal ICE memo from February outlined to expand capacity to 92,600 beds across the U.S.

Seven ICE-contracted detention facilities have been active in California in 2025, according to the DOJ; the eighth, the Central Valley Annex, began holding detainees in April 2026. The California Department of Justice says, affirming what families and attorneys are saying, that facilities are remote and hard to reach.

The Beverly Hills capital group’s reach extends beyond Gilroy: The state and county’s complaint alleges the firm leased at least two properties to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in Montana and Texas. In Billings, Montana, Elmwood’s portfolio lists a 14,444-square-foot GSA property; city records identify an ICE facility at 1711 6th Ave. N. A 2022 remodel permit lists Noah Zeligman as the owner of the property and describes jail processing spaces and holding cells.

The contracts reach beyond detention operators to surveillance firms, deportation contractors and property owners, as part of a broader detention-industrial complex. In the first year of Trump’s second term, ICE obligated about $5.4 billion to 679 contractors; the top ten received roughly $3.8 billion, according to a joint POGO–IRW analysis. Those top recipients included Palantir (surveillance analytics), CoreCivic and GEO Group (private detention), and CSI Aviation (deportation flights). ICE paid $129.3 million for a warehouse formerly majority-owned by Goldman Sachs and $68.2 million for one sold by a Carlyle-linked entity, CoStar and the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported. Those are sale prices, not the firms’ disclosed profits. WIRED found ICE and CBP had spent at least $515 million with Microsoft, Amazon, Google and Palantir since 2023. Some firms, executives or PACs donated to Trump-aligned campaigns or initiatives, and some lobbied on ICE-related issues. More than 50 members of Congress launched separate investigations into six contractors, brokers and property owners, Salon reported.

A Threat to Farmworkers

Armendáriz warned KTVU that construction of an ICE facility may push farmworkers to leave Gilroy: “Our community is going to live in fear because this is going to be so close.” Law enforcement pressure is already palpable at county jails: On October 28, federal agents pursued two men after they were released from Elmwood Correctional Facility in Milpitas; one was tased. Observers reported seeing 10 to 12 agents at county jails daily the week before. Sheriff’s office figures show about 70 people detained near county jails since June 2025, local reporting found.

Farmworkers have the legal right to organize, but only about 10,000 of California’s 800,000-plus farmworkers arecovered by union contracts, a UC Davis review estimated in 2025. In a UC Merced survey of farmworkers in the state, 19 percent of respondents said an employer had withheld payment of wages; 43 percent said employers never provided the required heat-illness prevention plan. A national study found that spikes in immigration arrests cut noncitizen farmworkers’ weekly hours by as much as 23.1 percent that month. The threat of detention compounds workers’ risk of retaliation when they report wage theft or unsafe conditions.

Mateo said early marches in May drew mostly white allies from San Jose, Santa Cruz, and Salinas. In a small town, he said, residents feared detention, violence, or provocations that could lead to mass arrests. As more Latino residents saw other communities stand with them, they began joining — and calling for more people to join them in the streets.

The organizing efforts drew people from beyond Gilroy — from Stockton to Salinas and across the Bay Area. Organizers say about 800 people joined an emergency online call to action on May 22 after news broke that the ICE processing center was being built. Union members joined rapid-response work; Pacific Printing donated thousands of red-and-yellow campaign materials; SEIU 2015 and other health-care workers’ unions helped organize actions, while nurses brought material aid and joined protests. SEIU-USWW and the local labor council also supported the campaign.

More recently, on October 25, the coalition screened When ICE Melts, a documentary about Minneapolis resistance to Operation Metro Surge, in San Jose. The film follows unions, immigrant groups, and rapid-response networks as they defend their neighbors and build toward a mass strike. The film’s organizing argument has a local echo: Immigrant defense belongs inside labor organizing.

A Data Center Approved Without a Vote

Amazon’s 56-acre data center at 8050 Camino Arroyo is a reported $2 billion project with two planned buildings. Its first phase requires a 49-megawatt connection to Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E). That is the first building’s peak demand; the full site could require 98 MW, with any effect on household bills depending on who pays for grid upgrades.On July 3, 2025, Gilroy’s Community Development Director approved it under existing industrial zoning, without a planning commission hearing or city council vote. The Council later adopted new public-notice and hearing requirements for future large projects; Amazon’s approval remains in force. Resident Georgine Scott-Codiga told KSBW, “What they have done is they shut the people down; the people have no voice.”

Gilroy’s approval findings say the project’s benefits outweighed its unavoidable environmental impacts, including converting prime farmland and increasing vehicle travel above California’s environmental review threshold, which increases pollution from employee commutes. The city described the parcel’s long period of underdevelopment as “detrimental to the economic development of the City as a whole” and cited its goal of attracting technology companies seeking less costly locations. The city projects $40 million in revenue over the first decade, about 70 percent from a 5 percent tax on electricity use, according to its revenue FAQ. The city’s tax revenue rises with the facility’s power consumption.

The project requires off-site PG&E transmission upgrades. Gilroy’s Community Development Director says Amazon will fund a dedicated substation, but the California Public Utilities Commission’s Public Advocates Office issued a statewide warning that ratepayers could bear transmission costs if projected demand falls short. The city says newer state protections may limit that risk, though it remains unclear whether they cover Gilroy’s approved project.

Kim Woo of SIREN says the centers will “drastically deplete our electricity and water resources.” The project’s Water Supply Assessment estimates up to 23 acre-feet of water a year — about 7.5 million gallons — for cooling, irrigation and domestic use. Once recycled-water service is connected, expected by 2030, potable use should fall to about 2 acre-feet annually. Amazon must pay for the recycled-water infrastructure, which the city says will also serve future customers.

Only Short-Term Jobs for the Build, Long-Term Unemployment Uncertain

Gilroy City Council’s jobs argument centers on construction: The city projects hundreds of temporary jobs under a project labor agreement that prioritizes local hiring and prevailing wages. Those jobs matter to workers, but they end when construction does. The approval report’s employment projections estimate up to 25 full-time employees initially and 50 after Phase II. At full buildout, up to 125 employees and contractors, including part-time workers, could be on site. The figure of up to 125 people on site includes part-time workers and contractors. Hundreds of workers may build the reported $2 billion project; only a few dozen are expected to run it.

That is the point. Data centers are a massive fixed-capital investment designed to produce more output with less workers. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said generative AI and agents will mean fewer people doing some of today’s jobs, while his company announced two rounds of cuts affecting about 30,000 office-based corporate roles: 14,000 in October 2025 and 16,000 in January 2026, according to its October notice and January notice. A Fairwork investigation documents how AI and robotics intensify warehouse work, while algorithmic monitoring narrows workers’ control over their pace and tasks.

Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) research director Alex Hanna describes AI as “making our expertise an add-on, and making us more interchangeable.” Alongside replacing some jobs, these systems can speed up work, expand surveillance and make the workers who remain easier to replace. A Truthout investigation found that Amazon’s Atlas model draws on hundreds of data points — including worker feedback, injuries and proximity to union activity — to assess “labor risk” and anticipate organizing. Workers build and power this infrastructure while Amazon gains new tools to reorganize their work and contain resistance.

From a Pause to a Lasting Win

After the court injunction paused work at Holsclaw Road, Gilroy’s Council passed a 45-day moratorium on new detention facilities on October 5, then extended it through October 4, 2027. The ordinance covers detention and custodial-facility applications where city authority applies, but not Holsclaw Road, outside city limits. Mateo calls the injunction and moratorium partial victories. The coalition’s tactic, he says, is “to delay these projects while we build a broader opposition.”

On October 5, 2026, a community-backed proposal to bar immigration-enforcement staging on city property failed to advance. Kim had pressed for no-staging zones: “Our city property belongs to us, the community, not the ICE agenda coming here to harass and kidnap us.”

On October 19, the Council extended its moratorium on new data-center applications through September 3, 2027, but Amazon’s project remains exempt. The coalition is using the pause to press for the Holsclaw project’s cancellation, and a permanent data-center moratorium.

As a result of this grassroots movement, Gilroy’s political representation is changing. Before district elections, its at-large Council had no Latino members despite a population that is nearly 60 percent Latino, according to local reporting. After a lawyer’s December 2024 letter threatened a California Voting Rights Act lawsuit, amid Latino residents’ calls for greater representation, the Council voted in February 2025 to switch to district elections. The first were held in November 2026, when voters chose three Latinas—Diana Sanchez Bentz, Christina Tovar, and Rebeca Armendáriz—for the three seats on the ballot. Armendáriz, ICE Out of Gilroy’s chair, was among those elected and campaigned on protecting residents from ICE.

The struggle also crosses city lines. Kim sees the proposed Gilroy facility and the former Dublin federal prison as parts of one regional system, with Gilroy processing people and Dublin detaining them. Armendáriz wants the newly elected Congress to defund ICE, reverse its inhumane policies, and end qualified immunity for ICE agents. She is looking ahead to 2027: “It is a key year, and the community is ready for a general strike.”

For Betty, a San Jose teacher who asked to use a pseudonym due to fears of state repression, said that fight must unite immigrant defense with civil liberties. “We need to fight these systems of mass surveillance now with a mass united front that brings immigrant defense together with the fight for civil liberties,” said Betty, who is active with Workers’ Voice. “That means unions, immigrant rights groups and civil liberties organizations organizing together across the Bay Area, across California and nationally.”
